content.summary: A small molecule that researchers developed to block an enzyme called nicotinamide N-methyltransferase. Studied in cultured mouse fat cells and in obese mice; those cell and mouse studies do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 50 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a small molecule that researchers developed to block one enzyme, nicotinamide N-methyltransferase. It is listed for laboratory study of that enzyme's activity. What the cited work establishes is in cultured mouse fat cells and in obese mice: less of a product of the enzyme's reaction and less fat accumulation in the cells, lower body weight and fat mass in the mice without a change in total food intake, and little or no effect on several related enzymes. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

5-Amino-1MQ is short for 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium, a small molecule from a series of methylquinolinium compounds that researchers developed to inhibit the cytosolic enzyme nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT). In one laboratory study, the team measured 1-methylnicotinamide (1-MNA), a product of the NNMT reaction, in cultured mouse 3T3-L1 fat cells exposed to the compound and found concentration-dependent reductions; in differentiating cells, the compound also reduced lipid accumulation in a concentration-dependent way. In the same study, the overall effect on intracellular S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) was significant, with a significant increase at one of the concentrations tested; intracellular NAD+ trended upward, but the overall comparison for NAD+ was inconclusive. In enzyme assays at the concentrations tested, it showed little or no inhibition of the related methyltransferases DNMT1, PRMT3 and COMT or of the NAD+ salvage enzymes NAMPT and SIRT1, which the authors interpreted as selectivity for NNMT. In diet-induced obese mice fed a high-fat diet, 5-amino-1MQ reduced body weight and white adipose tissue mass, decreased fat-cell size and lowered plasma total cholesterol without changing total food intake. A 2021 study from the same research group reported that, in obese mice switched to a lean diet, adding the compound produced greater body-weight and fat loss and less liver fat than the diet switch alone. These cell and mouse studies do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item at a listed strength of 50 mg.
content.purpose: Laboratory study of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase activity.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only.

content.summary: A synthetic chain of 15 amino acids, copying part of a protein first isolated from human gastric juice. Laboratory work has examined its effects on rat tendon cells; a 2025 review of that literature reported no clinical safety data. Listed at 500 mcg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic chain of fifteen amino acids whose sequence is part of a protein first isolated from human gastric juice. It is listed for laboratory study of receptor expression in rat tendon cells. What the cited work establishes is in rat tendon cells: it accelerated the outgrowth of tendon fibroblasts, improved their survival under hydrogen peroxide stress, increased their migration, and increased expression of the growth hormone receptor. What it does not establish is safety or benefit in people: a 2025 systematic review of 35 preclinical studies and one retrospective clinical report found no clinical safety data in the literature it reviewed, and the cell studies used the peptide itself. The full technical description follows.

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide (Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val) whose sequence is a partial sequence of body protection compound, a protein first isolated from human gastric juice. In cultured rat Achilles tendon explants, it accelerated the outgrowth of tendon fibroblasts. In isolated rat tendon fibroblasts, it did not directly change proliferation but improved cell survival under hydrogen peroxide stress, and it increased cell migration and spreading in a concentration-dependent way, with increased phosphorylation of the focal adhesion proteins FAK and paxillin. A published laboratory study then examined growth hormone receptor expression in fibroblasts isolated from rat Achilles tendons, finding that BPC-157 increased that expression and that adding growth hormone then increased proliferation and activated Janus kinase 2 signaling. A 2025 systematic review of BPC-157 in orthopaedic sports medicine included 35 preclinical studies and one retrospective clinical report, and reported that it found no clinical safety data in the literature it reviewed. The cell studies above used the peptide itself, and human use falls outside this listing's research scope. This BPC-157 configuration has a listed strength of 500 mcg.
content.purpose: Laboratory study of receptor expression in rat tendon cells.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only.

content.summary: A copper-bound form of a three-amino-acid peptide first reported in human serum in 1973. In cultured fibroblasts it increased collagen synthesis, and in a rat wound model it increased wound tissue; those findings do not establish effects of the listed research material in people. Listed at 2 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is GHK-Cu, the copper complex of GHK - a tripeptide, meaning a chain of three amino acids - which has a high affinity for copper ions. It is listed for laboratory study of collagen synthesis in cultured fibroblasts. What the cited work establishes is in cell culture and in a rat wound model: it increased collagen synthesis at very low concentrations without any change in cell number, and in the rat model it increased wound tissue, type I collagen and glycosaminoglycans. What it does not establish is any effect of the listed research material in a person. The full technical description follows.

GHK-Cu is formed by the three-amino-acid peptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine (GHK) and copper; the tripeptide has a high affinity for copper(II) ions. The tripeptide later identified as GHK was first reported in human serum in 1973 as a factor that prolonged the survival of normal liver cells. In a published fibroblast culture study, researchers measured collagen synthesis after exposing the cells to the complex and found stimulation beginning at picomolar concentrations and peaking near 1 nanomolar, independently of any change in cell number. Those authors noted that a GHK sequence occurs within the alpha 2 chain of type I collagen and proposed that proteases could release it at a wound site. In a rat experimental wound-chamber model, the copper complex increased wound tissue production, type I collagen and glycosaminoglycans, and it raised expression of the proteoglycan decorin in the wound tissue and in cultured rat dermal fibroblasts. These findings on the compound do not establish effects of the listed research material in people. This catalog configuration lists the material for nonclinical research, with a listed strength of 2 mg.
content.purpose: Laboratory study of collagen synthesis in cultured fibroblasts.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only.

content.summary: A three-amino-acid piece of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, a peptide with described anti-inflammatory effects. Studied in intestinal and immune cell models and in mice with chemically induced colitis; those studies do not establish effects in people. Listed at 500 mcg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is the tripeptide lysine-proline-valine - a chain of three amino acids - corresponding to residues 11 to 13 of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, a peptide with described anti-inflammatory effects. It is listed for laboratory study of peptide transport and cell signaling. What the cited work establishes is in intestinal and immune cell models and in mice: it reduced inflammatory signaling and the secretion of the cytokine IL-8 in cells, its uptake depended on the transporter PepT1, and in mice it reduced chemically induced colitis. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

KPV stands for lysine–proline–valine, the tripeptide corresponding to residues 11 to 13 of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), a melanocortin peptide with described anti-inflammatory effects. One published study used intestinal and immune cell models: in the Caco2-BBE human intestinal epithelial cell line, nanomolar KPV reduced NF-kappaB and MAP kinase inflammatory signaling and lowered secretion of the cytokine IL-8, and in Jurkat T cells it reduced inflammatory signaling and IL-8 mRNA. That study examined uptake of KPV by the peptide transporter PepT1, a di- and tripeptide transporter normally expressed in the small intestine and induced in the colon during inflammatory bowel disease, and found that uptake depended on it. In mice, KPV given in drinking water reduced colitis induced by dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) or TNBS. A separate mouse study reported earlier recovery, regain of body weight and fewer inflammatory infiltrates in DSS and T-cell transfer colitis. In mice with a nonfunctional melanocortin-1 receptor, that study reported that all KPV-treated animals survived DSS colitis, and the authors concluded that the effects were at least partly independent of that receptor. These cell and mouse studies do not establish effects in people. This configuration lists KPV with a listed strength of 500 mcg.
content.purpose: Laboratory study of peptide transport and cell signaling.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only.

These cell-culture findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item at 50 mg for nonclinical laboratory research.

In mice, KPV given in drinking water reduced colitis induced by dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) or TNBS. A separate mouse study reported earlier recovery, regain of body weight and fewer inflammatory infiltrates in DSS and T-cell transfer colitis. In mice with a nonfunctional melanocortin-1 receptor, that study reported that all KPV-treated animals survived DSS colitis, and the authors concluded that the effects were at least partly independent of that receptor. These are cell and mouse findings and do not establish effects in people. The catalog lists this item at 10 mg for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.label: For laboratory research use only.

content.summary: A 16-amino-acid peptide encoded inside mitochondrial DNA rather than in the cell nucleus. Studied in cell experiments and in mice for effects on muscle glucose uptake and physical performance; findings about the body's own peptide are not evidence about an administered one. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a 16-amino-acid peptide whose instructions sit in mitochondrial DNA rather than in the cell nucleus. It is listed for laboratory work on such peptides, on muscle metabolism and on insulin sensitivity in animals. What the cited work establishes is in cells and in mice: it restored insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in the muscle of middle-aged mice, and improved physical performance in mice of several ages. What it does not establish is any effect of an administered peptide in a person - and where exercise raised the body's own MOTS-c in people, that is a finding about the natural peptide, not about this material. The full technical description follows.

MOTS-c (mitochondrial open reading frame of the 12S rRNA-c) is a 16-amino-acid peptide, MRWQEMGYIFYPRKLR, encoded by a short open reading frame within the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene. It was identified after the discovery of humanin suggested that mitochondrial DNA might encode further signaling peptides. In cell experiments in the 2015 study that named it, MOTS-c inhibited the folate cycle and the linked de novo purine synthesis and activated AMPK, and the authors described skeletal muscle as its likely primary target organ. In middle-aged mice that had already developed reduced insulin sensitivity, seven days of MOTS-c restored insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in soleus muscle to levels seen in young mice; in a separate experiment, it prevented obesity and hyperinsulinemia in mice fed a high-fat diet. A 2021 study reported improved physical performance in young, middle-aged and old mice and greater physical capacity when MOTS-c was given intermittently starting late in life. The same study found that exercise raised the body's own MOTS-c in human skeletal muscle and circulation, a finding about the endogenous peptide rather than an administered one. These mouse findings do not establish the effects of administered MOTS-c in people. The catalog lists this item at 10 mg for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on mitochondrial-derived peptides, skeletal-muscle metabolism and insulin sensitivity in animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A synthetic chain of 15 amino acids, copying part of a protein first found in human stomach fluid. Laboratory and animal work has examined its effects on tendon cells; a 2025 review of that literature reported no clinical safety data. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic pentadecapeptide - a chain of fifteen amino acids - whose sequence is part of a protein first isolated from human gastric juice. It is listed for laboratory work on tissue-repair signaling, including tendon cell culture and rodent injury models. What the cited work establishes is in rat cells and animals: it accelerated the outgrowth of tendon fibroblasts, improved their survival under hydrogen peroxide stress and increased their migration, and in rats and beagle dogs it broke down within minutes into fragments and single amino acids. What it does not establish is safety or benefit in people - a 2025 systematic review of 35 preclinical studies and one retrospective clinical report found no clinical safety data in the literature it reviewed. The full technical description follows.

BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide (Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val) whose sequence is a partial sequence of body protection compound, a protein first isolated from human gastric juice. In cultured rat Achilles tendon explants, it accelerated the outgrowth of tendon fibroblasts. In isolated rat tendon fibroblasts, it did not directly change proliferation but improved cell survival under hydrogen peroxide stress, and it increased cell migration and spreading in a concentration-dependent way, with increased phosphorylation of the focal adhesion proteins FAK and paxillin. A follow-up study in these fibroblasts found that BPC-157 increased growth hormone receptor expression, and that adding growth hormone then increased proliferation and activated Janus kinase 2 signaling. A pharmacokinetic study measured a plasma elimination half-life of under 30 minutes for the intact peptide in rats and beagle dogs; in that study's separate experiment with tritium-labeled BPC-157 in rats, the excreted radioactivity was found mainly in urine and bile, and the authors reported that the peptide was broken down within minutes into small peptide fragments and, ultimately, single amino acids. A 2025 systematic review of BPC-157 in orthopaedic sports medicine included 35 preclinical studies and one retrospective clinical report, and reported that it found no clinical safety data in the literature it reviewed. These laboratory and animal results do not establish safety or benefit in people. The catalog lists this item at 10 mg for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research into tissue-repair signaling, including tendon fibroblast culture and rodent musculoskeletal injury models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use. BPC-157 is not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

content.summary: A synthetic seven-amino-acid molecule modelled on a fragment of adrenocorticotropic hormone. In rat studies it bound to specific sites in brain tissue and raised a nerve-growth protein; those rodent findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic seven-amino-acid peptide described as an analogue of the 4-10 fragment of adrenocorticotropic hormone, ACTH. It is listed for laboratory work on ACTH-derived peptides, on signaling by brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), on monoamine neurochemistry and on focal brain ischemia in rodents. What the cited work establishes is in rats: tritium-labelled Semax bound specific, reversible binding sites in forebrain membranes, a single administration raised BDNF and its receptor trkB in the hippocampus, and in a stroke model it mainly altered immune-system gene expression in the cortex. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

Semax is a synthetic seven-amino-acid peptide, Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro, described in the literature as an analogue of the N-terminal fragment 4-10 of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In membranes from the rat basal forebrain, tritium-labelled Semax bound to specific, reversible, calcium-dependent binding sites, and giving the peptide to rats raised brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) protein in the basal forebrain 3 hours later but not in the cerebellum. In the rat hippocampus, a single administration increased BDNF protein, tyrosine phosphorylation of its receptor trkB, and BDNF (exon III) and trkB mRNA levels, and rats that received it made more conditioned avoidance responses. In rodents, Semax raised striatal levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA without changing dopamine or its metabolites on its own, but it enhanced the dopamine release and locomotor activity produced by D-amphetamine. In a rat model of permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion, a genome-wide analysis of the cortex found that Semax mainly altered the expression of immune-system genes, notably those encoding immunoglobulins and chemokines, as well as genes related to the vascular system. These rodent findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item at 10 mg for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on ACTH-derived peptides, BDNF/trkB signaling, monoamine neurochemistry and focal brain ischemia in rodent models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A peptide derived from the product of the KISS1 gene, acting on a receptor called GPR54 that controls release of reproductive hormones. The catalog does not state which form this is - the 54-amino-acid version or the shorter 10-amino-acid fragment - so the exact peptide is not established. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a peptide derived from the protein made by the KISS1 gene, first identified as a metastasis suppressor gene for melanoma cells. It is listed for laboratory work on KISS1 and GPR54 signaling and on the brain's control of reproductive hormone release. What the cited work establishes is in cells and animals: kisspeptins are natural ligands of the receptor GPR54, loss-of-function mutations in that receptor impair pubertal maturation and reproductive function in affected families and in mice, and kisspeptin delivered into a brain ventricle raised luteinizing hormone in mice. What it does not establish is any effect of this listing in a person - and the catalog does not state which form this is, the 54-amino-acid or the shorter 10-amino-acid one. The full technical description follows.

Kisspeptins are peptides derived from the protein product of the KISS1 gene, first identified as a metastasis suppressor gene for melanoma cells, and they share a common Arg-Phe-amide (RF-amide) C-terminus. The catalog listing names this item only as kisspeptin and does not state which form it is, for example the 54-amino-acid kisspeptin-54 or the 10-amino-acid C-terminal fragment kisspeptin-10. In 2001, kisspeptins were isolated from human placenta as natural ligands of the orphan G protein-coupled receptor GPR54; in hamster ovary cells expressing rat or human GPR54 they bound with low nanomolar affinity, mobilized calcium, activated ERK1/2 and p38 MAP kinases and inhibited cell proliferation. Loss-of-function mutations in GPR54 were later found to cause isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, in which pubertal maturation and reproductive function are impaired, in affected human families and in Gpr54-deficient mice. In mice, kisspeptin-54 and kisspeptin-10 delivered into a lateral brain ventricle both stimulated luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, the kisspeptin-54 effect was blocked by a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist, and KISS1 mRNA was mapped to hypothalamic areas that regulate gonadotropin secretion. In a separate study, kisspeptin that stimulated LH and follicle-stimulating hormone release in normal mice had no effect in mice lacking GPR54, and in sheep it released GnRH into the cerebrospinal fluid, which the authors interpret as a direct action at the level of GnRH release. These cell and animal findings, and the human genetic studies of its receptor, do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item at 10 mg for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on KISS1/GPR54 signaling and the hypothalamic control of gonadotropin secretion in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A nine-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary, known for its role in labor and milk release. Mice bred without it could not nurse and lacked social memory; those findings do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a nine-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary, best known for driving contractions in labor and milk release during nursing. It is listed for laboratory work on its receptor, on lactation and reproduction, and on social behavior in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is largely in mice: those bred without the hormone gave birth normally but could not nurse, and giving it back restored milk release; males bred without it failed to form social memory of other mice, which the hormone restored. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. Synthetic oxytocin is also the active ingredient of prescription medicines used in labor and delivery; this listing is a laboratory research material, not those medicines. The full technical description follows.

Oxytocin is a nine-amino-acid peptide hormone, Cys-Tyr-Ile-Gln-Asn-Cys-Pro-Leu-Gly-NH2, with a disulfide bridge between its two cysteines; its gene is expressed mainly in magnocellular neurons of the hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei, and the peptide is released from the posterior pituitary. Its receptor is a class I G protein-coupled receptor that signals mainly through Gq proteins and phospholipase C-beta, and its classical actions are contraction of uterine smooth muscle during labor and milk ejection during lactation. Oxytocin is also made in peripheral tissues such as the uterus, placenta, corpus luteum, testis and heart, and its receptors have been found in the kidney, heart, thymus, pancreas and fat cells. Mice engineered to lack the oxytocin gene were viable and fertile and gave birth without obvious deficits, but all their pups died shortly after birth because the mothers could not nurse, and giving the mothers oxytocin after delivery restored milk ejection and rescued the pups. Male mice lacking the oxytocin gene failed to develop social memory of other mice although their detection of non-social odors and their spatial memory appeared intact, and oxytocin, but not vasopressin, restored their social memory. Synthetic oxytocin is also the active ingredient of prescription medicines used in labor and delivery; this listing is a laboratory research material, not those medicines. These animal findings, and the medical use of those separate products, do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item at 5 mg for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on oxytocin receptor signaling, lactation and reproductive physiology, and social behavior in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A nine-amino-acid molecule first isolated in 1977 from the blood of rabbits, named for its effect on brain-wave recordings. A later review found the sleep link was never confirmed, and suggests a different, unidentified peptide may account for it. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a nine-amino-acid peptide isolated in 1977 from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits and named for its effect on the electroencephalogram, or EEG, a recording of brain-wave activity. It is listed for laboratory work on this peptide and related ones, on sleep physiology, and on where such peptides occur in the hypothalamus. What the cited work establishes is in rabbits: infused into the brain ventricles it increased delta-wave and spindle EEG activity compared with controls. What it does not establish is a confirmed role in sleep at all - a 2006 review notes the link was never further characterized, that no gene, precursor protein or receptor had been isolated, and proposes that a different, still unidentified peptide may account for the activity attributed to it. The full technical description follows.

Delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP) is a nine-amino-acid peptide, Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu, isolated in 1977 from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits by a research group in Basel and named for its effect on the electroencephalogram (EEG). In the original double-blind study in rabbits, synthetic DSIP infused into the brain ventricles significantly increased delta-wave and spindle EEG activity compared with controls. Of the other eight peptides tested, rabbits given one of the three shortest (two fragments and a related tripeptide) showed less significant differences from controls, and rabbits given one of the remaining five, three longer fragments and two analogues with two amino acids exchanged, did not differ significantly from controls. A 2006 review noted that this link to sleep had never been further characterized, partly because no gene, precursor protein or receptor for DSIP had been isolated by then, and that its natural occurrence and biological activity remained unclear. The same review describes the structure of DSIP as unlike any other known peptide family, and notes that DSIP-like immunoreactivity has a highly specific distribution in neurosecretory nuclei of the hypothalamus in several vertebrate species, regions not particularly relevant to sleep regulation. The review's authors also report that certain synthetic DSIP analogues, but not DSIP itself, promoted slow-wave sleep in their own rabbit and rat studies, and they propose that a related, still unidentified peptide may account, at least in part, for the activity attributed to DSIP. These animal findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item at 10 mg for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on DSIP and DSIP-like peptides, EEG and sleep physiology, and hypothalamic neuropeptide distribution in animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: The synthetic form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, the ten-amino-acid signal from the hypothalamus that prompts the pituitary gland to release reproductive hormones. Animal studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is the synthetic form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, GnRH - the ten-amino-acid hypothalamic signal that makes the anterior pituitary release luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. It is listed for laboratory work on that hypothalamic-pituitary signaling in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes dates from 1971 and 1972 and is in animals and cells: the structure was determined from porcine and ovine hypothalami, a synthetic decapeptide with that sequence matched the natural factor's activities, and analogues altered at the histidine in position 2 were partial agonists or inactive. What it does not establish is any effect in a person, and the separate approved veterinary products for cattle are approved on their own evidence, which does not transfer to this research listing. The full technical description follows.

Gonadorelin is the synthetic form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the hypothalamic decapeptide pGlu-His-Trp-Ser-Tyr-Gly-Leu-Arg-Pro-Gly-NH2 that causes the anterior pituitary to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Its structure was established in 1971 and 1972 from porcine and ovine hypothalami; the ovine sequence was determined by enzymatic hydrolysis, Edman sequencing and mass spectrometry, a synthetic decapeptide with that sequence had the same biological activities as the native factor, and the ovine and porcine sequences were identical. In 1971, the synthetic porcine decapeptide stimulated LH release and induced ovulation in hamsters whose spontaneous ovulation had been blocked with phenobarbital, and in 1972 two analogues altered at the histidine in position 2 were tested in cultured rat anterior pituitary cells: the analogue with glycine in place of histidine was a partial agonist, releasing less than half of the maximal LH response to the native factor, the analogue lacking that histidine had no significant agonist activity, and at molar ratios of a thousand to ten thousand times the native factor both reduced the LH secreted in response to it. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine; separately, gonadorelin is the active ingredient of veterinary products approved in the United States for cattle, for ovarian follicular cysts and, within certain approved regimens that also include another veterinary medicine, for synchronizing estrous cycles to allow fixed-time artificial insemination. The animal findings above, and the approval of those separate veterinary products, do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotropin signaling in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A synthetic, ring-shaped peptide of seven amino acids, a modified version of the hormone α-MSH, acting on melanocortin receptors. Also known as bremelanotide. Animal studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic cyclic heptapeptide - a ring-shaped chain of seven amino acids - modelled on alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, and the development code of bremelanotide. It is listed for laboratory work on melanocortin receptor signaling and on melanocortin-regulated behavior in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is in female rats: it selectively stimulated solicitational behaviors without affecting lordosis or other sexual behaviors, without general motor activation and without altering the perception of sexual reward. What it does not establish is any effect in a person, and the separate prescription medicine made with this compound is approved on its own evidence, which does not transfer to this research listing. The full technical description follows.

PT-141, the development code of bremelanotide, is a synthetic cyclic heptapeptide analogue of α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), Ac-Nle-cyclo(Asp-His-D-Phe-Arg-Trp-Lys)-OH, with an acetylated N-terminus, a lactam bridge between the aspartate and lysine side chains and a free carboxyl group at the C-terminus. It is an agonist at melanocortin receptors with high affinity for the melanocortin type 4 receptor, and by the PubChem records it differs from the related research compound Melanotan II only in having a carboxylic acid rather than an amide at the C-terminal lysine. In a 2004 study in female rats, PT-141 selectively stimulated solicitational behaviors without affecting lordosis, pacing or other sexual behaviors, did not cause generalized motor activation and did not alter the perception of sexual reward, which the authors took as evidence that central melanocortin systems regulate appetitive sexual behavior. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine; separately, bremelanotide is the active ingredient of a prescription medicine approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2019 for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder. The animal findings above, and the approval of that separate medicine, do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on melanocortin receptor signaling and melanocortin-regulated behavior in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A copper-bound form of a three-amino-acid peptide first reported in human serum in 1973. In cell cultures it increased collagen production by connective-tissue cells, which is a cell-culture result only. Listed at 75 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a chain of three amino acids bound to copper. It is listed for laboratory work on how skin and connective tissue repair themselves, and in particular on the production of collagen. What the cited work establishes is narrow: in dishes of cultured connective-tissue cells, the copper complex increased collagen production at very low concentrations, without the cells multiplying more. What it does not establish is any effect in a person, because a result in cultured cells is not a result in people. The full technical description follows.

GHK (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine) is a tripeptide with high affinity for copper(II) ions, and GHK-Cu is its copper complex. The tripeptide later identified as GHK was first reported in human serum in 1973 as a factor that prolonged the survival of normal liver cells. In fibroblast cultures, the copper complex GHK-Cu stimulated collagen synthesis beginning at picomolar concentrations and peaking near 1 nanomolar, independently of any change in cell number. Those authors noted that a GHK sequence occurs within the alpha 2 chain of type I collagen and proposed that proteases could release it at a wound site. These cell-culture findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 75 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on extracellular-matrix and wound-repair biology, including collagen synthesis in fibroblast culture.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

Semax is a synthetic seven-amino-acid peptide, Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro, described in the literature as an analogue of the N-terminal fragment 4-10 of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In membranes from the rat basal forebrain, tritium-labelled Semax bound to specific, reversible, calcium-dependent binding sites, and giving the peptide to rats raised brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) protein in the basal forebrain 3 hours later but not in the cerebellum. In the rat hippocampus, a single administration increased BDNF protein, tyrosine phosphorylation of its receptor trkB, and BDNF (exon III) and trkB mRNA levels, and rats that received it made more conditioned avoidance responses. In rodents, Semax raised striatal levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA without changing dopamine or its metabolites on its own, but it enhanced the dopamine release and locomotor activity produced by D-amphetamine. In a rat model of permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion, a genome-wide analysis of the cortex found that Semax mainly altered the expression of immune-system genes, notably those encoding immunoglobulins and chemokines, as well as genes related to the vascular system. These rodent findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 30 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on ACTH-derived peptides, BDNF/trkB signaling, monoamine neurochemistry and focal brain ischemia in rodent models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: Two-subunit glycoprotein hormone, described in the published record as an alpha and beta dimer and studied as recombinant subunits in cell assays. The exact labeled strength is under review.
content.overview: Human chorionic gonadotropin, written hCG, is a glycoprotein hormone made of two different subunits rather than a single chain. A 2020 study describes hCG as a dimer of two highly glycosylated subunits, an alpha subunit and a beta subunit, and notes that the beta protein is encoded by the CGB3, CGB5, CGB7 and CGB8 genes, that CGB3, CGB5 and CGB8 encode an identical protein, and that CGB7 differs from it in three amino acids. That study produced and isolated recombinant alpha, CGB7 and CGB3/5/8 proteins and compared their glycosylation, finding the N- and O-glycosylation patterns of the two beta variants quite similar. Testing activation of the ERK1/2 pathway, it reported the two beta variants to be functionally redundant isoforms, with a slight difference in the kinetics of that activation, and recorded biological activity for CGB7 for the first time. Reference records give the alpha subunit as a 116-residue precursor with a signal region at 1 to 24 and the mature chain at 25 to 116, and the choriogonadotropin beta subunit as a 165-residue precursor with a signal region at 1 to 20 and the mature chain at 21 to 165; those records name the alpha subunit as the chain shared with the other glycoprotein hormones, so the beta subunit is what distinguishes this hormone from them. The exact labeled strength and the basis for that amount are being verified. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on glycoprotein hormone subunit chemistry, glycosylation and receptor pathway activation in cell assays.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A synthetic six-amino-acid peptide, also called pralmorelin, that mimics ghrelin, a natural hormone involved in growth-hormone release. Published records treat it as a different compound from the similarly named GHRP-6. The cell and animal findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic hexapeptide - a chain of six amino acids - also called pralmorelin, described as mimicking the actions of ghrelin, the stomach peptide that regulates growth hormone release. It is a different compound from GHRP-6, with a different sequence. It is listed for laboratory work on the growth hormone secretagogue receptor in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is in rats and mice: reducing that receptor's transcript cut its growth hormone effect while leaving the response to growth hormone-releasing hormone unaltered, and in conscious rats it raised adrenocorticotropic hormone by acting through the hypothalamus. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

GHRP-2, also called pralmorelin, is a synthetic hexapeptide, D-Ala-D-2-Nal-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2, and by the PubChem records it is a different compound from the hexapeptide GHRP-6, whose sequence is His-D-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2. A 2004 profile of the compound describes it as a synthetic growth hormone-releasing peptide from a series of small, highly active peptides, and as mimicking the actions of ghrelin, the 28-amino-acid peptide, octanoylated at its third residue, that regulates the release of growth hormone. In primary cultured rat pituitary cells, antisense knockdown of the secretagogue receptor transcript reduced but did not abolish GHRP-2-induced growth hormone secretion and left the response to growth hormone-releasing hormone unaltered; knockdown of that hormone's own receptor transcript abolished its response while leaving GHRP-2's unaffected; and knocking down both inhibited both responses. In conscious rats, GHRP-2 raised plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone but did not stimulate its release from rat primary pituitary cells; a corticotropin-releasing factor antagonist markedly inhibited that rise while a vasopressin antagonist and an anti-vasopressin antiserum did not, from which the authors concluded that the peptide acts through the hypothalamus mainly by releasing corticotropin-releasing factor. In rats with thermal injury, GHRP-2 lessened the injury-induced rise in the messenger RNA of interleukin-6 and of the E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF-1 and MAFbx in skeletal muscle and reduced total and myofibrillar protein breakdown; in mice, it produced a concentration- and time-related antinociceptive effect in a tail-immersion test that an antagonist of the secretagogue receptor fully reversed and that δ- and κ-opioid receptor antagonists markedly attenuated. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The cell and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on growth hormone secretagogue receptor signaling in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A synthetic six-amino-acid peptide that prompts release of growth hormone. In the 1984 report describing it, it did so in pituitary tissue and in several animal species; those animal findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic hexapeptide - a chain of six amino acids - whose structure is that of an analogue described in 1984 as a growth hormone-releasing peptide. It is listed for laboratory work on the growth hormone secretagogue receptor and on growth hormone release in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is in animals: it released growth hormone in pituitary incubates and in rats, monkeys, lambs and calves without releasing luteinizing, follicle-stimulating or thyroid-stimulating hormone or prolactin, and immature rats given it gained more weight than controls. What it does not establish is any effect in a person - and the natural hormone whose action these peptides were thought to reflect was only identified later, as ghrelin, in 1999. The full technical description follows.

GHRP-6 is a synthetic hexapeptide, His-D-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2, whose structure is that of the analogue described in 1984 as [His1,Lys6] growth hormone-releasing peptide. In that 1984 report the hexapeptide released growth hormone in pituitary incubates at 1 to 10 nanograms per millilitre and in rats, monkeys, lambs, calves and, under special experimental conditions, chicks, without a concomitant release of luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone or prolactin, and in limited work insulin or glucagon; its growth hormone response lasted longer than that of the larger growth hormone-releasing factors of 44 and 40 residues, and both the 14- and 28-residue forms of somatotropin release-inhibiting factor suppressed it, the longer form being about four times as active in pituitary incubates and about seven and a half times as active in animals. In the same report, body weight gain in immature rats given the peptide for 9 or 25 days rose above that of controls, and the pituitary remained fully responsive to the peptide at the end of those studies. A 1998 review by the author of that 1984 report described growth hormone-releasing peptides as a class of synthetic growth hormone secretagogues that act on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary, and argued that, although the peptides themselves are of unnatural origin, their action reflects that of a natural hypothalamic hormone not yet isolated at the time. The receptor through which such secretagogues act was cloned from the pituitary and hypothalamus of swine and humans in 1996, and in 1999 an endogenous ligand for it was purified from rat stomach and named ghrelin, a 28-amino-acid peptide whose serine 3 is octanoylated, an acylation the authors found essential for its activity. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on growth hormone secretagogue receptor signaling and growth hormone release in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: The synthetic form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, the ten-amino-acid signal from the hypothalamus that prompts the pituitary gland to release reproductive hormones. Animal studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is the synthetic form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, GnRH - the ten-amino-acid hypothalamic signal that makes the anterior pituitary release luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. It is listed for laboratory work on that hypothalamic-pituitary signaling in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes dates from 1971 and 1972 and is in animals and cells: the structure was determined from porcine and ovine hypothalami, a synthetic decapeptide with that sequence matched the natural factor's activities, and analogues altered at the histidine in position 2 were partial agonists or inactive. What it does not establish is any effect in a person, and the separate approved veterinary products for cattle are approved on their own evidence, which does not transfer to this research listing. The full technical description follows.

Gonadorelin is the synthetic form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the hypothalamic decapeptide pGlu-His-Trp-Ser-Tyr-Gly-Leu-Arg-Pro-Gly-NH2 that causes the anterior pituitary to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Its structure was established in 1971 and 1972 from porcine and ovine hypothalami; the ovine sequence was determined by enzymatic hydrolysis, Edman sequencing and mass spectrometry, a synthetic decapeptide with that sequence had the same biological activities as the native factor, and the ovine and porcine sequences were identical. In 1971, the synthetic porcine decapeptide stimulated LH release and induced ovulation in hamsters whose spontaneous ovulation had been blocked with phenobarbital, and in 1972 two analogues altered at the histidine in position 2 were tested in cultured rat anterior pituitary cells: the analogue with glycine in place of histidine was a partial agonist, releasing less than half of the maximal LH response to the native factor, the analogue lacking that histidine had no significant agonist activity, and at molar ratios of a thousand to ten thousand times the native factor both reduced the LH secreted in response to it. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine; separately, gonadorelin is the active ingredient of veterinary products approved in the United States for cattle, for ovarian follicular cysts and, within certain approved regimens that also include another veterinary medicine, for synchronizing estrous cycles to allow fixed-time artificial insemination. The animal findings above, and the approval of those separate veterinary products, do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotropin signaling in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A synthetic peptide of 13 amino acids that acts on pigment cells, a modified version of the hormone α-MSH. Also known as afamelanotide. Laboratory studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic 13-amino-acid version of a natural hormone that drives pigment production, altered at two positions. It is listed for laboratory work on the receptor it acts on and on pigment formation in cells and tissue. What the cited work establishes is laboratory work from 1980 onward: it resisted breakdown by serum enzymes, darkened frog skin with prolonged activity, and was about 26 times as potent as α-MSH at activating adenylate cyclase in mouse melanoma cells. What it does not establish is any effect in a person, and the separate prescription medicine made with this compound is approved on its own evidence, which does not transfer to this research listing. The full technical description follows.

Melanotan I is the research name of afamelanotide, [Nle4, D-Phe7]-α-MSH, a synthetic 13-amino-acid analogue of α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone in which norleucine replaces methionine at position 4 and D-phenylalanine replaces L-phenylalanine at position 7. In the 1980 report that first described it, the analogue was resistant to degradation by serum enzymes, darkened frog skin with prolonged activity, and was about 26 times as potent as α-MSH at activating adenylate cyclase in mouse melanoma cells. It is an agonist at the melanocortin 1 receptor on melanocytes and stimulates eumelanin synthesis independently of ultraviolet exposure. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine; separately, afamelanotide is the active ingredient of a prescription medicine authorized in the European Union in 2014 for the prevention of phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, and approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with a history of phototoxic reactions from erythropoietic protoporphyria. The laboratory findings above, and the approval of that separate medicine, do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on melanocortin 1 receptor signaling and melanogenesis in cell and tissue models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A three-amino-acid piece of a natural signaling hormone with described anti-inflammatory effects. Studied in human intestinal and immune cell models and in mice; those cell and mouse findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is the tripeptide lysine-proline-valine - a chain of three amino acids - corresponding to residues 11 to 13 of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, a peptide with described anti-inflammatory effects. It is listed for laboratory work on peptide transport and inflammatory signaling in intestinal models. What the cited work establishes is in human intestinal cell lines and in mice: it reduced inflammatory signaling and the secretion of the cytokine IL-8 in cells, its uptake depended on the transporter PepT1, and in mice it reduced chemically induced colitis. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

KPV is the tripeptide lysine-proline-valine, corresponding to residues 11 to 13 of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), a melanocortin peptide with described anti-inflammatory effects. In the Caco2-BBE human intestinal epithelial cell line, nanomolar KPV reduced NF-kappaB and MAP kinase inflammatory signaling and lowered secretion of the cytokine IL-8; in Jurkat T cells it reduced inflammatory signaling and IL-8 mRNA. Its uptake depended on PepT1, a di- and tripeptide transporter normally expressed in the small intestine and induced in the colon during inflammatory bowel disease. In mice, KPV given in drinking water reduced colitis induced by dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) or TNBS. A separate mouse study reported earlier recovery, regain of body weight and fewer inflammatory infiltrates in DSS and T-cell transfer colitis. In mice with a nonfunctional melanocortin-1 receptor, that study reported that all KPV-treated animals survived DSS colitis, and the authors concluded that the effects were at least partly independent of that receptor. These are cell and mouse findings and do not establish effects in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on peptide transport and inflammatory signaling in intestinal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.

content.summary: A small synthetic molecule designed to block an enzyme called nicotinamide N-methyltransferase. Studied in cultured mouse fat cells and in obese mice; those cell and mouse findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a small synthetic molecule made to block one enzyme, nicotinamide N-methyltransferase. It is listed for laboratory work on that enzyme's activity in cells and in animals. What the cited work establishes is in cultured mouse fat cells and in obese mice: less of the enzyme's product, less fat accumulation in the cells, and lower body weight and fat mass in the mice, with little or no effect on several related enzymes. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

5-Amino-1MQ is short for 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium, a small molecule from a series of methylquinolinium compounds that researchers developed to inhibit the cytosolic enzyme nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT). In one laboratory study, the team measured 1-methylnicotinamide (1-MNA), a product of the NNMT reaction, in cultured mouse 3T3-L1 fat cells exposed to the compound and found concentration-dependent reductions; in differentiating cells, the compound also reduced lipid accumulation in a concentration-dependent way. In the same study, the overall effect on intracellular S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) was significant, with a significant increase at one of the concentrations tested; intracellular NAD+ trended upward, but the overall comparison for NAD+ was inconclusive. In enzyme assays at the concentrations tested, it showed little or no inhibition of the related methyltransferases DNMT1, PRMT3 and COMT or of the NAD+ salvage enzymes NAMPT and SIRT1, which the authors interpreted as selectivity for NNMT. In diet-induced obese mice fed a high-fat diet, 5-amino-1MQ reduced body weight and white adipose tissue mass, decreased fat-cell size and lowered plasma total cholesterol without changing total food intake. A 2021 study from the same research group reported that, in obese mice switched to a lean diet, adding the compound produced greater body-weight and fat loss and less liver fat than the diet switch alone. These cell and mouse findings do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Laboratory study of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase activity in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.

content.summary: A nine-amino-acid molecule known as delta sleep-inducing peptide, first isolated in 1977 from the blood of rabbits. In rabbit experiments it increased slow brain-wave and spindle activity; those animal findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a nine-amino-acid peptide isolated in 1977 from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits and named for its effect on the electroencephalogram, or EEG, a recording of brain-wave activity. It is listed for laboratory work on this peptide and related ones, on sleep physiology, and on where such peptides occur in the hypothalamus. What the cited work establishes is in rabbits: infused into the brain ventricles it increased delta-wave and spindle EEG activity compared with controls. What it does not establish is a confirmed role in sleep at all - a 2006 review notes the link was never further characterized, that no gene, precursor protein or receptor had been isolated, and proposes that a different, still unidentified peptide may account for the activity attributed to it. The full technical description follows.

Delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP) is a nine-amino-acid peptide, Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu, isolated in 1977 from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits by a research group in Basel and named for its effect on the electroencephalogram (EEG). In the original double-blind study in rabbits, synthetic DSIP infused into the brain ventricles significantly increased delta-wave and spindle EEG activity compared with controls. Of the other eight peptides tested, rabbits given one of the three shortest (two fragments and a related tripeptide) showed less significant differences from controls, and rabbits given one of the remaining five, three longer fragments and two analogues with two amino acids exchanged, did not differ significantly from controls. A 2006 review noted that this link to sleep had never been further characterized, partly because no gene, precursor protein or receptor for DSIP had been isolated by then, and that its natural occurrence and biological activity remained unclear. The same review describes the structure of DSIP as unlike any other known peptide family, and notes that DSIP-like immunoreactivity has a highly specific distribution in neurosecretory nuclei of the hypothalamus in several vertebrate species, regions not particularly relevant to sleep regulation. The review's authors also report that certain synthetic DSIP analogues, but not DSIP itself, promoted slow-wave sleep in their own rabbit and rat studies, and they propose that a related, still unidentified peptide may account, at least in part, for the activity attributed to DSIP. These animal findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on DSIP and DSIP-like peptides, EEG and sleep physiology, and hypothalamic neuropeptide distribution in animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A peptide derived from the product of the KISS1 gene, first identified as a metastasis-suppressor gene for melanoma cells. The catalog does not state which form this is — the 54-amino-acid version or the shorter 10-amino-acid fragment — so the exact peptide here is not established. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a peptide derived from the protein made by the KISS1 gene, first identified as a metastasis suppressor gene for melanoma cells. It is listed for laboratory work on KISS1 and GPR54 signaling and on the brain's control of reproductive hormone release. What the cited work establishes is in cells and animals: kisspeptins are natural ligands of the receptor GPR54, loss-of-function mutations in that receptor impair pubertal maturation and reproductive function in affected families and in mice, and kisspeptin delivered into a brain ventricle raised luteinizing hormone in mice. What it does not establish is any effect of this listing in a person - and the catalog does not state which form this is, the 54-amino-acid or the shorter 10-amino-acid one. The full technical description follows.

Kisspeptins are peptides derived from the protein product of the KISS1 gene, first identified as a metastasis suppressor gene for melanoma cells, and they share a common Arg-Phe-amide (RF-amide) C-terminus. The catalog listing names this item only as kisspeptin and does not state which form it is, for example the 54-amino-acid kisspeptin-54 or the 10-amino-acid C-terminal fragment kisspeptin-10. In 2001, kisspeptins were isolated from human placenta as natural ligands of the orphan G protein-coupled receptor GPR54; in hamster ovary cells expressing rat or human GPR54 they bound with low nanomolar affinity, mobilized calcium, activated ERK1/2 and p38 MAP kinases and inhibited cell proliferation. Loss-of-function mutations in GPR54 were later found to cause isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, in which pubertal maturation and reproductive function are impaired, in affected human families and in Gpr54-deficient mice. In mice, kisspeptin-54 and kisspeptin-10 delivered into a lateral brain ventricle both stimulated luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, the kisspeptin-54 effect was blocked by a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist, and KISS1 mRNA was mapped to hypothalamic areas that regulate gonadotropin secretion. In a separate study, kisspeptin that stimulated LH and follicle-stimulating hormone release in normal mice had no effect in mice lacking GPR54, and in sheep it released GnRH into the cerebrospinal fluid, which the authors interpret as a direct action at the level of GnRH release. These cell and animal findings, and the human genetic studies of its receptor, do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on KISS1/GPR54 signaling and the hypothalamic control of gonadotropin secretion in cell and animal models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A synthetic seven-amino-acid molecule modelled on tuftsin, a short natural peptide the body makes itself. Studied in rodent and tissue models for signaling involving GABA, a chemical messenger in the brain; those findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic heptapeptide - a chain of seven amino acids - designed as an analogue of tuftsin, a peptide the body makes itself. It is listed for laboratory work on GABA-related signaling, on gene expression and on stress-related behavior in rodents. What the cited work establishes is in rodent and tissue models: in brain membrane assays it changed GABA binding in a way consistent with positive allosteric modulation, it altered many neurotransmission-related genes in the rat frontal cortex, and in rats given ethanol for 30 weeks it prevented memory and attention deficits during withdrawal. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

Selank is a synthetic heptapeptide (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro) designed as an analogue of the endogenous peptide tuftsin. The selected studies examine GABA-related signaling, gene expression and behavior in rodent and tissue models. In brain membrane binding assays, Selank changed [3H]GABA binding in a way consistent with positive allosteric modulation of GABA receptors, and it blocked the modulatory effect of diazepam and olanzapine on that binding. In the rat frontal cortex, Selank altered the expression of many of 84 neurotransmission-related genes at one and three hours; the one-hour changes correlated positively with those produced by GABA, and the three-hour changes correlated negatively. In mouse spleen, Selank and its C-terminal Gly-Pro fragment changed the expression of immune-related genes such as complement C3 within 30 to 90 minutes, with similar profiles for both peptides. In rats given ethanol as their only fluid for 30 weeks, Selank prevented memory and attention deficits during withdrawal and prevented the ethanol-related rise in BDNF in the hippocampus and frontal cortex. These findings come from rodent and tissue studies and do not establish effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on GABAergic signaling, neurotransmission-related gene expression and stress-related behavior in rodent models.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: A laboratory-made version of amylin, a hormone produced by the pancreas, altered to be more stable and longer-acting. Studied in receptor experiments and in rodents; those laboratory and animal findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a lipidated analogue of amylin, a pancreatic hormone, built to be stable and long-acting where the natural form readily forms amyloid fibrils. It is listed for laboratory work on amylin and calcitonin receptor signaling and on feeding behavior in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is structural and in rodents: it binds both the amylin-1 receptor and the calcitonin receptor as a dual agonist, it reduced food intake in normal-weight rats, and in diet-induced obese rats it markedly reduced food intake and body weight, mainly through loss of fat mass. What it does not establish is any effect in a person - as of reports through 2026 it was in clinical development, alone and in a combination. The full technical description follows.

Cagrilintide is a lipidated analogue of amylin, a pancreatic hormone whose native form readily forms amyloid fibrils; its developer reported it in 2021 as a stable, long-acting amylin analogue selected for clinical development. The PubChem record describes it as a 37-amino-acid peptide amide with one disulfide bridge and a C20 fatty diacid attached through a γ-glutamyl spacer to its N-terminal lysine. A 2026 structural study reported cryo-electron-microscopy structures of cagrilintide bound to the amylin-1 receptor and to the calcitonin receptor, each with a Gs protein, and described it as a dual agonist that activates Gs signaling through both receptors with a similar binding mode at each; the authors noted a salt bridge between residues 14 and 17 that stabilizes its helix and a phenylalanine at position 23 that anchors the peptide at the receptor's transmembrane bundle. In a 2025 report from its developer, cagrilintide and a closely related tool compound reduced food intake in normal-weight rats after acute administration, had small and transient effects on food intake and body weight in diet-induced obese mice, and in diet-induced obese rats markedly reduced food intake and body weight, mainly through loss of fat mass, while adding to the effects of semaglutide. As of its developer's 2025 report and a 2026 systematic review of trials published to March 2026, cagrilintide was in clinical development alone and in a combination with semaglutide; this listing is a laboratory research material, not a medicine. The laboratory and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.summary: A laboratory-made version of the human hormone glucagon-like peptide-1, altered by attaching a fatty acid so that it persists longer. Studied in receptor experiments and in rodent models of body-weight regulation; those findings do not establish any effect in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a laboratory-made version of a human hormone called glucagon-like peptide-1, with a fatty acid attached so that it stays in circulation longer. It is listed for laboratory work on that hormone's receptor, on the design of peptides that bind to albumin, and on how the brain regulates body weight. What the cited work establishes is in cells and rodents: the fatty acid binds albumin reversibly, and in mice and rats the labeled peptide reached specific regions of the hypothalamus, which the authors propose explains its effect on body weight in those animals. What it does not establish is any effect in a person, and the separate prescription medicines made with this compound are approved on their own evidence, which does not transfer to this research listing. The full technical description follows.

Liraglutide is an analogue of human glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) in which arginine replaces lysine at position 34 and a C16 fatty acid, palmitic acid, is attached through a glutamic acid spacer to the lysine at position 26; the fatty acid binds albumin reversibly, which prolongs the peptide's presence in circulation. In the developer's 2000 report, GLP-1 derivatives carrying fatty acids of 12 or more carbons were markedly protracted compared with GLP-1, many of them with similar or higher potency at the cloned human GLP-1 receptor, derivatives with two fatty acids lost potency, and palmitate with a γ-glutamate linker was later judged the best combination of protraction and receptor potency, leading to the selection of liraglutide. Although its N-terminus is unchanged from GLP-1, liraglutide is partly protected from rapid degradation by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, which its developers attribute to reversible albumin binding or steric hindrance. In a 2014 study, liraglutide-dependent body-weight reduction in rats did not depend on GLP-1 receptors in the vagus nerve, area postrema or paraventricular nucleus; in mice, fluorescently labeled liraglutide given peripherally produced a receptor-dependent signal in circumventricular organs and in selected hypothalamic regions including the arcuate and paraventricular nuclei, with no signal in mice lacking the GLP-1 receptor; in rat hypothalamic sections, labeled liraglutide accumulated inside CART-positive arcuate cells, and in mouse brain slices GLP-1 itself depolarized pro-opiomelanocortin neurons, from which the authors propose that GLP-1 receptors on these arcuate neurons mediate liraglutide's effect on body weight. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine; separately, liraglutide is the active ingredient of prescription medicines approved in the European Union in 2009 and in the United States as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in type 2 diabetes mellitus and, in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease, to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events; later approvals cover other indications for specific medicines. The cell and animal findings above, and the approval of those separate medicines, do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.
