content.summary: Tadalafil SR 12 mg capsules, a prescription capsule form of tadalafil, a PDE5 inhibitor; the listing does not say what “SR” means. CIALIS labeling, written for 5, 10 and 20 mg tablets and not this capsule, says tadalafil helps blood flow into the penis during sexual stimulation and covers erectile dysfunction and enlarged-prostate symptoms. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
Each capsule is listed at 12 mg of tadalafil, a PDE5 inhibitor; a capsule is a different form from the CIALIS tablets cited here. The listing does not say what “SR” stands for or how the capsule releases tadalafil. According to the CIALIS prescribing information, sexual stimulation releases nitric oxide, which relaxes smooth muscle so more blood flows into the penis; blocking PDE5 strengthens this, and the effect needs sexual stimulation. CIALIS is labeled for erectile dysfunction (ED), for the signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH, an enlarged prostate), and for both together. That labeling describes 5, 10 and 20 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed at 12 mg of tadalafil, a phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) inhibitor. A capsule is a different dosage form from the tablets covered by the CIALIS prescribing information cited here. The catalog name for this capsule includes “SR”; the listing does not say what that stands for or how the capsule releases tadalafil, and this page makes no claim about its release profile. According to the CIALIS prescribing information, erection during sexual stimulation comes from increased penile blood flow: nitric oxide released from nerve terminals and endothelial cells stimulates cGMP synthesis in smooth muscle cells, and cGMP relaxes that muscle so more blood flows into the corpus cavernosum. Inhibiting PDE5 enhances erectile function by increasing the amount of cGMP, and because sexual stimulation is needed to start the local release of nitric oxide, this erectile effect requires sexual stimulation. The CIALIS prescribing information describes CIALIS tablets in 5, 10 and 20 mg strengths and indicates CIALIS for erectile dysfunction, for the signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia, and for both together. Those indications describe CIALIS tablets; they do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule or how it is prepared; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.

content.purpose: Labeled indications (CIALIS prescribing information, which describes CIALIS tablets, not this capsule): erectile dysfunction (ED), the signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and ED with the signs and symptoms of BPH. content.cautions: The CIALIS prescribing information contraindicates CIALIS with any form of organic nitrate, taken regularly or intermittently, with guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat, and in people with a known serious hypersensitivity to tadalafil. It notes a degree of cardiac risk associated with sexual activity, and states that treatments for erectile dysfunction, including CIALIS, should not be used in men for whom sexual activity is inadvisable because of their underlying cardiovascular status. It advises emergency medical attention for an erection lasting more than 4 hours, and stopping all PDE5 inhibitors and seeking medical attention after a sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes. It also warns about sudden hearing loss, additive blood-pressure lowering with alpha-blockers or other blood-pressure medicines, orthostatic symptoms with substantial alcohol (for example, 5 units or more), and interactions with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors. It states that the safety and efficacy of combinations of CIALIS with other PDE5 inhibitors or other treatments for erectile dysfunction have not been studied, and that patients should be told not to take CIALIS with other PDE5 inhibitors. It also states that CIALIS offers no protection against sexually transmitted diseases.

content.cautions:
The PROMETRIUM prescribing information contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with hypersensitivity to its ingredients and, because PROMETRIUM capsules contain peanut oil, in patients allergic to peanuts; this listing does not state the capsule's ingredients or vehicle.

It also contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with abnormal genital bleeding of unknown etiology; known, suspected, or history of breast cancer; active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease (for example, stroke and myocardial infarction) or a history of these conditions; or known liver dysfunction or disease.

Its warnings state that PROMETRIUM should be immediately discontinued if a pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction occurs or is suspected, and that, if feasible, it should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization.

The labeling states that the safety and efficacy of estrogen plus progestogen for the prevention of cardiovascular disorders has not been established, and that the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin trial reported increased risks of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke and myocardial infarction in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age, average age 63.4 years) during 5.6 years of treatment with daily oral conjugated estrogens (0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (2.5 mg), relative to placebo.

It states that only daily oral 0.625 mg conjugated estrogens and 2.5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate were studied in that trial, so the relevance of the WHI findings regarding adverse cardiovascular events to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, and that without such data it is not possible to definitively exclude these risks or determine their extent for other products.

For venous thromboembolism in the overall WHI study population, the labeling reports a relative risk for pulmonary embolism of 1.98 (95% CI, 1.36, 2.87) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (18 versus 9), and a relative risk for deep vein thrombosis of 1.87 (95% CI, 1.37, 2.54), with a risk difference of 12 per 10,000 women-years (25 versus 14).

For the overall WHI population it also reports a relative risk for stroke of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.07, 1.76) with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (33 versus 24), and a relative risk of coronary heart disease of 1.18 (95% CI, 0.95, 1.45) with a risk difference of 6 per 10,000 women-years (41 versus 35), for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo.

Its breast cancer warning states that PROMETRIUM is contraindicated in women with breast cancer, a history of breast cancer, or estrogen-dependent neoplasia, that PROMETRIUM should be discontinued if a hormone-sensitive malignancy is diagnosed, and that the use of estrogen plus progestin therapy has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation.

In the overall WHI population, the labeling reports a relative risk for invasive breast cancer of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01, 1.53) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (43 versus 35); it states that invasive breast cancers were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage in that group, and that the trial did not show a statistically significant difference in breast cancer mortality.

It adds that, consistent with the WHI trial, observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy, and that a large meta-analysis including 24 prospective studies of postmenopausal women comparing current use of estrogen plus progestin products for 5 to 14 years (average of 9 years) versus never use reported a relative risk for breast cancer of 2.08 (95% CI, 2.02 to 2.15). It states that these studies have not generally found significant variation in the risk of breast cancer among different estrogen plus progestin combinations, doses, or routes of administration, and that the relevance of the WHI findings regarding breast cancer to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, so that these risks cannot be definitively excluded or their extent determined for other products.

Its ovarian cancer warning reports, for the overall WHI population, a relative risk for ovarian cancer of 1.41 (95% CI, 0.75 to 2.66) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate versus placebo after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, with a risk difference of 1 per 10,000 women-years (5 versus 4), and a large meta-analysis of 17 prospective studies of postmenopausal women reporting a relative risk of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.26 to 1.48) for current use of estrogen plus progestin products versus never use; it states that the duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown.

Its vision warning states that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogen, that estrogen plus progestin therapy should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that it should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions.

Its precautions state that progesterone may cause some degree of fluid retention, so women with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation.

They also state that PROMETRIUM capsules may cause transient dizziness and drowsiness and should be used with caution when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery; the patient information adds that some women may experience extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness during initial therapy, in a few cases with blurred vision, difficulty speaking, difficulty with walking and feeling abnormal, and says to discuss these symptoms with the healthcare provider right away.

Its drug-interaction section reports that the metabolism of progesterone by human liver microsomes was inhibited by ketoconazole, a known inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, so these data suggest that ketoconazole or other known inhibitors of this enzyme may increase the bioavailability of progesterone, and that the clinical relevance of the in vitro findings is unknown.

It reports that coadministration of conjugated estrogens and PROMETRIUM capsules to 29 postmenopausal women over a 12-day period increased total estrone and total equilin concentrations and decreased circulating 17β estradiol concentrations, while the half-life of the conjugated estrogens was similar with coadministration.

Its precautions also list laboratory results that may be altered by estrogen plus progestin therapy: increased sulfobromophthalein retention and other hepatic function tests; coagulation tests (an increase in prothrombin factors VII, VIII, IX and X); pregnanediol determination; and thyroid function (an increase in PBI and butanol extractable protein bound iodine and a decrease in T3 uptake values).

Its precautions state that exogenously administered progesterone has been shown to inhibit ovulation in a number of species, and that high doses given for an extended duration are expected to impair fertility until the cessation of treatment.

The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules should not be used during pregnancy, and its patient information lists, among serious but less common side effects, risk to the fetus: cases of cleft palate, cleft lip, hypospadias, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, and other congenital heart defects.

It states that detectable amounts of progestin have been identified in the milk of nursing women receiving progestins, that caution should be exercised when PROMETRIUM capsules are administered to a nursing woman, and, in the patient information, that the hormone in PROMETRIUM capsules can pass into breast milk.

It states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children, that clinical studies have not been conducted in the pediatric population, and that there have not been sufficient numbers of geriatric women in clinical studies to determine whether those over 65 years of age differ from younger subjects in their response.

For women over 65, it reports that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy showed a higher relative risk of nonfatal stroke and invasive breast cancer. It also reports that the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study of postmenopausal women 65 to 79 years of age found an increased risk of developing probable dementia with estrogen plus progestin compared to placebo (after an average follow-up of 4 years, a relative risk of 2.05, 95 percent CI 1.21 to 3.48, and an absolute risk of 45 versus 22 per 10,000 women-years), and that it is unknown whether these findings apply to younger postmenopausal women.

Its table of adverse reactions comes from a 3-year, placebo-controlled trial of cyclic PROMETRIUM capsules 200 mg with conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg in postmenopausal women (875 women studied; the table's arms are n = 178 and placebo n = 174) and lists the reactions reported by 2% or more of women. Those are headache (31% versus 27% on placebo), breast tenderness (27% versus 6%), joint pain (20% versus 29%), depression (19% versus 12%), dizziness (15% versus 9%), abdominal bloating (12% versus 5%), hot flashes (11% versus 35%), urinary problems (11% versus 9%), abdominal pain (10% versus 10%), vaginal discharge (10% versus 3%), nausea or vomiting (8% versus 7%), worry (8% versus 4%), chest pain (7% versus 5%), diarrhea (7% versus 4%), night sweats (7% versus 17%), breast pain (6% versus 2%), swelling of hands and feet (6% versus 9%), vaginal dryness (6% versus 10%), constipation (3% versus 2%), and breast carcinoma, breast excisional biopsy and cholecystectomy (2% each versus less than 1%).

In a placebo-controlled trial of PROMETRIUM capsules at 400 mg/day in 49 estrogen-primed postmenopausal women, its table of adverse reactions reported by 5% or more lists fatigue (8% versus 4% on placebo), headache (16% versus 8%), dizziness (24% versus 4%), abdominal distention or bloating (8% versus 8%), abdominal pain or cramping (20% versus 13%), diarrhea (8% versus 4%), nausea (8% versus 0%), back pain (8% versus 8%), musculoskeletal pain (12% versus 4%), irritability (8% versus 4%), breast pain (16% versus 8%), viral infection (12% versus 0%) and coughing (8% versus 0%).

In an open-label postmarketing study of 220 premenopausal women with secondary amenorrhea who received conjugated estrogens with PROMETRIUM capsules, the labeling lists the most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse reactions (5% or more) as nausea, fatigue, vaginal mycosis, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness, abdominal distension, acne, dysmenorrhea, mood swing, and urinary tract infection.

Among additional adverse reactions reported with PROMETRIUM capsules after marketing, which the labeling notes are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size so that their frequency or a causal relationship to drug exposure cannot always be reliably established, it lists genitourinary reactions (endometrial carcinoma, hypospadia, intra-uterine death, menorrhagia, menstrual disorder, metrorrhagia, ovarian cyst, spontaneous abortion) and cardiovascular reactions (circulatory collapse, congenital heart disease including ventricular septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus, hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia).

It also lists gastrointestinal reactions (acute pancreatitis, cholestasis, cholestatic hepatitis, dysphagia, hepatic failure, hepatic necrosis, hepatitis, increased liver function tests, jaundice, swollen tongue), skin reactions (alopecia, pruritus, urticaria) and eye reactions (blurred vision, diplopia, visual disturbance).

Its central nervous system list includes aggression, convulsion, depersonalization, depressed consciousness, disorientation, dysarthria, loss of consciousness, paresthesia, sedation, stupor, syncope (with and without hypotension), transient ischemic attack and suicidal ideation, and it notes that during initial therapy a few women have experienced a constellation of many or all of the following: extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness, blurred vision, slurred speech, difficulty walking, loss of consciousness, vertigo, confusion, disorientation, feeling drunk, and shortness of breath.

Among miscellaneous postmarketing reactions it lists abnormal gait, anaphylactic reaction, arthralgia, blood glucose increased, choking, cleft lip, cleft palate, difficulty walking, dyspnea, face edema, feeling abnormal, feeling drunk, hypersensitivity, asthma, muscle cramp, throat tightness, tinnitus and vertigo, among others.

Its patient information lists abnormal blood clotting (stroke, heart attack, pulmonary embolus, visual loss or blindness) among serious but less common side effects, gives changes in vision or speech, sudden new severe headaches, severe pains in the chest or legs with or without shortness of breath, weakness and fatigue, dizziness and faintness, and vomiting as warning signs of serious side effects, and says to call the healthcare provider right away for any of these warning signs or any other unusual symptoms that concern the patient.

Its patient information lists these less serious but common side effects: headaches; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach or abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; hair loss; fluid retention; and vaginal yeast infection.

Its patient information advises seeing the healthcare provider right away for unusual vaginal bleeding while taking PROMETRIUM capsules. It advises a pelvic exam, breast exam and mammogram every year unless the healthcare provider says otherwise, and says that women whose family members have had breast cancer, or who have ever had breast lumps or an abnormal mammogram, may need breast exams more often. It also advises telling the healthcare provider about all medical problems, since closer checks may be needed with conditions such as asthma, epilepsy, diabetes, migraine, endometriosis, lupus, problems with the heart, liver, thyroid or kidneys, or high calcium levels in the blood, and about all medicines taken, including nonprescription medicines, vitamins and herbal supplements, since some medicines may affect how PROMETRIUM capsules work and PROMETRIUM capsules may affect how other medicines work.

It also advises telling the healthcare provider about all medical problems, since closer checks may be needed with conditions such as asthma, epilepsy, diabetes, migraine, endometriosis, lupus, problems with the heart, liver, thyroid or kidneys, or high calcium levels in the blood, and about all medicines taken, including nonprescription medicines, vitamins and herbal supplements, since some medicines may affect how PROMETRIUM capsules work and PROMETRIUM capsules may affect how other medicines work.

content.summary: Estradiol 1 mg tablets are a prescription estrogen. The estradiol tablets labeling covers moderate to severe hot flashes and vulvar and vaginal atrophy symptoms of menopause, among other uses, and its boxed warning states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These tablets are listed at 1 mg of estradiol, a prescription estrogen. The labeling calls estradiol the principal human estrogen inside cells; estrogens act through receptors in the body's tissues and lower the high levels of the pituitary hormones LH and FSH seen after menopause. The estradiol tablets labeling covers moderate to severe hot flashes (vasomotor symptoms) and vulvar and vaginal atrophy symptoms of menopause, low estrogen from certain causes, prevention of osteoporosis in some women, and relief (palliation only) of some advanced cancers. Its boxed warning states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer (cancer of the uterine lining), and the labeling also addresses heart and other risks. This listing does not name the tablet's maker or say whether its estradiol is micronized; the dispensed product's own label governs. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each tablet is listed at 1 mg of estradiol, an estrogen. The estradiol tablets prescribing information describes tablets for oral administration that contain 0.5, 1 or 2 mg of micronized estradiol, USP per tablet. The same labeling states that estradiol is the principal intracellular human estrogen, that estrogens act through binding to nuclear receptors in estrogen-responsive tissues, and that two estrogen receptors have been identified to date, which vary in proportion from tissue to tissue. It adds that circulating estrogens modulate the pituitary secretion of the gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), through a negative feedback mechanism, and that estrogens act to reduce the elevated levels of these hormones seen in postmenopausal women. The same labeling lists as indications the treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms associated with the menopause, the treatment of moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy associated with the menopause, and the treatment of hypoestrogenism due to hypogonadism, castration or primary ovarian failure; it states that when prescribing solely for the treatment of symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy, topical vaginal products should be considered. Its other listed indications are the treatment of breast cancer (for palliation only) in appropriately selected women and men with metastatic disease, the treatment of advanced androgen-dependent carcinoma of the prostate (for palliation only), and the prevention of osteoporosis; it states that when prescribing solely for the prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, therapy should only be considered for women at significant risk of osteoporosis and for whom non-estrogen medications are not considered to be appropriate. Its boxed warning states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer, and it also addresses cardiovascular and other risks, including findings from the Women’s Health Initiative studies. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state the tablet's manufacturer, whether it is a brand or generic product, or whether its estradiol is micronized as described in the estradiol tablets prescribing information; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (estradiol tablets prescribing information): treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms associated with the menopause; treatment of moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy associated with the menopause; treatment of hypoestrogenism due to hypogonadism, castration or primary ovarian failure; treatment of breast cancer (for palliation only) in appropriately selected women and men with metastatic disease; treatment of advanced androgen-dependent carcinoma of the prostate (for palliation only); and prevention of osteoporosis. For vulvar and vaginal atrophy alone, the labeling states that topical vaginal products should be considered. For prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis alone, it states that therapy should only be considered for women at significant risk of osteoporosis and for whom non-estrogen medications are not considered to be appropriate. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The boxed warning in the estradiol tablets prescribing information states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer, that close clinical surveillance of all women taking estrogens is important, and that adequate diagnostic measures, including endometrial sampling when indicated, should be undertaken to rule out malignancy in all cases of undiagnosed persistent or recurring abnormal vaginal bleeding.

It adds that there is no evidence that the use of “natural” estrogens results in a different endometrial risk profile than “synthetic” estrogens at equivalent estrogen doses.

The boxed warning states that estrogens with or without progestins should not be used for the prevention of cardiovascular disease, and that the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study reported increased risks of myocardial infarction, stroke, invasive breast cancer, pulmonary emboli and deep vein thrombosis in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age) during 5 years of treatment with oral conjugated estrogens (CE 0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA 2.5 mg) relative to placebo.

It also states that the Women’s Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS), a substudy of WHI, reported increased risk of developing probable dementia in postmenopausal women 65 years of age or older during 4 years of treatment with oral conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate relative to placebo, and that it is unknown whether this finding applies to younger postmenopausal women or to women taking estrogen alone therapy.

It adds that other doses of oral conjugated estrogens with medroxyprogesterone acetate, and other combinations and dosage forms of estrogens and progestins, were not studied in the WHI clinical trials and that, in the absence of comparable data, these risks should be assumed to be similar.

The labeling states that estrogens should not be used in individuals with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding; known, suspected or history of cancer of the breast, except in appropriately selected patients being treated for metastatic disease; known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia; or active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or history of these conditions.

Its list of conditions in which estrogens should not be used also includes active or recent (e.g., within the past year) arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), liver dysfunction or disease, and known or suspected pregnancy, and it states that estradiol tablets should not be used in patients with known hypersensitivity to their ingredients.

Its endometrial cancer warning states that the use of unopposed estrogens in women with intact uteri has been associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer, and that the reported endometrial cancer risk among unopposed estrogen users is about 2- to 12-fold greater than in non-users and appears dependent on duration of treatment and on estrogen dose.

It adds that most studies show no significant increased risk associated with use of estrogens for less than one year, that the greatest risk appears associated with prolonged use, with increased risks of 15- to 24-fold for five to ten years or more, and that this risk persists for 8 to over 15 years after estrogen therapy is discontinued.

The labeling states that adding a progestin to estrogen therapy has been shown to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, which may be a precursor to endometrial cancer, and that there are possible risks which may be associated with the use of progestins with estrogens compared to estrogen-alone regimens, including a possible increased risk of breast cancer.

Its cardiovascular warning states that estrogen and estrogen/progestin therapy has been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke, as well as venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and that should any of these occur or be suspected, estrogens should be discontinued immediately.

It states that risk factors for arterial vascular disease and/or venous thromboembolism should be managed appropriately.

It reports that large doses of estrogen (5 mg conjugated estrogens per day), comparable to those used to treat cancer of the prostate and breast, have been shown in a large prospective clinical trial in men to increase the risks of nonfatal myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism and thrombophlebitis.

The labeling states that, if feasible, estrogens should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization.

Its breast cancer warning states that, after a mean follow-up of 5.6 years, the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy reported an increased risk of invasive breast cancer in women who took daily CE plus MPA (relative risk 1.24; absolute risk 41 versus 33 cases per 10,000 women-years compared with placebo), and that invasive breast cancers in the CE plus MPA group were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage than in the placebo group.

It states that in the WHI estrogen-alone substudy, after an average follow-up of 7.1 years, daily CE (0.625 mg)-alone was not associated with an increased risk of invasive breast cancer (relative risk 0.80).

It adds that observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer for estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller, but still increased, risk for estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use, and that one large meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies reported increased risks that were dependent upon duration of use and could last up to more than 10 years after discontinuation of estrogen plus progestin therapy and estrogen-alone therapy.

It notes that the use of estrogen-alone and estrogen plus progestin has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation, and it states that all women should receive yearly breast examinations by a healthcare provider and perform monthly breast self-examinations, and that mammography examinations should be scheduled based on patient age, risk factors and prior mammogram results.

Its ovarian cancer warning states that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy reported a statistically non-significant increased risk of ovarian cancer: after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, the relative risk for CE plus MPA versus placebo was 1.58 (95 percent CI, 0.77-3.24), and the absolute risk was 4 versus 3 cases per 10,000 women-years.

It adds that a meta-analysis of 17 prospective and 35 retrospective epidemiology studies found that women who used hormonal therapy for menopausal symptoms had an increased risk for ovarian cancer (relative risk 1.41 with current use), that the elevated risk with combined current and recent use (discontinued use within 5 years before cancer diagnosis) was significant for both estrogen-alone and estrogen plus progestin products, and that the exact duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown.

Its gallbladder disease warning states that a 2- to 4-fold increase in the risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery has been reported in postmenopausal women receiving estrogens.

Its hypercalcemia warning states that estrogen administration may lead to severe hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and bone metastases, and that if hypercalcemia occurs, use of the drug should be stopped and appropriate measures taken to reduce the serum calcium level.

Its visual abnormalities warning notes that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogens, and it states that medication should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that estrogens should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions.

Its precautions section notes that, in a small number of case reports, substantial increases in blood pressure have been attributed to idiosyncratic reactions to estrogens and that a generalized effect of estrogens on blood pressure was not seen in a large, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial, and it states that blood pressure should be monitored at regular intervals with estrogen use.

It states that in patients with pre-existing hypertriglyceridemia, estrogen therapy may be associated with elevations of plasma triglycerides leading to pancreatitis and other complications.

Under its precautions, the labeling notes that estrogens may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function, and that for patients with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or with pregnancy, caution should be exercised and, in the case of recurrence, medication should be discontinued.

It states that estrogen administration leads to increased thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels, that patients dependent on thyroid hormone replacement therapy who are also receiving estrogens may require increased doses of their thyroid replacement therapy, and that these patients should have their thyroid function monitored in order to maintain their free thyroid hormone levels in an acceptable range.

It states that because estrogens may cause some degree of fluid retention, patients with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as asthma, epilepsy, migraine, and cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation when estrogens are prescribed, and that estrogens should be used with caution in individuals with severe hypocalcemia.

It notes that endometriosis may be exacerbated with administration of estrogens and that a few cases of malignant transformation of residual endometrial implants have been reported in women treated post-hysterectomy with estrogen alone therapy, and it states that for patients known to have residual endometriosis post-hysterectomy, the addition of progestin should be considered.

It states that estrogens may cause an exacerbation of asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraine or porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas and should be used with caution in women with these conditions.

Its clinical pharmacology section states that estrogens are metabolized partially by cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), and that inducers or inhibitors of CYP3A4 may therefore affect estrogen drug metabolism.

It gives St. John’s Wort preparations (Hypericum perforatum), phenobarbital, carbamazepine and rifampin as examples of CYP3A4 inducers that may reduce plasma concentrations of estrogens, possibly resulting in a decrease in therapeutic effects and/or changes in the uterine bleeding profile.

It gives erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice as examples of CYP3A4 inhibitors that may increase plasma concentrations of estrogens and may result in side effects.

The labeling states that estrogen administration to nursing mothers has been shown to decrease the quantity and quality of the milk, that detectable amounts of estrogens have been identified in the milk of mothers receiving this drug, and that caution should be exercised when estradiol is administered to a nursing woman.

Its patient information lists these common side effects: headache; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach/abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; and hair loss.

It also lists these other side effects: high blood pressure; liver problems; high blood sugar; fluid retention; enlargement of benign tumors (“fibroids”) of the uterus; a spotty darkening of the skin, particularly on the face; and vaginal yeast infection.

Its patient information advises calling the doctor immediately if any of the warning signals it lists, or any other unusual symptoms, happen while using estrogens; those signals include abnormal bleeding from the vagina (possible uterine cancer); pains in the calves or chest, sudden shortness of breath, or coughing blood (possible clot in the legs, or lungs); and severe headache or vomiting, dizziness, faintness, changes in vision or speech, weakness or numbness of an arm or leg (possible clot in the brain or eye).

The other warning signals it lists are breast lumps (possible breast cancer; it advises asking a doctor or health professional to show how to examine the breasts monthly); yellowing of the skin or eyes (possible liver problem); and pain, swelling, or tenderness in the abdomen (possible gallbladder problem).

content.summary: Progesterone 125 mg capsules are a prescription hormone. Their reference labeling, for 100 mg and 200 mg PROMETRIUM capsules rather than this one, covers preventing endometrial hyperplasia (overgrowth of the uterine lining) in women after menopause who still have a uterus and take conjugated estrogens tablets, and secondary amenorrhea (periods that have stopped). Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These capsules are listed at 125 mg of progesterone, a prescription hormone. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information cited here describes 100 mg and 200 mg capsules of micronized progesterone made with peanut oil; it does not describe this capsule, and the listing does not say whether this capsule's progesterone is micronized or what its vehicle is. PROMETRIUM is labeled for preventing endometrial hyperplasia (overgrowth of the uterine lining) in women after menopause who still have a uterus and take conjugated estrogens tablets, and for secondary amenorrhea (periods that have stopped); it is not for children. Because PROMETRIUM capsules are made with peanut oil, that labeling rules them out for people allergic to peanuts; the listing does not state this capsule's ingredients. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed at 125 mg of progesterone. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the reference label cited here, describes capsules containing 100 mg or 200 mg of micronized progesterone with peanut oil among their inactive ingredients. 125 mg is not a strength it describes, and the listing does not state whether this capsule's progesterone is micronized, what its vehicle is or how it is prepared, so the label's statements describe PROMETRIUM capsules and do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. According to the PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the progesterone in PROMETRIUM capsules is synthesized from a starting material from a plant source and is chemically identical to progesterone of human ovarian origin, and the oral bioavailability of progesterone is increased through micronization. For PROMETRIUM's micronized soft-gelatin capsules, it reports that maximum serum concentrations were attained within 3 hours after oral administration, and that the absolute bioavailability of micronized progesterone is not known. It states that progesterone is approximately 96 percent to 99 percent bound to serum proteins, that it is metabolized primarily by the liver largely to pregnanediols and pregnanolones, and that its metabolites are eliminated mainly by the kidneys. The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules are indicated for use in the prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets, and also for use in secondary amenorrhea. It notes that the effect of hepatic impairment and of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of PROMETRIUM capsules has not been studied. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule, how it is prepared, or whether its progesterone is micronized or its vehicle contains peanut oil as PROMETRIUM capsules do; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (PROMETRIUM prescribing information), which describe PROMETRIUM capsules of 100 mg or 200 mg micronized progesterone and not this capsule: prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets; and secondary amenorrhea. The labeling also states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The PROMETRIUM prescribing information contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with hypersensitivity to its ingredients and, because PROMETRIUM capsules contain peanut oil, in patients allergic to peanuts; this listing does not state the capsule's ingredients or vehicle.

It also contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with abnormal genital bleeding of unknown etiology; known, suspected, or history of breast cancer; active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease (for example, stroke and myocardial infarction) or a history of these conditions; or known liver dysfunction or disease.

Its warnings state that PROMETRIUM should be immediately discontinued if a pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction occurs or is suspected, and that, if feasible, it should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization.

The labeling states that the safety and efficacy of estrogen plus progestogen for the prevention of cardiovascular disorders has not been established, and that the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin trial reported increased risks of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke and myocardial infarction in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age, average age 63.4 years) during 5.6 years of treatment with daily oral conjugated estrogens (0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (2.5 mg), relative to placebo.

It states that only daily oral 0.625 mg conjugated estrogens and 2.5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate were studied in that trial, so the relevance of the WHI findings regarding adverse cardiovascular events to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, and that without such data it is not possible to definitively exclude these risks or determine their extent for other products.

For venous thromboembolism in the overall WHI study population, the labeling reports a relative risk for pulmonary embolism of 1.98 (95% CI, 1.36, 2.87) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (18 versus 9), and a relative risk for deep vein thrombosis of 1.87 (95% CI, 1.37, 2.54), with a risk difference of 12 per 10,000 women-years (25 versus 14).

For the overall WHI population it also reports a relative risk for stroke of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.07, 1.76) with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (33 versus 24), and a relative risk of coronary heart disease of 1.18 (95% CI, 0.95, 1.45) with a risk difference of 6 per 10,000 women-years (41 versus 35), for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo.

Its breast cancer warning states that PROMETRIUM is contraindicated in women with breast cancer, a history of breast cancer, or estrogen-dependent neoplasia, that PROMETRIUM should be discontinued if a hormone-sensitive malignancy is diagnosed, and that the use of estrogen plus progestin therapy has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation.

In the overall WHI population, the labeling reports a relative risk for invasive breast cancer of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01, 1.53) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (43 versus 35); it states that invasive breast cancers were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage in that group, and that the trial did not show a statistically significant difference in breast cancer mortality.

It adds that, consistent with the WHI trial, observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy, and that a large meta-analysis including 24 prospective studies of postmenopausal women comparing current use of estrogen plus progestin products for 5 to 14 years (average of 9 years) versus never use reported a relative risk for breast cancer of 2.08 (95% CI, 2.02 to 2.15). It states that these studies have not generally found significant variation in the risk of breast cancer among different estrogen plus progestin combinations, doses, or routes of administration, and that the relevance of the WHI findings regarding breast cancer to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, so that these risks cannot be definitively excluded or their extent determined for other products.

Its ovarian cancer warning reports, for the overall WHI population, a relative risk for ovarian cancer of 1.41 (95% CI, 0.75 to 2.66) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate versus placebo after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, with a risk difference of 1 per 10,000 women-years (5 versus 4), and a large meta-analysis of 17 prospective studies of postmenopausal women reporting a relative risk of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.26 to 1.48) for current use of estrogen plus progestin products versus never use; it states that the duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown.

Its vision warning states that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogen, that estrogen plus progestin therapy should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that it should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions.

Its precautions state that progesterone may cause some degree of fluid retention, so women with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation.

They also state that PROMETRIUM capsules may cause transient dizziness and drowsiness and should be used with caution when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery; the patient information adds that some women may experience extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness during initial therapy, in a few cases with blurred vision, difficulty speaking, difficulty with walking and feeling abnormal, and says to discuss these symptoms with the healthcare provider right away.

Its drug-interaction section reports that the metabolism of progesterone by human liver microsomes was inhibited by ketoconazole, a known inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, so these data suggest that ketoconazole or other known inhibitors of this enzyme may increase the bioavailability of progesterone, and that the clinical relevance of the in vitro findings is unknown.

It reports that coadministration of conjugated estrogens and PROMETRIUM capsules to 29 postmenopausal women over a 12-day period increased total estrone and total equilin concentrations and decreased circulating 17β estradiol concentrations, while the half-life of the conjugated estrogens was similar with coadministration.

Its precautions also list laboratory results that may be altered by estrogen plus progestin therapy: increased sulfobromophthalein retention and other hepatic function tests; coagulation tests (an increase in prothrombin factors VII, VIII, IX and X); pregnanediol determination; and thyroid function (an increase in PBI and butanol extractable protein bound iodine and a decrease in T3 uptake values).

Its precautions state that exogenously administered progesterone has been shown to inhibit ovulation in a number of species, and that high doses given for an extended duration are expected to impair fertility until the cessation of treatment.

The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules should not be used during pregnancy, and its patient information lists, among serious but less common side effects, risk to the fetus: cases of cleft palate, cleft lip, hypospadias, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, and other congenital heart defects.

It states that detectable amounts of progestin have been identified in the milk of nursing women receiving progestins, that caution should be exercised when PROMETRIUM capsules are administered to a nursing woman, and, in the patient information, that the hormone in PROMETRIUM capsules can pass into breast milk.

It states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children, that clinical studies have not been conducted in the pediatric population, and that there have not been sufficient numbers of geriatric women in clinical studies to determine whether those over 65 years of age differ from younger subjects in their response.

For women over 65, it reports that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy showed a higher relative risk of nonfatal stroke and invasive breast cancer. It also reports that the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study of postmenopausal women 65 to 79 years of age found an increased risk of developing probable dementia with estrogen plus progestin compared to placebo (after an average follow-up of 4 years, a relative risk of 2.05, 95 percent CI 1.21 to 3.48, and an absolute risk of 45 versus 22 per 10,000 women-years), and that it is unknown whether these findings apply to younger postmenopausal women.

Its table of adverse reactions comes from a 3-year, placebo-controlled trial of cyclic PROMETRIUM capsules 200 mg with conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg in postmenopausal women (875 women studied; the table's arms are n = 178 and placebo n = 174) and lists the reactions reported by 2% or more of women. Those are headache (31% versus 27% on placebo), breast tenderness (27% versus 6%), joint pain (20% versus 29%), depression (19% versus 12%), dizziness (15% versus 9%), abdominal bloating (12% versus 5%), hot flashes (11% versus 35%), urinary problems (11% versus 9%), abdominal pain (10% versus 10%), vaginal discharge (10% versus 3%), nausea or vomiting (8% versus 7%), worry (8% versus 4%), chest pain (7% versus 5%), diarrhea (7% versus 4%), night sweats (7% versus 17%), breast pain (6% versus 2%), swelling of hands and feet (6% versus 9%), vaginal dryness (6% versus 10%), constipation (3% versus 2%), and breast carcinoma, breast excisional biopsy and cholecystectomy (2% each versus less than 1%).

In a placebo-controlled trial of PROMETRIUM capsules at 400 mg/day in 49 estrogen-primed postmenopausal women, its table of adverse reactions reported by 5% or more lists fatigue (8% versus 4% on placebo), headache (16% versus 8%), dizziness (24% versus 4%), abdominal distention or bloating (8% versus 8%), abdominal pain or cramping (20% versus 13%), diarrhea (8% versus 4%), nausea (8% versus 0%), back pain (8% versus 8%), musculoskeletal pain (12% versus 4%), irritability (8% versus 4%), breast pain (16% versus 8%), viral infection (12% versus 0%) and coughing (8% versus 0%).

In an open-label postmarketing study of 220 premenopausal women with secondary amenorrhea who received conjugated estrogens with PROMETRIUM capsules, the labeling lists the most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse reactions (5% or more) as nausea, fatigue, vaginal mycosis, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness, abdominal distension, acne, dysmenorrhea, mood swing, and urinary tract infection.

Among additional adverse reactions reported with PROMETRIUM capsules after marketing, which the labeling notes are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size so that their frequency or a causal relationship to drug exposure cannot always be reliably established, it lists genitourinary reactions (endometrial carcinoma, hypospadia, intra-uterine death, menorrhagia, menstrual disorder, metrorrhagia, ovarian cyst, spontaneous abortion) and cardiovascular reactions (circulatory collapse, congenital heart disease including ventricular septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus, hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia).

It also lists gastrointestinal reactions (acute pancreatitis, cholestasis, cholestatic hepatitis, dysphagia, hepatic failure, hepatic necrosis, hepatitis, increased liver function tests, jaundice, swollen tongue), skin reactions (alopecia, pruritus, urticaria) and eye reactions (blurred vision, diplopia, visual disturbance).

Its central nervous system list includes aggression, convulsion, depersonalization, depressed consciousness, disorientation, dysarthria, loss of consciousness, paresthesia, sedation, stupor, syncope (with and without hypotension), transient ischemic attack and suicidal ideation, and it notes that during initial therapy a few women have experienced a constellation of many or all of the following: extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness, blurred vision, slurred speech, difficulty walking, loss of consciousness, vertigo, confusion, disorientation, feeling drunk, and shortness of breath.

Among miscellaneous postmarketing reactions it lists abnormal gait, anaphylactic reaction, arthralgia, blood glucose increased, choking, cleft lip, cleft palate, difficulty walking, dyspnea, face edema, feeling abnormal, feeling drunk, hypersensitivity, asthma, muscle cramp, throat tightness, tinnitus and vertigo, among others.

Its patient information lists abnormal blood clotting (stroke, heart attack, pulmonary embolus, visual loss or blindness) among serious but less common side effects, gives changes in vision or speech, sudden new severe headaches, severe pains in the chest or legs with or without shortness of breath, weakness and fatigue, dizziness and faintness, and vomiting as warning signs of serious side effects, and says to call the healthcare provider right away for any of these warning signs or any other unusual symptoms that concern the patient.

Its patient information lists these less serious but common side effects: headaches; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach or abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; hair loss; fluid retention; and vaginal yeast infection.

Its patient information advises seeing the healthcare provider right away for unusual vaginal bleeding while taking PROMETRIUM capsules. It advises a pelvic exam, breast exam and mammogram every year unless the healthcare provider says otherwise, and says that women whose family members have had breast cancer, or who have ever had breast lumps or an abnormal mammogram, may need breast exams more often. It also advises telling the healthcare provider about all medical problems, since closer checks may be needed with conditions such as asthma, epilepsy, diabetes, migraine, endometriosis, lupus, problems with the heart, liver, thyroid or kidneys, or high calcium levels in the blood, and about all medicines taken, including nonprescription medicines, vitamins and herbal supplements, since some medicines may affect how PROMETRIUM capsules work and PROMETRIUM capsules may affect how other medicines work.

content.summary: Tadalafil 24 mg capsules, a prescription capsule form of tadalafil, a PDE5 inhibitor. CIALIS labeling, written for 5, 10 and 20 mg tablets and not this capsule, says tadalafil helps blood flow into the penis during sexual stimulation and covers erectile dysfunction and enlarged-prostate symptoms (BPH). Clinical review required.
content.overview:
Each capsule is listed at 24 mg of tadalafil, a PDE5 inhibitor; a capsule is a different form from the CIALIS tablets cited here. According to the CIALIS prescribing information, sexual stimulation releases nitric oxide, which relaxes smooth muscle so more blood flows into the penis; blocking PDE5 strengthens this, and the effect needs sexual stimulation. CIALIS is labeled for erectile dysfunction (ED), for the signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH, an enlarged prostate), and for both together. That labeling describes 5, 10 and 20 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed at 24 mg of tadalafil, a phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) inhibitor. A capsule is a different dosage form from the tablets covered by the CIALIS prescribing information cited here. According to the CIALIS prescribing information, erection during sexual stimulation comes from increased penile blood flow: nitric oxide released from nerve terminals and endothelial cells stimulates cGMP synthesis in smooth muscle cells, and cGMP relaxes that muscle so more blood flows into the corpus cavernosum. Inhibiting PDE5 enhances erectile function by increasing the amount of cGMP, and because sexual stimulation is needed to start the local release of nitric oxide, this erectile effect requires sexual stimulation. The CIALIS prescribing information describes CIALIS tablets in 5, 10 and 20 mg strengths and indicates CIALIS for erectile dysfunction, for the signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia, and for both together. content.overview:
The catalog lists each capsule as sildenafil 110 mg, a PDE5 inhibitor; a capsule is a different form from the VIAGRA tablets cited here. The listing does not say what “SR” stands for or how the capsule releases sildenafil. According to the VIAGRA prescribing information, sexual stimulation releases nitric oxide, which relaxes smooth muscle so blood can flow into the penis; sildenafil strengthens this by blocking PDE5 and, at the doses the label recommends for VIAGRA tablets, has no effect without sexual stimulation. VIAGRA is labeled for the treatment of erectile dysfunction. That labeling describes 25, 50 and 100 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

The catalog lists each capsule as sildenafil 110 mg. Sildenafil is a selective inhibitor of cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5). A capsule is a different dosage form from the film-coated tablets covered by the VIAGRA prescribing information cited here. The catalog name for this capsule includes “SR”; the listing does not say what that stands for or how the capsule releases sildenafil, and this page makes no claim about its release profile. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. It reports prolonged erections lasting more than 4 hours and priapism, and states that a patient with an erection that persists longer than 4 hours should seek immediate medical assistance, because priapism that is not treated immediately could result in penile tissue damage and permanent loss of potency.
