content.summary: Anastrozole 1 mg tablets are a prescription medicine that lowers estrogen by blocking the aromatase enzyme. ARIMIDEX's labeling covers certain breast cancers in women after menopause, and its patient information states that ARIMIDEX does not work in women with breast cancer who have not gone through menopause. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
Anastrozole 1 mg tablets are a prescription medicine called an aromatase inhibitor. According to the ARIMIDEX prescribing information, many breast cancers grow in response to estrogen, which after menopause comes mainly from the aromatase enzyme; anastrozole blocks that enzyme and lowers estradiol, an estrogen. ARIMIDEX is labeled for certain breast cancers in women after menopause, including early hormone receptor-positive breast cancer and advanced breast cancer, and its patient information states that ARIMIDEX does not work in women with breast cancer who have not gone through menopause. This listing does not name the tablet's maker; the dispensed product's own label governs. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each tablet is listed at 1 mg of anastrozole, a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor. According to the ARIMIDEX prescribing information, the growth of many breast cancers is stimulated or maintained by estrogens, and in postmenopausal women estrogens come mainly from the aromatase enzyme, which converts adrenal androgens (primarily androstenedione and testosterone) to estrone and estradiol. The same labeling describes anastrozole as a selective non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor that significantly lowers serum estradiol concentrations and has no detectable effect on the formation of adrenal corticosteroids or aldosterone. The ARIMIDEX prescribing information indicates ARIMIDEX for adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer, for first-line treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive or hormone receptor-unknown locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer, and for treatment of advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease progression following tamoxifen therapy. It notes that patients with estrogen receptor-negative disease, and patients who did not respond to previous tamoxifen therapy, rarely responded to ARIMIDEX. Its patient information states that ARIMIDEX does not work in women with breast cancer who have not gone through menopause. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state the tablet's manufacturer or whether it is a brand or generic product; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (ARIMIDEX prescribing information): adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer; first-line treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive or hormone receptor-unknown locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer; and treatment of advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease progression following tamoxifen therapy; the labeling notes that patients with estrogen receptor-negative disease and patients who did not respond to previous tamoxifen therapy rarely responded to ARIMIDEX. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The ARIMIDEX prescribing information contraindicates ARIMIDEX in any patient who has shown a hypersensitivity reaction to the drug or to any of its excipients; observed reactions include anaphylaxis, angioedema and urticaria.

Based on findings from animal studies and its mechanism of action, the labeling states that ARIMIDEX can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman, and it notes that there are no studies of ARIMIDEX use in pregnant women; it advises verifying the pregnancy status of females of reproductive potential before starting and using effective contraception during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose, and it advises females to contact their healthcare provider if they become pregnant, or if pregnancy is suspected, during treatment.

Based on studies in female animals, the labeling says ARIMIDEX may impair fertility in females of reproductive potential.

It advises lactating women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 2 weeks after the last dose.

It states that tamoxifen should not be administered with anastrozole, and that estrogen-containing therapies should not be used with ARIMIDEX because they may diminish its pharmacological action.

The labeling reports that in the ATAC trial, women with pre-existing ischemic heart disease had more ischemic cardiovascular events on ARIMIDEX than on tamoxifen (17% versus 10%), and it advises considering the risks and benefits of ARIMIDEX therapy in these patients.

Its patient counseling information says to inform patients of the possibility of serious allergic reactions with swelling of the face, lips, tongue and/or throat, which may cause difficulty in swallowing and/or breathing, and to seek medical attention immediately; it also says that patients with pre-existing ischemic heart disease should be informed that an increased incidence of cardiovascular events has been observed with ARIMIDEX use compared to tamoxifen use, and it advises patients to seek medical attention immediately if new or worsening chest pain or shortness of breath occurs.

It reports that patients receiving ARIMIDEX in the ATAC bone substudy had mean decreases in lumbar spine and total hip bone mineral density, and it advises considering bone mineral density monitoring; it also reports that more patients on ARIMIDEX than on tamoxifen had elevated serum cholesterol (9% versus 3.5%), and its patient counseling information says to inform patients that an increased level of cholesterol might be seen while receiving ARIMIDEX.

It also reports that in the adjuvant trial patients receiving ARIMIDEX had an increase in the incidence of all fractures (specifically fractures of the spine, hip and wrist), 10% versus 7% on tamoxifen, and its patient counseling information notes that a possible consequence of decreased mineral content of bones is an increase in the risk of fractures.

The labeling lists the serious adverse reactions occurring in fewer than 1 in 10,000 patients as skin reactions such as lesions, ulcers or blisters; allergic reactions with swelling of the face, lips, tongue and/or throat, which may cause difficulty swallowing and/or breathing; and changes in liver function blood tests, including inflammation of the liver.

Its patient information says to stop taking ARIMIDEX and call the healthcare provider right away for any skin lesions, ulcers or blisters, or for signs or symptoms of a liver problem such as a general feeling of not being well, yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, or pain on the right side of the stomach area.

It lists the common adverse reactions (10% or more) in women taking ARIMIDEX as hot flashes, asthenia, arthritis, pain, arthralgia, hypertension, depression, nausea and vomiting, rash, osteoporosis, fractures, back pain, insomnia, headache, bone pain, peripheral edema, increased cough, dyspnea, pharyngitis and lymphedema.

The labeling reports that in the adjuvant trial, patients receiving ARIMIDEX had a higher incidence of carpal tunnel syndrome (2.5%) than patients receiving tamoxifen (0.7%), and it says patients should be informed that if they experience tickling, tingling or numbness they should notify their health care provider.

Post-marketing reports, which the labeling says come from a population of uncertain size and cannot always be used to estimate frequency or establish causation, include hepatobiliary events (increases in alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, gamma-GT and bilirubin; hepatitis), rash including erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, allergic reactions including angioedema, urticaria and anaphylaxis, myalgia and hypercalcemia (with or without an increase in parathyroid hormone), and tendon disorders including tendon rupture, tendonitis, tenosynovitis and trigger finger.

content.summary: Clomiphene 25 mg capsules, a prescription nonsteroidal ovulatory stimulant. The CLOMID labeling, written for 50 mg tablets and not this capsule, covers ovulation problems in women who want to become pregnant and states that no adequate studies show it works for male infertility. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These capsules are listed at 25 mg of clomiphene, a prescription ovulatory stimulant. According to the CLOMID prescribing information, clomiphene may compete with estrogen at receptors in the brain and reproductive organs, and it starts a chain of hormone events, beginning with more pituitary hormone release, that ends in ovulation. CLOMID is labeled for ovulatory dysfunction in women who want to become pregnant, after other barriers to pregnancy are ruled out or treated, and must not be used during pregnancy. The labeling states that no adequate studies show it works for male infertility, and it describes 50 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed at 25 mg of clomiphene, a nonsteroidal ovulatory stimulant. A capsule is a different dosage form from the tablets covered by the CLOMID prescribing information cited here, which describes 50 mg tablets of clomiphene citrate; the statements below describe those tablets and do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. According to the CLOMID prescribing information, clomiphene citrate is capable of interacting with estrogen-receptor-containing tissues, including the hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary, endometrium, vagina and cervix, and it may compete with estrogen for estrogen-receptor-binding sites and may delay replenishment of intracellular estrogen receptors. The same labeling states that clomiphene citrate initiates a series of endocrine events culminating in a preovulatory gonadotropin surge and subsequent follicular rupture, beginning with an increase in the release of pituitary gonadotropins. It states that clomiphene citrate is a mixture of two geometric isomers, cis (zuclomiphene) and trans (enclomiphene), containing between 30% and 50% of the cis-isomer, and that the two isomers have been found to have mixed estrogenic and antiestrogenic effects, which may vary from one species to another. It also states that clomiphene citrate has no apparent progestational, androgenic or antiandrogenic effects and does not appear to interfere with pituitary-adrenal or pituitary-thyroid function. The CLOMID prescribing information indicates clomiphene citrate for the treatment of ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy, only in patients with demonstrated ovulatory dysfunction who are not pregnant, are without ovarian cysts (it should not be used in patients with ovarian enlargement except those with polycystic ovary syndrome), are without abnormal vaginal bleeding and have normal liver function; it states that impediments to achieving pregnancy must be excluded or adequately treated before beginning therapy. It states that there are no adequate or well-controlled studies that demonstrate the effectiveness of clomiphene citrate in the treatment of male infertility, that testicular tumors and gynecomastia have been reported in males using clomiphene and that the cause and effect relationship between reports of testicular tumors and the administration of clomiphene citrate is not known, and that clomiphene citrate is not recommended for combined therapy with other ovulation-inducing drugs or for ovulation induction in in vitro fertilization programs, for which no standard regimen exists. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule, how it is prepared, or whether its clomiphene is the citrate salt described in the CLOMID prescribing information; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indication (CLOMID prescribing information), which describes clomiphene citrate tablets and not this capsule: treatment of ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy, only in patients with demonstrated ovulatory dysfunction who are not pregnant, without ovarian cysts (other than polycystic ovary syndrome), without abnormal vaginal bleeding and with normal liver function, after impediments to achieving pregnancy have been excluded or adequately treated. The labeling adds that patients should have adequate levels of endogenous estrogen, although reduced estrogen levels, while less favorable, do not preclude successful therapy, and that the patients most likely to achieve success include those with polycystic ovary syndrome, amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome, psychogenic amenorrhea, post-oral-contraceptive amenorrhea and certain cases of secondary amenorrhea of undetermined etiology. It states that therapy cannot be expected to substitute for specific treatment of other causes of ovulatory failure, such as primary pituitary or ovarian failure. It also states that there are no adequate or well-controlled studies demonstrating effectiveness in the treatment of male infertility, and that clomiphene citrate is not recommended for combined therapy with other ovulation-inducing drugs or for ovulation induction in in vitro fertilization programs. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The CLOMID prescribing information contraindicates clomiphene citrate in patients with a known hypersensitivity or allergy to clomiphene citrate or to any of its ingredients; in pregnant women, because it does not offer benefit in this population; in patients with liver disease or a history of liver dysfunction; in patients with abnormal uterine bleeding of undetermined origin; in patients with ovarian cysts or enlargement not due to polycystic ovarian syndrome; and in patients with uncontrolled thyroid or adrenal dysfunction or in the presence of an organic intracranial lesion such as pituitary tumor.

On pregnancy, it states that available human data do not suggest an increased risk for congenital anomalies above the background population risk when used as indicated, that animal reproductive toxicology studies showed increased embryo-fetal loss and structural malformations in offspring, and that if the drug is used during pregnancy, or if the patient becomes pregnant while taking it, the patient should be apprised of the potential risks to the fetus; it adds that appropriate tests should be used during each treatment cycle to determine whether ovulation and/or pregnancy occurs, to avoid inadvertent administration during early pregnancy.

Its pharmacokinetics section states that in single-dose studies in normal volunteers detectable levels of zuclomiphene persisted for longer than a month, so it is possible that some active drug may remain in the body during early pregnancy in women who conceive in the menstrual cycle during clomiphene citrate therapy.

Its visual symptoms warning states that blurring or other visual symptoms such as spots or flashes (scintillating scotomata) may occasionally occur during therapy, that these symptoms increase in incidence with increasing total dose or therapy duration, that they are usually reversible but that cases of prolonged visual disturbance have been reported, some occurring after discontinuation, and that the visual disturbances may be irreversible, especially with increased dosage or duration of therapy.

It warns that these visual symptoms may render activities such as driving a car or operating machinery more hazardous than usual, particularly under conditions of variable lighting, and states that patients with any visual symptoms should discontinue treatment and have a complete ophthalmological evaluation carried out promptly.

Its ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome warning states that OHSS has been reported in patients receiving clomiphene citrate therapy for ovulation induction, that it may progress rapidly (within 24 hours to several days) and become a serious medical disorder, that in some cases it occurred following cyclic use or when clomiphene citrate was used in combination with gonadotropins, and that transient liver function test abnormalities suggestive of hepatic dysfunction have been reported in association with OHSS.

It gives abdominal pain and distention, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and weight gain as the early warning signs of OHSS, and states that death due to hypovolemic shock, hemoconcentration or thromboembolism has occurred.

It describes the clinical signs of severe cases as gross ovarian enlargement, gastrointestinal symptoms, ascites, dyspnea, oliguria and pleural effusion, with pericardial effusion, anasarca, hydrothorax, acute abdomen, hypotension, renal failure, pulmonary edema, intraperitoneal and ovarian hemorrhage, deep venous thrombosis, torsion of the ovary and acute respiratory distress also reported.

It states that if conception results, rapid progression to the severe form of the syndrome may occur; that, due to the fragility of enlarged ovaries in severe cases, abdominal and pelvic examination should be performed very cautiously; and that some patients with polycystic ovary syndrome who are unusually sensitive to gonadotropin may have an exaggerated response to usual doses of clomiphene citrate.

It states that if enlargement of the ovary occurs, additional clomiphene citrate therapy should not be given until the ovaries have returned to pretreatment size, that maximal enlargement of the ovary, whether physiologic or abnormal, may not occur until several days after discontinuation, that ovarian enlargement and cyst formation associated with therapy usually regress spontaneously within a few days or weeks after discontinuing treatment, and that if ovarian cysts do not regress spontaneously a thorough evaluation should be performed to rule out the presence of ovarian neoplasia.

It states that a causal relationship between ovarian hyperstimulation and ovarian cancer has not been determined, and that prolonged use of clomiphene citrate tablets may increase the risk of a borderline or invasive ovarian tumor.

Its information for patients says that the patient should be instructed to inform the physician whenever any unusual visual symptoms occur, and to inform the physician of any abdominal or pelvic pain, weight gain, discomfort or distention after taking clomiphene citrate.

It reports cases of hypertriglyceridemia, states that pre-existing or family history of hyperlipidemia and use of higher than recommended dose and/or longer duration of treatment are associated with a risk of hypertriglyceridemia, recommends periodic monitoring of plasma triglycerides in patients with pre-existing or family history of hyperlipidemia and pretreatment screening of triglyceride levels, and reports cases of pancreatitis.

It advises informing the patient that there is an increased chance of multiple pregnancy, including bilateral tubal pregnancy and coexisting tubal and intrauterine pregnancy, when conception occurs in relation to clomiphene citrate therapy; in its clinical trials the incidence of multiple pregnancies among reported pregnancies was 7.98% (6.9% twin, 0.5% triplet, 0.3% quadruplet, 0.1% quintuplet).

It advises informing the patient that the available data suggest no increase in the rates of spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) or congenital anomalies with maternal clomiphene citrate use compared to rates in the general population, while noting that among birth anomalies spontaneously reported since commercial availability the proportion of neural tube defects has been high among pregnancies associated with ovulation induced by clomiphene citrate, which has not been supported by data from population-based studies.

It states that drug interactions with clomiphene citrate have not been documented.

It states that it is not known whether clomiphene citrate is excreted in human milk, that caution should be exercised if it is administered to a nursing woman, and that in some patients it may reduce lactation.

It advises caution in patients with uterine fibroids due to the potential for further enlargement of the fibroids; states that, because the incidence of endometriosis and endometrial carcinoma increases with age, as does the incidence of ovulatory disorders, endometrial biopsy should always be performed prior to therapy in this population; states that pelvic examination is necessary prior to the first and each subsequent course of treatment; and states that if abnormal vaginal bleeding is present, the patient should be carefully evaluated to ensure that neoplastic lesions are not present.

The labeling states that testicular tumors and gynecomastia have been reported in males using clomiphene, and that the cause and effect relationship between reports of testicular tumors and the administration of clomiphene citrate is not known.

In clinical studies (n = 8029), the adverse events the labeling reports in more than 1% of patients were ovarian enlargement (13.6%), vasomotor flushes (10.4%), abdominal-pelvic discomfort, distention or bloating (5.5%), nausea and vomiting (2.2%), breast discomfort (2.1%), visual symptoms (1.5%; blurred vision, lights, floaters, waves, unspecified visual complaints, photophobia, diplopia, scotomata, phosphenes), headache (1.3%) and abnormal uterine bleeding (1.3%; intermenstrual spotting, menorrhagia).

Postmarketing reports, which the labeling says come from a population of uncertain size and cannot always be used to estimate frequency or establish causation, include pulmonary embolism, thrombophlebitis, stroke, seizure, erythema multiforme, pancreatitis, hepatitis and increased transaminases, ovarian hemorrhage, tubal pregnancy, psychosis, and visual disorders including cataract, optic neuritis, retinal thrombosis and temporary or prolonged loss of vision, possibly irreversible; neoplasms, including ovarian, endometrial, breast and liver tumors, have also been reported, as have fetal and neonatal anomalies including skeletal and cardiac malformations and neural tube defects.

Its ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome warning states that OHSS has been reported in patients receiving clomiphene citrate therapy for ovulation induction, that it may progress rapidly (within 24 hours to several days) and become a serious medical disorder, that in some cases it occurred following cyclic use or when clomiphene citrate was used in combination with gonadotropins, and that transient liver function test abnormalities suggestive of hepatic dysfunction have been reported in association with OHSS.

It gives abdominal pain and distention, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and weight gain as the early warning signs of OHSS, and states that death due to hypovolemic shock, hemoconcentration or thromboembolism has occurred.

It describes the clinical signs of severe cases as gross ovarian enlargement, gastrointestinal symptoms, ascites, dyspnea, oliguria and pleural effusion, with pericardial effusion, anasarca, hydrothorax, acute abdomen, hypotension, renal failure, pulmonary edema, intraperitoneal and ovarian hemorrhage, deep venous thrombosis, torsion of the ovary and acute respiratory distress also reported.

It states that if conception results, rapid progression to the severe form of the syndrome may occur; that, due to the fragility of enlarged ovaries in severe cases, abdominal and pelvic examination should be performed very cautiously; and that some patients with polycystic ovary syndrome who are unusually sensitive to gonadotropin may have an exaggerated response to usual doses of clomiphene citrate.

It states that if enlargement of the ovary occurs, additional clomiphene citrate therapy should not be given until the ovaries have returned to pretreatment size, that maximal enlargement of the ovary, whether physiologic or abnormal, may not occur until several days after discontinuation, that ovarian enlargement and cyst formation associated with therapy usually regress spontaneously within a few days or weeks after discontinuing treatment, and that if ovarian cysts do not regress spontaneously a thorough evaluation should be performed to rule out the presence of ovarian neoplasia.

It states that a causal relationship between ovarian hyperstimulation and ovarian cancer has not been determined, and that prolonged use of clomiphene citrate tablets may increase the risk of a borderline or invasive ovarian tumor.

Its information for patients says that the patient should be instructed to inform the physician whenever any unusual visual symptoms occur, and to inform the physician of any abdominal or pelvic pain, weight gain, discomfort or distention after taking clomiphene citrate.

It reports cases of hypertriglyceridemia, states that pre-existing or family history of hyperlipidemia and use of higher than recommended dose and/or longer duration of treatment are associated with a risk of hypertriglyceridemia, recommends periodic monitoring of plasma triglycerides in patients with pre-existing or family history of hyperlipidemia and pretreatment screening of triglyceride levels, and reports cases of pancreatitis.

It advises informing the patient that there is an increased chance of multiple pregnancy, including bilateral tubal pregnancy and coexisting tubal and intrauterine pregnancy, when conception occurs in relation to clomiphene citrate therapy; in its clinical trials the incidence of multiple pregnancies among reported pregnancies was 7.98% (6.9% twin, 0.5% triplet, 0.3% quadruplet, 0.1% quintuplet).

It advises informing the patient that the available data suggest no increase in the rates of spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) or congenital anomalies with maternal clomiphene citrate use compared to rates in the general population, while noting that among birth anomalies spontaneously reported since commercial availability the proportion of neural tube defects has been high among pregnancies associated with ovulation induced by clomiphene citrate, which has not been supported by data from population-based studies.

It states that drug interactions with clomiphene citrate have not been documented.

It states that it is not known whether clomiphene citrate is excreted in human milk, that caution should be exercised if it is administered to a nursing woman, and that in some patients it may reduce lactation.

It advises caution in patients with uterine fibroids due to the potential for further enlargement of the fibroids; states that, because the incidence of endometriosis and endometrial carcinoma increases with age, as does the incidence of ovulatory disorders, endometrial biopsy should always be performed prior to therapy in this population; states that pelvic examination is necessary prior to the first and each subsequent course of treatment; and states that if abnormal vaginal bleeding is present, the patient should be carefully evaluated to ensure that neoplastic lesions are not present.

The labeling states that testicular tumors and gynecomastia have been reported in males using clomiphene, and that the cause and effect relationship between reports of testicular tumors and the administration of clomiphene citrate is not known.

In clinical studies (n = 8029), the adverse events the labeling reports in more than 1% of patients were ovarian enlargement (13.6%), vasomotor flushes (10.4%), abdominal-pelvic discomfort, distention or bloating (5.5%), nausea and vomiting (2.2%), breast discomfort (2.1%), visual symptoms (1.5%; blurred vision, lights, floaters, waves, unspecified visual complaints, photophobia, diplopia, scotomata, phosphenes), headache (1.3%) and abnormal uterine bleeding (1.3%; intermenstrual spotting, menorrhagia).

Postmarketing reports, which the labeling says come from a population of uncertain size and cannot always be used to estimate frequency or establish causation, include pulmonary embolism, thrombophlebitis, stroke, seizure, erythema multiforme, pancreatitis, hepatitis and increased transaminases, ovarian hemorrhage, tubal pregnancy, psychosis, and visual disorders including cataract, optic neuritis, retinal thrombosis and temporary or prolonged loss of vision, possibly irreversible; neoplasms, including ovarian, endometrial, breast and liver tumors, have also been reported, as have fetal and neonatal anomalies including skeletal and cardiac malformations and neural tube defects.

content.summary: Estradiol 1.25 mg capsules are a prescription estrogen. The estradiol tablets labeling, written for tablets and not this capsule, covers moderate to severe hot flashes and vulvar and vaginal atrophy symptoms of menopause, among other uses, and warns that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These capsules are listed at 1.25 mg of estradiol, a prescription estrogen. The labeling calls estradiol the principal human estrogen inside cells; estrogens act through receptors in the body's tissues and lower the high levels of the pituitary hormones LH and FSH seen after menopause. The estradiol tablets labeling covers moderate to severe hot flashes (vasomotor symptoms) and vulvar and vaginal atrophy symptoms of menopause, low estrogen from certain causes, prevention of osteoporosis in some women, and relief (palliation only) of some advanced cancers. Its boxed warning states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer (cancer of the uterine lining), and the labeling also addresses heart and other risks. That labeling describes 0.5, 1 and 2 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed at 1.25 mg of estradiol, an estrogen. A capsule is a different dosage form from the tablets covered by the estradiol tablets prescribing information cited here, which describes 0.5, 1 and 2 mg tablets of micronized estradiol; the statements below describe those tablets and do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. The same labeling states that estradiol is the principal intracellular human estrogen, that estrogens act through binding to nuclear receptors in estrogen-responsive tissues, and that two estrogen receptors have been identified to date, which vary in proportion from tissue to tissue. It adds that circulating estrogens modulate the pituitary secretion of the gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), through a negative feedback mechanism, and that estrogens act to reduce the elevated levels of these hormones seen in postmenopausal women. The same labeling lists as indications the treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms associated with the menopause, the treatment of moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy associated with the menopause, and the treatment of hypoestrogenism due to hypogonadism, castration or primary ovarian failure; it states that when prescribing solely for the treatment of symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy, topical vaginal products should be considered. Its other listed indications are the treatment of breast cancer (for palliation only) in appropriately selected women and men with metastatic disease, the treatment of advanced androgen-dependent carcinoma of the prostate (for palliation only), and the prevention of osteoporosis; it states that when prescribing solely for the prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, therapy should only be considered for women at significant risk of osteoporosis and for whom non-estrogen medications are not considered to be appropriate. Its boxed warning states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer, and it also addresses cardiovascular and other risks, including findings from the Women’s Health Initiative studies. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule, how it is prepared, or whether its estradiol is micronized as described in the estradiol tablets prescribing information; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (estradiol tablets prescribing information), which describe estradiol tablets and not this capsule: treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms associated with the menopause; treatment of moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy associated with the menopause; treatment of hypoestrogenism due to hypogonadism, castration or primary ovarian failure; treatment of breast cancer (for palliation only) in appropriately selected women and men with metastatic disease; treatment of advanced androgen-dependent carcinoma of the prostate (for palliation only); and prevention of osteoporosis. For vulvar and vaginal atrophy alone, the labeling states that topical vaginal products should be considered. For prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis alone, it states that therapy should only be considered for women at significant risk of osteoporosis and for whom non-estrogen medications are not considered to be appropriate. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The boxed warning in the estradiol tablets prescribing information states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer, that close clinical surveillance of all women taking estrogens is important, and that adequate diagnostic measures, including endometrial sampling when indicated, should be undertaken to rule out malignancy in all cases of undiagnosed persistent or recurring abnormal vaginal bleeding.

It adds that there is no evidence that the use of “natural” estrogens results in a different endometrial risk profile than “synthetic” estrogens at equivalent estrogen doses.

The boxed warning states that estrogens with or without progestins should not be used for the prevention of cardiovascular disease, and that the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study reported increased risks of myocardial infarction, stroke, invasive breast cancer, pulmonary emboli and deep vein thrombosis in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age) during 5 years of treatment with oral conjugated estrogens (CE 0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA 2.5 mg) relative to placebo.

It also states that the Women’s Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS), a substudy of WHI, reported increased risk of developing probable dementia in postmenopausal women 65 years of age or older during 4 years of treatment with oral conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate relative to placebo, and that it is unknown whether this finding applies to younger postmenopausal women or to women taking estrogen alone therapy.

It adds that other doses of oral conjugated estrogens with medroxyprogesterone acetate, and other combinations and dosage forms of estrogens and progestins, were not studied in the WHI clinical trials and that, in the absence of comparable data, these risks should be assumed to be similar.

The labeling states that estrogens should not be used in individuals with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding; known, suspected or history of cancer of the breast, except in appropriately selected patients being treated for metastatic disease; known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia; or active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or history of these conditions.

Its list of conditions in which estrogens should not be used also includes active or recent (e.g., within the past year) arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), liver dysfunction or disease, and known or suspected pregnancy, and it states that estradiol tablets should not be used in patients with known hypersensitivity to their ingredients.

Its endometrial cancer warning states that the use of unopposed estrogens in women with intact uteri has been associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer, and that the reported endometrial cancer risk among unopposed estrogen users is about 2- to 12-fold greater than in non-users and appears dependent on duration of treatment and on estrogen dose.

It adds that most studies show no significant increased risk associated with use of estrogens for less than one year, that the greatest risk appears associated with prolonged use, with increased risks of 15- to 24-fold for five to ten years or more, and that this risk persists for 8 to over 15 years after estrogen therapy is discontinued.

The labeling states that adding a progestin to estrogen therapy has been shown to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, which may be a precursor to endometrial cancer, and that there are possible risks which may be associated with the use of progestins with estrogens compared to estrogen-alone regimens, including a possible increased risk of breast cancer.

Its cardiovascular warning states that estrogen and estrogen/progestin therapy has been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke, as well as venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and that should any of these occur or be suspected, estrogens should be discontinued immediately.

It states that risk factors for arterial vascular disease and/or venous thromboembolism should be managed appropriately.

It reports that large doses of estrogen (5 mg conjugated estrogens per day), comparable to those used to treat cancer of the prostate and breast, have been shown in a large prospective clinical trial in men to increase the risks of nonfatal myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism and thrombophlebitis.

The labeling states that, if feasible, estrogens should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization.

Its breast cancer warning states that, after a mean follow-up of 5.6 years, the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy reported an increased risk of invasive breast cancer in women who took daily CE plus MPA (relative risk 1.24; absolute risk 41 versus 33 cases per 10,000 women-years compared with placebo), and that invasive breast cancers in the CE plus MPA group were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage than in the placebo group.

It states that in the WHI estrogen-alone substudy, after an average follow-up of 7.1 years, daily CE (0.625 mg)-alone was not associated with an increased risk of invasive breast cancer (relative risk 0.80).

It adds that observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer for estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller, but still increased, risk for estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use, and that one large meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies reported increased risks that were dependent upon duration of use and could last up to more than 10 years after discontinuation of estrogen plus progestin therapy and estrogen-alone therapy.

It notes that the use of estrogen-alone and estrogen plus progestin has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation, and it states that all women should receive yearly breast examinations by a healthcare provider and perform monthly breast self-examinations, and that mammography examinations should be scheduled based on patient age, risk factors and prior mammogram results.

Its ovarian cancer warning states that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy reported a statistically non-significant increased risk of ovarian cancer: after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, the relative risk for CE plus MPA versus placebo was 1.58 (95 percent CI, 0.77-3.24), and the absolute risk was 4 versus 3 cases per 10,000 women-years.

It adds that a meta-analysis of 17 prospective and 35 retrospective epidemiology studies found that women who used hormonal therapy for menopausal symptoms had an increased risk for ovarian cancer (relative risk 1.41 with current use), that the elevated risk with combined current and recent use (discontinued use within 5 years before cancer diagnosis) was significant for both estrogen-alone and estrogen plus progestin products, and that the exact duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown.

Its gallbladder disease warning states that a 2- to 4-fold increase in the risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery has been reported in postmenopausal women receiving estrogens.

Its hypercalcemia warning states that estrogen administration may lead to severe hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and bone metastases, and that if hypercalcemia occurs, use of the drug should be stopped and appropriate measures taken to reduce the serum calcium level.

Its visual abnormalities warning notes that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogens, and it states that medication should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that estrogens should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions.

Its precautions section notes that, in a small number of case reports, substantial increases in blood pressure have been attributed to idiosyncratic reactions to estrogens and that a generalized effect of estrogens on blood pressure was not seen in a large, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial, and it states that blood pressure should be monitored at regular intervals with estrogen use.

It states that in patients with pre-existing hypertriglyceridemia, estrogen therapy may be associated with elevations of plasma triglycerides leading to pancreatitis and other complications.

Under its precautions, the labeling notes that estrogens may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function, and that for patients with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or with pregnancy, caution should be exercised and, in the case of recurrence, medication should be discontinued.

It states that estrogen administration leads to increased thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels, that patients dependent on thyroid hormone replacement therapy who are also receiving estrogens may require increased doses of their thyroid replacement therapy, and that these patients should have their thyroid function monitored in order to maintain their free thyroid hormone levels in an acceptable range.

It states that because estrogens may cause some degree of fluid retention, patients with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as asthma, epilepsy, migraine, and cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation when estrogens are prescribed, and that estrogens should be used with caution in individuals with severe hypocalcemia.

It notes that endometriosis may be exacerbated with administration of estrogens and that a few cases of malignant transformation of residual endometrial implants have been reported in women treated post-hysterectomy with estrogen alone therapy, and it states that for patients known to have residual endometriosis post-hysterectomy, the addition of progestin should be considered.

It states that estrogens may cause an exacerbation of asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraine or porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas and should be used with caution in women with these conditions.

Its clinical pharmacology section states that estrogens are metabolized partially by cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), and that inducers or inhibitors of CYP3A4 may therefore affect estrogen drug metabolism.

It gives St. John’s Wort preparations (Hypericum perforatum), phenobarbital, carbamazepine and rifampin as examples of CYP3A4 inducers that may reduce plasma concentrations of estrogens, possibly resulting in a decrease in therapeutic effects and/or changes in the uterine bleeding profile.

It gives erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice as examples of CYP3A4 inhibitors that may increase plasma concentrations of estrogens and may result in side effects.

The labeling states that estrogen administration to nursing mothers has been shown to decrease the quantity and quality of the milk, that detectable amounts of estrogens have been identified in the milk of mothers receiving this drug, and that caution should be exercised when estradiol is administered to a nursing woman.

Its patient information lists these common side effects: headache; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach/abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; and hair loss.

It also lists these other side effects: high blood pressure; liver problems; high blood sugar; fluid retention; enlargement of benign tumors (“fibroids”) of the uterus; a spotty darkening of the skin, particularly on the face; and vaginal yeast infection.

Its patient information advises calling the doctor immediately if any of the warning signals it lists, or any other unusual symptoms, happen while using estrogens; those signals include abnormal bleeding from the vagina (possible uterine cancer); pains in the calves or chest, sudden shortness of breath, or coughing blood (possible clot in the legs, or lungs); and severe headache or vomiting, dizziness, faintness, changes in vision or speech, weakness or numbness of an arm or leg (possible clot in the brain or eye).

The other warning signals it lists are breast lumps (possible breast cancer; it advises asking a doctor or health professional to show how to examine the breasts monthly); yellowing of the skin or eyes (possible liver problem); and pain, swelling, or tenderness in the abdomen (possible gallbladder problem).

content.summary: Sildenafil SR 36 mg capsules, a prescription capsule form of sildenafil, a PDE5 inhibitor; the listing does not say what “SR” means. VIAGRA labeling, written for 25, 50 and 100 mg tablets and not this capsule, says sildenafil helps blood flow into the penis during sexual stimulation and covers erectile dysfunction. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
The catalog lists each capsule as sildenafil 36 mg, a PDE5 inhibitor; a capsule is a different form from the VIAGRA tablets cited here. The listing does not say what “SR” stands for or how the capsule releases sildenafil. According to the VIAGRA prescribing information, sexual stimulation releases nitric oxide, which relaxes smooth muscle so blood can flow into the penis; sildenafil strengthens this by blocking PDE5 and, at the doses the label recommends for VIAGRA tablets, has no effect without sexual stimulation. VIAGRA is labeled for the treatment of erectile dysfunction. That labeling describes 25, 50 and 100 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

The catalog lists each capsule as sildenafil 36 mg. Sildenafil is a selective inhibitor of cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5). A capsule is a different dosage form from the film-coated tablets covered by the VIAGRA prescribing information cited here. The catalog name for this capsule includes “SR”; the listing does not say what that stands for or how the capsule releases sildenafil, and this page makes no claim about its release profile. According to the VIAGRA prescribing information, erection involves the release of nitric oxide in the corpus cavernosum during sexual stimulation; nitric oxide activates the enzyme guanylate cyclase, which raises cyclic GMP (cGMP), relaxing smooth muscle and allowing blood to flow in. The VIAGRA label states that sildenafil enhances the effect of nitric oxide by inhibiting PDE5, the enzyme responsible for breaking down cGMP in the corpus cavernosum, and that sildenafil at the doses it recommends for VIAGRA tablets has no effect in the absence of sexual stimulation. The VIAGRA prescribing information indicates VIAGRA for the treatment of erectile dysfunction and describes its tablets as containing sildenafil citrate equivalent to 25 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg of sildenafil. Those statements describe VIAGRA tablets; they do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule, how it is prepared, or whether its strength is expressed as sildenafil or as the citrate salt; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.

specifications.value: Capsule, listed as “SR” (release profile not stated)

specifications.label: Listed strength
specifications.value: 36 mg per capsule (whether as sildenafil or as the citrate salt is not stated)

specifications.label: Reference prescribing information
specifications.value: VIAGRA (sildenafil citrate) tablets, Viatris Specialty LLC; it describes its own 25, 50 and 100 mg film-coated tablets, not this capsule.

content.purpose: Labeled indication (VIAGRA prescribing information, which describes VIAGRA tablets, not this capsule): treatment of erectile dysfunction. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions: The VIAGRA prescribing information contraindicates VIAGRA with nitric oxide donors such as organic nitrates or nitrites in any form, taken regularly or intermittently, with guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat, and in people with a known hypersensitivity to sildenafil or any component of the tablet. It notes a potential cardiac risk of sexual activity in people with preexisting cardiovascular disease, and advises stopping all PDE5 inhibitors and seeking prompt medical attention after a sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes or a sudden decrease or loss of hearing. It states that treatments for erectile dysfunction, including VIAGRA, should not generally be used in men for whom sexual activity is inadvisable because of their underlying cardiovascular status. It reports prolonged erections lasting more than 4 hours and priapism, and states that a patient with an erection that persists longer than 4 hours should seek immediate medical assistance, because priapism that is not treated immediately could result in penile tissue damage and permanent loss of potency. It also advises caution with alpha-blockers and other blood-pressure medicines, and notes that ritonavir substantially increases sildenafil levels. The VIAGRA label states that the safety and efficacy of combinations of VIAGRA with other PDE5 inhibitors, including REVATIO or other pulmonary arterial hypertension treatments containing sildenafil, or with other treatments for erectile dysfunction have not been studied. The VIAGRA label states that such combinations may further lower blood pressure and that their use is not recommended. The VIAGRA label also notes postmarketing reports of bleeding events in patients who have taken VIAGRA, and states that a causal relationship between VIAGRA and these events has not been established. It also states that VIAGRA offers no protection against sexually transmitted diseases.

content.summary: Progesterone 100 mg sustained-release capsules are a prescription hormone. Their reference labeling, for 100 mg and 200 mg PROMETRIUM capsules and no sustained-release product, covers preventing endometrial hyperplasia (overgrowth of the uterine lining) in women after menopause who still have a uterus and take conjugated estrogens tablets, and secondary amenorrhea (periods that have stopped). Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These sustained-release capsules are listed at 100 mg of progesterone, a prescription hormone. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information cited here describes 100 mg and 200 mg capsules of micronized progesterone made with peanut oil and no sustained-release product, and the listing does not say how this capsule releases its progesterone or what its vehicle is. PROMETRIUM is labeled for preventing endometrial hyperplasia (overgrowth of the uterine lining) in women after menopause who still have a uterus and take conjugated estrogens tablets, and for secondary amenorrhea (periods that have stopped); it is not for children. Because PROMETRIUM capsules are made with peanut oil, that labeling rules them out for people allergic to peanuts; the listing does not state this capsule's ingredients. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed as a sustained-release capsule at 100 mg of progesterone. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the reference label cited here, describes capsules containing 100 mg or 200 mg of micronized progesterone with peanut oil among their inactive ingredients. It describes no sustained-release product, and the listing does not state how this capsule releases its progesterone, whether the progesterone is micronized, what the vehicle is or how the capsule is prepared, so the label's statements describe PROMETRIUM capsules and do not establish how this sustained-release capsule releases or absorbs progesterone or how it performs. According to the PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the progesterone in PROMETRIUM capsules is synthesized from a starting material from a plant source and is chemically identical to progesterone of human ovarian origin, and the oral bioavailability of progesterone is increased through micronization. For PROMETRIUM's micronized soft-gelatin capsules, it reports that maximum serum concentrations were attained within 3 hours after oral administration, and that the absolute bioavailability of micronized progesterone is not known. It states that progesterone is approximately 96 percent to 99 percent bound to serum proteins, that it is metabolized primarily by the liver largely to pregnanediols and pregnanolones, and that its metabolites are eliminated mainly by the kidneys. The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules are indicated for use in the prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets, and also for use in secondary amenorrhea. It notes that the effect of hepatic impairment and of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of PROMETRIUM capsules has not been studied. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule, how it is prepared, or whether its progesterone is micronized or its vehicle contains peanut oil as PROMETRIUM capsules do; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (PROMETRIUM prescribing information), which describe PROMETRIUM capsules of 100 mg or 200 mg micronized progesterone and not this sustained-release capsule: prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets; and secondary amenorrhea. The labeling also states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The PROMETRIUM prescribing information contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with hypersensitivity to its ingredients and, because PROMETRIUM capsules contain peanut oil, in patients allergic to peanuts; this listing does not state the capsule's ingredients or vehicle.

It also contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with abnormal genital bleeding of unknown etiology; known, suspected, or history of breast cancer; active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease (for example, stroke and myocardial infarction) or a history of these conditions; or known liver dysfunction or disease.

Its warnings state that PROMETRIUM should be immediately discontinued if a pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction occurs or is suspected, and that, if feasible, it should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization.

The labeling states that the safety and efficacy of estrogen plus progestogen for the prevention of cardiovascular disorders has not been established, and that the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin trial reported increased risks of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke and myocardial infarction in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age, average age 63.4 years) during 5.6 years of treatment with daily oral conjugated estrogens (0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (2.5 mg), relative to placebo.

It states that only daily oral 0.625 mg conjugated estrogens and 2.5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate were studied in that trial, so the relevance of the WHI findings regarding adverse cardiovascular events to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, and that without such data it is not possible to definitively exclude these risks or determine their extent for other products.

For venous thromboembolism in the overall WHI study population, the labeling reports a relative risk for pulmonary embolism of 1.98 (95% CI, 1.36, 2.87) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (18 versus 9), and a relative risk for deep vein thrombosis of 1.87 (95% CI, 1.37, 2.54), with a risk difference of 12 per 10,000 women-years (25 versus 14).

For the overall WHI population it also reports a relative risk for stroke of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.07, 1.76) with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (33 versus 24), and a relative risk of coronary heart disease of 1.18 (95% CI, 0.95, 1.45) with a risk difference of 6 per 10,000 women-years (41 versus 35), for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo.

Its breast cancer warning states that PROMETRIUM is contraindicated in women with breast cancer, a history of breast cancer, or estrogen-dependent neoplasia, that PROMETRIUM should be discontinued if a hormone-sensitive malignancy is diagnosed, and that the use of estrogen plus progestin therapy has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation.

In the overall WHI population, the labeling reports a relative risk for invasive breast cancer of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01, 1.53) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (43 versus 35); it states that invasive breast cancers were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage in that group, and that the trial did not show a statistically significant difference in breast cancer mortality.

It adds that, consistent with the WHI trial, observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy, and that a large meta-analysis including 24 prospective studies of postmenopausal women comparing current use of estrogen plus progestin products for 5 to 14 years (average of 9 years) versus never use reported a relative risk for breast cancer of 2.08 (95% CI, 2.02 to 2.15). It states that these studies have not generally found significant variation in the risk of breast cancer among different estrogen plus progestin combinations, doses, or routes of administration, and that the relevance of the WHI findings regarding breast cancer to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, so that these risks cannot be definitively excluded or their extent determined for other products.

Its ovarian cancer warning reports, for the overall WHI population, a relative risk for ovarian cancer of 1.41 (95% CI, 0.75 to 2.66) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate versus placebo after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, with a risk difference of 1 per 10,000 women-years (5 versus 4), and a large meta-analysis of 17 prospective studies of postmenopausal women reporting a relative risk of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.26 to 1.48) for current use of estrogen plus progestin products versus never use; it states that the duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown.

content.summary: Anastrozole 0.5 mg capsules, a prescription aromatase inhibitor. ARIMIDEX's labeling, written for 1 mg tablets and not this capsule, says anastrozole lowers estrogen and covers certain breast cancers in women after menopause. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These capsules are listed at 0.5 mg of anastrozole, a prescription medicine called an aromatase inhibitor. According to the ARIMIDEX prescribing information, many breast cancers grow in response to estrogen, which after menopause comes mainly from the aromatase enzyme; anastrozole blocks that enzyme and lowers estradiol, an estrogen. ARIMIDEX is labeled for certain breast cancers in women after menopause, including early hormone receptor-positive breast cancer and advanced breast cancer, and its patient information states that ARIMIDEX does not work in women with breast cancer who have not gone through menopause. That labeling describes 1 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed at 0.5 mg of anastrozole, a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor. A capsule is a different dosage form from the tablets covered by the ARIMIDEX prescribing information cited here, which describes 1 mg tablets; the statements below describe those tablets and do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. According to the ARIMIDEX prescribing information, the growth of many breast cancers is stimulated or maintained by estrogens, and in postmenopausal women estrogens come mainly from the aromatase enzyme, which converts adrenal androgens (primarily androstenedione and testosterone) to estrone and estradiol. The same labeling describes anastrozole as a selective non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor that significantly lowers serum estradiol concentrations and has no detectable effect on the formation of adrenal corticosteroids or aldosterone. The ARIMIDEX prescribing information indicates ARIMIDEX for adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer, for first-line treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive or hormone receptor-unknown locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer, and for treatment of advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease progression following tamoxifen therapy. It notes that patients with estrogen receptor-negative disease, and patients who did not respond to previous tamoxifen therapy, rarely responded to ARIMIDEX. Its patient information states that ARIMIDEX does not work in women with breast cancer who have not gone through menopause. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule or how it is prepared; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (ARIMIDEX prescribing information), which describe ARIMIDEX tablets and not this capsule: adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer; first-line treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive or hormone receptor-unknown locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer; and treatment of advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease progression following tamoxifen therapy; the labeling notes that patients with estrogen receptor-negative disease and patients who did not respond to previous tamoxifen therapy rarely responded to ARIMIDEX. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The ARIMIDEX prescribing information contraindicates ARIMIDEX in any patient who has shown a hypersensitivity reaction to the drug or to any of its excipients; observed reactions include anaphylaxis, angioedema and urticaria.

Based on findings from animal studies and its mechanism of action, the labeling states that ARIMIDEX can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman, and it notes that there are no studies of ARIMIDEX use in pregnant women; it advises verifying the pregnancy status of females of reproductive potential before starting and using effective contraception during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose, and it advises females to contact their healthcare provider if they become pregnant, or if pregnancy is suspected, during treatment.

Based on studies in female animals, the labeling says ARIMIDEX may impair fertility in females of reproductive potential.

It advises lactating women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 2 weeks after the last dose.

It states that tamoxifen should not be administered with anastrozole, and that estrogen-containing therapies should not be used with ARIMIDEX because they may diminish its pharmacological action.

The labeling reports that in the ATAC trial, women with pre-existing ischemic heart disease had more ischemic cardiovascular events on ARIMIDEX than on tamoxifen (17% versus 10%), and it advises considering the risks and benefits of ARIMIDEX therapy in these patients.

Its patient counseling information says to inform patients of the possibility of serious allergic reactions with swelling of the face, lips, tongue and/or throat, which may cause difficulty in swallowing and/or breathing, and to seek medical attention immediately; it also says that patients with pre-existing ischemic heart disease should be informed that an increased incidence of cardiovascular events has been observed with ARIMIDEX use compared to tamoxifen use, and it advises patients to seek medical attention immediately if new or worsening chest pain or shortness of breath occurs.

It reports that patients receiving ARIMIDEX in the ATAC bone substudy had mean decreases in lumbar spine and total hip bone mineral density, and it advises considering bone mineral density monitoring; it also reports that more patients on ARIMIDEX than on tamoxifen had elevated serum cholesterol (9% versus 3.5%), and its patient counseling information says to inform patients that an increased level of cholesterol might be seen while receiving ARIMIDEX.

It also reports that in the adjuvant trial patients receiving ARIMIDEX had an increase in the incidence of all fractures (specifically fractures of the spine, hip and wrist), 10% versus 7% on tamoxifen, and its patient counseling information notes that a possible consequence of decreased mineral content of bones is an increase in the risk of fractures.

The labeling lists the serious adverse reactions occurring in fewer than 1 in 10,000 patients as skin reactions such as lesions, ulcers or blisters; allergic reactions with swelling of the face, lips, tongue and/or throat, which may cause difficulty swallowing and/or breathing; and changes in liver function blood tests, including inflammation of the liver.

Its patient information says to stop taking ARIMIDEX and call the healthcare provider right away for any skin lesions, ulcers or blisters, or for signs or symptoms of a liver problem such as a general feeling of not being well, yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, or pain on the right side of the stomach area.

It lists the common adverse reactions (10% or more) in women taking ARIMIDEX as hot flashes, asthenia, arthritis, pain, arthralgia, hypertension, depression, nausea and vomiting, rash, osteoporosis, fractures, back pain, insomnia, headache, bone pain, peripheral edema, increased cough, dyspnea, pharyngitis and lymphedema.

The labeling reports that in the adjuvant trial, patients receiving ARIMIDEX had a higher incidence of carpal tunnel syndrome (2.5%) than patients receiving tamoxifen (0.7%), and it says patients should be informed that if they experience tickling, tingling or numbness they should notify their health care provider.

Post-marketing reports, which the labeling says come from a population of uncertain size and cannot always be used to estimate frequency or establish causation, include hepatobiliary events (increases in alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, gamma-GT and bilirubin; hepatitis), rash including erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, allergic reactions including angioedema, urticaria and anaphylaxis, myalgia and hypercalcemia (with or without an increase in parathyroid hormone), and tendon disorders including tendon rupture, tendonitis, tenosynovitis and trigger finger.

content.summary: Prescription solution listed at minoxidil 5% and tretinoin 0.025% in a 60 mL fill. Minoxidil 5% alone is labeled to regrow hair on the top of the scalp in men and tretinoin for acne; no label cited covers tretinoin for hair loss or the two combined. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
This prescription solution is listed at minoxidil 5% and tretinoin 0.025% in a 60 mL fill. The Rogaine Extra Strength label is for regrowing hair on the top of the scalp in men only; it says results can take at least 4 months and differ for each person, that it will not work for all men, and that hair loss begins again if use stops. The RETIN-A labeling is for acne and states that long-term safety and efficacy for other conditions have not been established. Neither label describes tretinoin for hair loss or the two combined, so neither shows how this solution performs. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

This solution is listed at minoxidil 5% and tretinoin 0.025% in a 60 mL fill. This description draws on two single-ingredient reference labels, the Drug Facts label for Men's Rogaine Extra Strength Unscented and the RETIN-A tretinoin cream and gel prescribing information; neither label describes tretinoin for hair loss or minoxidil and tretinoin combined. Each label describes its own single-ingredient product, not this combined solution, so what either label says about its own product does not establish how this solution performs. The Rogaine label lists that product's use as regrowing hair on the top of the scalp (vertex only) and says that product is for use by men only and is not intended for frontal baldness or receding hairline. The Rogaine label says it takes time to regrow hair and that some men may need to use that product for at least 4 months before they see results; the label adds that the amount of hair regrowth is different for each person and that the Rogaine product will not work for all men. The Rogaine label also states that continued use of that product is necessary to increase and keep hair regrowth, or hair loss will begin again, and that hair regrowth has not been shown to last longer than 48 weeks in large clinical trials with continuous treatment with 5% minoxidil topical solution for men. The RETIN-A prescribing information describes RETIN-A gel and cream as containing tretinoin, chemically all-trans-retinoic acid, and indicates RETIN-A for topical application in the treatment of acne vulgaris. The same labeling states that the safety and efficacy of the long-term use of RETIN-A in the treatment of other disorders have not been established. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the solution, how it is prepared, or whether its percentages are by weight or by volume; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
