content.purpose: Labeled indications and uses below are the ones two single-ingredient reference labels give for their own products; neither label describes a use for this combined solution, and neither describes tretinoin for hair loss or minoxidil and tretinoin combined. The Men's Rogaine Extra Strength Unscented Drug Facts label gives that product's purpose as a hair regrowth treatment for men and its use as regrowing hair on the top of the scalp (vertex only); it says that product is for use by men only and is not intended for frontal baldness or receding hairline. The Rogaine label adds that the amount of hair regrowth is different for each person and that the Rogaine product will not work for all men. The Rogaine label says some men may need to use that product for at least 4 months before they see results, and that continued use of that product is necessary to increase and keep hair regrowth, or hair loss will begin again. The Rogaine label also states that hair regrowth has not been shown to last longer than 48 weeks in large clinical trials with continuous treatment with 5% minoxidil topical solution for men. The RETIN-A prescribing information indicates RETIN-A for topical application in the treatment of acne vulgaris and states that the safety and efficacy of the long-term use of RETIN-A in the treatment of other disorders have not been established. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make.
content.cautions: The cautions below are the ones two single-ingredient reference labels state for their own products; neither label addresses this combined solution, the dispensed product's own label governs, and the prescribing clinician decides whether the solution is appropriate. The Men's Rogaine Extra Strength Unscented Drug Facts label says not to use that product if you are a woman, if your amount of hair loss is different from that shown on its carton or your hair loss is on the front of the scalp, or if you have no family history of hair loss. The Rogaine label also says not to use that product if your hair loss is sudden and/or patchy, if you do not know the reason for your hair loss, or if you use other medicines on the scalp. The Rogaine label says not to use that product if you are under 18 years of age or if your scalp is red, inflamed, infected, irritated or painful, and not to use it on babies and children. The Rogaine label says to ask a doctor before using that product if you have heart disease. The Rogaine label says that product is for external use only; when using it, the label says not to apply it on other parts of the body and to avoid contact with the eyes, rinsing the eyes with large amounts of cool tap water after accidental contact. The Rogaine label notes that some people have experienced changes in hair color and/or texture when using that product. The Rogaine label's directions state that using that product more, or more often, than those directions say will not improve results. The Rogaine label says to stop using that product and ask a doctor if chest pain, rapid heartbeat, faintness or dizziness occurs, if sudden, unexplained weight gain occurs, or if your hands or feet swell. The Rogaine label also says to stop using that product and ask a doctor if scalp irritation or redness occurs, if unwanted facial hair growth occurs, or if you do not see hair regrowth in 4 months. The Rogaine label says that product may be harmful if used when pregnant or breast-feeding. The Rogaine label says to keep that product out of reach of children and, if it is swallowed, to get medical help or contact a Poison Control Center right away. The RETIN-A prescribing information says the following should be used with caution because of possible interaction with tretinoin: concomitant topical medication; medicated or abrasive soaps and cleansers; soaps and cosmetics that have a strong drying effect; and products with high concentrations of alcohol, astringents, spices or lime. The RETIN-A prescribing information says particular caution should be exercised in using preparations containing sulfur, resorcinol or salicylic acid with RETIN-A. The patient instructions in the RETIN-A labeling say RETIN-A is to be used only according to your doctor's instructions and should not be applied to other areas of the body or to other growths or lesions. The RETIN-A patient instructions also say not to use other medications with RETIN-A that are not recommended by your doctor, not to allow anyone else to use RETIN-A, and to keep RETIN-A out of reach of children. The RETIN-A patient instructions also say to avoid preparations that may dry or irritate the skin, which may include certain astringents, toiletries containing alcohol, spices or lime, or certain medicated soaps, shampoos and hair permanent solutions. The RETIN-A prescribing information says that use of RETIN-A should be discontinued if hypersensitivity to any of its ingredients is noted or if a reaction suggesting sensitivity or chemical irritation occurs, and its patient instructions say to discontinue RETIN-A and consult your physician if you are experiencing severe or persistent irritation. The RETIN-A prescribing information says RETIN-A should be kept away from the eyes, the mouth, angles of the nose and mucous membranes, and its patient instructions also say to keep RETIN-A away from open wounds. The RETIN-A prescribing information also says topical use of RETIN-A may induce severe local erythema and peeling at the site of application, and that tretinoin has been reported to cause severe irritation on eczematous skin and should be used with utmost caution in patients with this condition. The RETIN-A dosage section says application of RETIN-A may cause a transitory feeling of warmth or slight stinging. The RETIN-A prescribing information says exposure to sunlight, including sunlamps, should be minimized during the use of RETIN-A, and that patients with sunburn should not use RETIN-A until fully recovered because of heightened susceptibility to sunlight as a result of the use of tretinoin. The RETIN-A prescribing information recommends sunscreen products and protective clothing over treated areas when exposure cannot be avoided. The RETIN-A prescribing information adds that patients who may be required to have considerable sun exposure due to occupation, and those with inherent sensitivity to the sun, should exercise particular caution, and that weather extremes, such as wind or cold, also may be irritating to patients under treatment with tretinoin. The RETIN-A patient instructions say not to use artificial sunlamps while using RETIN-A and, if you do become sunburned, to stop therapy with RETIN-A until your skin has recovered. The RETIN-A patient instructions also say that areas treated with RETIN-A should be protected when outside, even on hazy days, and that an effective sunscreen should be used any time you are outside, consulting your physician for a recommended SPF level that gives the necessary high level of protection. The RETIN-A patient instructions add that protective clothing, like a hat, should be worn for extended sun exposure. The RETIN-A labeling reports that studies in hairless albino mice suggest that concurrent exposure to tretinoin may enhance the tumorigenic potential of carcinogenic doses of UVB and UVA light from a solar simulator. The RETIN-A labeling reports that this effect has been confirmed in a later study in pigmented mice, and that dark pigmentation did not overcome the enhancement of photocarcinogenesis by 0.05% tretinoin. The RETIN-A labeling says that, although the significance of these studies to humans is not clear, patients should minimize exposure to sunlight or artificial ultraviolet irradiation sources. In a 91-week dermal study in which CD-1 mice were given 0.017% and 0.035% tretinoin formulations, the RETIN-A labeling reports cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and papillomas in the treatment area in some female mice and a dose-related incidence of liver tumors in male mice at those same doses. The RETIN-A labeling states that the maximum systemic doses associated with those two formulations, 0.5 and 1.0 mg/kg/day (milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day) respectively, are two and four times the maximum human systemic dose, when adjusted for total body surface area. For its comparisons of animal exposure with human systemic exposure, the RETIN-A label defines the maximum human systemic dose using its own 0.1% RETIN-A product. The RETIN-A labeling says the biological significance of these findings is not clear because they occurred at doses that exceeded the dermal maximally tolerated dose and were within the background natural occurrence rate for these tumors in this strain of mice. The RETIN-A labeling also reports no evidence of carcinogenic potential when tretinoin was given topically to mice at a dose of 0.025 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day (0.1 times the maximum human systemic dose, adjusted for total body surface area). The RETIN-A labeling reports that the mutagenic potential of tretinoin was evaluated in the Ames assay and in the in vivo mouse micronucleus assay, both of which were negative. In dermal Segment I fertility studies of another tretinoin formulation in rats, the RETIN-A labeling reports slight, not statistically significant decreases in sperm count and motility at 0.5 mg/kg/day (4 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area). In the same studies, the RETIN-A labeling reports slight, not statistically significant increases in the number and percent of nonviable embryos in females treated with 0.25 mg/kg/day (2 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area) and above. The RETIN-A labeling notes that a dermal Segment III study with RETIN-A has not been performed in any species. The RETIN-A labeling reports decreased survival of neonates and growth retardation in oral Segment I and Segment III studies in rats at doses in excess of 2 mg/kg/day (16 times the human topical dose adjusted for total body surface area). The RETIN-A adverse reactions section says the skin of certain sensitive individuals may become excessively red, edematous, blistered or crusted, and that true contact allergy to topical tretinoin is rarely encountered. The RETIN-A adverse reactions section also says temporary hyper- or hypopigmentation has been reported with repeated application of RETIN-A, and that to date all adverse effects of RETIN-A have been reversible upon discontinuance of therapy. The RETIN-A overdosage section states that if RETIN-A is applied excessively, no more rapid or better results will be obtained and marked redness, peeling or discomfort may occur. The RETIN-A overdosage section also states that oral ingestion of RETIN-A may lead to the same side effects as those associated with excessive oral intake of vitamin A. On pregnancy, the RETIN-A labeling says there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women and that tretinoin should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. The RETIN-A patient instructions say to consult your physician before using RETIN-A if you are pregnant, think you are pregnant, or are nursing a baby. The RETIN-A labeling reports that oral tretinoin has been shown to be teratogenic in rats, mice, hamsters and subhuman primates. The RETIN-A labeling reports that tretinoin was teratogenic and fetotoxic in Wistar rats when given orally or topically in doses greater than 1 mg/kg/day (8 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area). The RETIN-A labeling notes that variations in teratogenic doses among various strains of rats have been reported. In the cynomolgus monkey, which the RETIN-A labeling describes as metabolically closer to humans for tretinoin than the other species examined, the labeling reports fetal malformations at doses of 10 mg/kg/day or greater but none at 5 mg/kg/day (83 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area). For the cynomolgus monkey, the RETIN-A labeling also reports increased skeletal variations at all doses and a dose-related increase in embryolethality and abortion, with similar results in pigtail macaques. For topical tretinoin, the RETIN-A labeling says animal teratogenicity tests have generated equivocal results. The RETIN-A labeling reports evidence of teratogenicity (shortened or kinked tail) of topical tretinoin in Wistar rats at doses greater than 1 mg/kg/day (8 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area). The RETIN-A labeling also reports anomalies (humerus: short 13%, bent 6%, os parietale incompletely ossified 14%) when 10 mg/kg/day was topically applied. In New Zealand White rabbits given doses greater than 0.2 mg/kg/day (3.3 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area), the RETIN-A labeling cites other reports of an increased incidence of domed head and hydrocephaly, typical of retinoid-induced fetal malformations in this species. The RETIN-A labeling states that several well-controlled animal studies have shown that dermally applied tretinoin may be fetotoxic, but not overly teratogenic, in rats and rabbits at doses of 1.0 and 0.5 mg/kg/day, respectively (8 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area in both species). The RETIN-A labeling also reports that topical tretinoin has been shown to be fetotoxic in rabbits at 0.5 mg/kg/day (8 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area). The RETIN-A labeling reports that oral tretinoin has been shown to be fetotoxic in rats at 2.5 mg/kg/day (20 times the maximum human systemic dose adjusted for total body surface area), resulting in skeletal variations and increased intrauterine death. The RETIN-A labeling notes that, with widespread use of any drug, a small number of birth defect reports associated temporally with its administration would be expected by chance alone, and it reports thirty human cases of temporally associated congenital malformations during two decades of clinical use of RETIN-A. The RETIN-A labeling says no definite pattern of teratogenicity and no causal association have been established from these cases, but that five of the reports describe the rare birth defect category holoprosencephaly (defects associated with incomplete midline development of the forebrain). The RETIN-A labeling says the significance of these spontaneous reports in terms of risk to the fetus is not known. The RETIN-A labeling says it is not known whether tretinoin is excreted in human milk and that caution should be exercised when RETIN-A is administered to a nursing woman. The RETIN-A labeling says safety and effectiveness of RETIN-A have not been established in pediatric patients below the age of 12 or in a geriatric population, and that clinical studies of RETIN-A did not include sufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 and over to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. The Rogaine label warns that the Rogaine product is flammable and should be kept away from fire or flame, and the RETIN-A patient instructions say RETIN-A gels are flammable and to avoid fire, flame or smoking during use. This listing does not state the listed solution's route, vehicle, inactive ingredients, directions for use or storage, or whether the listed solution is flammable.

content.summary: Bi-Est 5 mg (50/50) capsules, prescription only; the catalog does not name the ingredients or say what the ratio refers to. A National Academies report lists other Bi-Est preparations as estradiol with estriol but does not describe this capsule; the FDA states there are no FDA-approved estriol drugs. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
The catalog lists Bi-Est 5 mg (50/50) capsules but does not name the ingredients, say which ingredient each figure of the ratio refers to, or say whether the milligram amount is the total or that of one ingredient. A National Academies analysis done for the FDA lists “Bi-Est” preparations as estradiol with estriol, but it does not describe this capsule. The FDA states that there are no FDA-approved estriol drugs and that it does not have evidence that estriol drugs are safe and effective or are “safer forms of estrogen.” The estradiol tablets labeling cited for estradiol was written for tablets, not this capsule, and its boxed warning states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

The catalog lists Bi-Est 5 mg (50/50) capsules; it does not name the ingredients, say which ingredient each figure of the ratio refers to, or say whether the stated milligram amount is the total of the ingredients or that of one of them. The FDA reports that, at its request, the National Academies (NASEM) evaluated the scientific evidence and in July 2020 provided the FDA with an analysis of compounded bioidentical hormone therapy. That report includes an appendix table of such formulations with two or more active ingredients, drawn from resources its note lists (peer-reviewed literature, adverse event reports, information provided by practitioners, outsourcing facility preparation reports and pharmacies’ online marketing); the table lists “Bi-Estrogen” and “Bi-Est” preparations whose active ingredients are estradiol and estriol, writes the ratios of a capsule entry and a cream entry as estriol/estradiol (for example 80/20) and describes “Bi-Est 50:50” as 50% estradiol and 50% estriol, but it does not describe this capsule, and the catalog does not say that its ratio follows the same order. The FDA’s menopause page (content current as of 12/14/2023) states that there are no FDA-approved drugs containing estriol, that marketed drugs containing estriol are compounded drugs, which are not FDA-approved, and that it does not have evidence that drugs containing estriol are safe and effective, or are “safer forms of estrogen.” For estradiol, this description cites the estradiol tablets prescribing information, which describes 0.5, 1 and 2 mg tablets of micronized estradiol; a capsule is a different dosage form, and although many of the label’s statements are made about estrogens in general, the label was written for those tablets, does not address this capsule, mentions estriol only as a metabolite of estradiol and not as an ingredient, and does not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. The same labeling states that estradiol is the principal intracellular human estrogen, that estrogens act through binding to nuclear receptors in estrogen-responsive tissues, and that two estrogen receptors have been identified to date, which vary in proportion from tissue to tissue. It adds that circulating estrogens modulate the pituitary secretion of the gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), through a negative feedback mechanism, and that estrogens act to reduce the elevated levels of these hormones seen in postmenopausal women. Its boxed warning states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer, and it also addresses cardiovascular and other risks, including findings from the Women’s Health Initiative studies. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule or how it is prepared; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.

specifications.value: Estradiol Tablets, USP prescribing information (Epic Pharma, Rev. 01-2026-00; SPL version 13, effective 2/26/2026), for estradiol, describing its own tablets; FDA, Women’s Health Topics: Menopause (content current as of 12/14/2023); FDA page on the National Academies study it requested; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2020 report (doi 10.17226/25791), Appendix G. content.purpose: The FDA states that there are no FDA-approved drugs containing estriol; the sources cited here give no prescribing information for estriol or for any combination of estrogens. Labeled indications for estradiol alone (estradiol tablets prescribing information), which describe estradiol tablets and not this capsule: treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms associated with the menopause; treatment of moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy associated with the menopause; treatment of hypoestrogenism due to hypogonadism, castration or primary ovarian failure; treatment of breast cancer (for palliation only) in appropriately selected women and men with metastatic disease; treatment of advanced androgen-dependent carcinoma of the prostate (for palliation only); and prevention of osteoporosis. For vulvar and vaginal atrophy alone, the labeling states that topical vaginal products should be considered. For prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis alone, it states that therapy should only be considered for women at significant risk of osteoporosis and for whom non-estrogen medications are not considered to be appropriate. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make.
content.cautions: The cautions below come from the estradiol tablets prescribing information, which states cautions for its own estradiol tablets, and from FDA statements on hormone therapy for menopause, on estriol, on products called “bioidentical hormones” and on a National Academies analysis the FDA requested. The FDA states that there are no FDA-approved drugs containing estriol, so no FDA-approved labeling covers estriol or a combination of estradiol and estriol; the dispensed product's own label governs, and the prescribing clinician decides whether the capsule is appropriate. The FDA states that many marketed products called “bioidentical hormones” are compounded drugs, which are not FDA-approved, and that it does not have evidence that compounded “bioidentical hormones” are safe and effective, and no evidence that they are safer or more effective than FDA-approved hormone therapy. The FDA reports that NASEM, in its analysis of compounded bioidentical hormone therapy, determined there was a lack of rigorous evidence of safety and effectiveness from well-designed or properly controlled clinical studies and found that information about safety and effectiveness came mostly from low quality data, such as anecdotal claims, patient reports and prescriber testimonies; that there is limited federal and state-level oversight of the quality and use of these preparations; and that NASEM concluded that, given the lack of high-quality clinical evidence and minimal oversight, their wide-spread use poses a public health concern. The FDA adds that it has been concerned that health care professionals and patients may not be aware of the uncertainties of the benefits and potential safety risks with these products. The FDA’s menopause page also states that hormone therapy should not be used to prevent heart attacks or strokes, or to prevent memory loss or Alzheimer’s disease, and that studies have not shown that hormone therapy prevents aging and wrinkles or increases sex drive. The boxed warning in the estradiol tablets prescribing information states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer, that close clinical surveillance of all women taking estrogens is important, and that adequate diagnostic measures, including endometrial sampling when indicated, should be undertaken to rule out malignancy in all cases of undiagnosed persistent or recurring abnormal vaginal bleeding. It adds that there is no evidence that the use of “natural” estrogens results in a different endometrial risk profile than “synthetic” estrogens at equivalent estrogen doses. The boxed warning states that estrogens with or without progestins should not be used for the prevention of cardiovascular disease, and that the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study reported increased risks of myocardial infarction, stroke, invasive breast cancer, pulmonary emboli and deep vein thrombosis in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age) during 5 years of treatment with oral conjugated estrogens (CE 0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA 2.5 mg) relative to placebo. It also states that the Women’s Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS), a substudy of WHI, reported increased risk of developing probable dementia in postmenopausal women 65 years of age or older during 4 years of treatment with oral conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate relative to placebo, and that it is unknown whether this finding applies to younger postmenopausal women or to women taking estrogen alone therapy. The estradiol tablet label describes the specific doses of oral conjugated estrogens with medroxyprogesterone acetate studied in the WHI combination trial. For other doses and other estrogen plus progestin combinations or dosage forms, it advises prescribers to assume similar risks when comparable data are unavailable. The labeling states that estrogens should not be used in individuals with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding; known, suspected or history of cancer of the breast, except in appropriately selected patients being treated for metastatic disease; known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia; or active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or history of these conditions. Its list of conditions in which estrogens should not be used also includes active or recent (e.g., within the past year) arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), liver dysfunction or disease, and known or suspected pregnancy, and it states that estradiol tablets should not be used in patients with known hypersensitivity to their ingredients. Its endometrial cancer warning states that the use of unopposed estrogens in women with intact uteri has been associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer, and that the reported endometrial cancer risk among unopposed estrogen users is about 2- to 12-fold greater than in non-users and appears dependent on duration of treatment and on estrogen dose. It adds that most studies show no significant increased risk associated with use of estrogens for less than one year, that the greatest risk appears associated with prolonged use, with increased risks of 15- to 24-fold for five to ten years or more, and that this risk persists for 8 to over 15 years after estrogen therapy is discontinued. The labeling states that adding a progestin to estrogen therapy has been shown to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, which may be a precursor to endometrial cancer, and that there are possible risks which may be associated with the use of progestins with estrogens compared to estrogen-alone regimens, including a possible increased risk of breast cancer. Its cardiovascular warning states that estrogen and estrogen/progestin therapy has been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke, as well as venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and that should any of these occur or be suspected, estrogens should be discontinued immediately. It states that risk factors for arterial vascular disease and/or venous thromboembolism should be managed appropriately. It reports that large doses of estrogen (5 mg conjugated estrogens per day), comparable to those used to treat cancer of the prostate and breast, have been shown in a large prospective clinical trial in men to increase the risks of nonfatal myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism and thrombophlebitis. The labeling states that, if feasible, estrogens should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization. Its breast cancer warning states that, after a mean follow-up of 5.6 years, the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy reported an increased risk of invasive breast cancer in women who took daily CE plus MPA (relative risk 1.24; absolute risk 41 versus 33 cases per 10,000 women-years compared with placebo), and that invasive breast cancers in the CE plus MPA group were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage than in the placebo group. It states that in the WHI estrogen-alone substudy, after an average follow-up of 7.1 years, daily CE (0.625 mg)-alone was not associated with an increased risk of invasive breast cancer (relative risk 0.80). It adds that observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer for estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller, but still increased, risk for estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use, and that one large meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies reported increased risks that were dependent upon duration of use and could last up to more than 10 years after discontinuation of estrogen plus progestin therapy and estrogen-alone therapy. It notes that the use of estrogen-alone and estrogen plus progestin has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation, and it states that all women should receive yearly breast examinations by a healthcare provider and perform monthly breast self-examinations, and that mammography examinations should be scheduled based on patient age, risk factors and prior mammogram results. Its ovarian cancer warning states that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy reported a statistically non-significant increased risk of ovarian cancer: after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, the relative risk for CE plus MPA versus placebo was 1.58 (95 percent CI, 0.77-3.24), and the absolute risk was 4 versus 3 cases per 10,000 women-years. It adds that a meta-analysis of 17 prospective and 35 retrospective epidemiology studies found that women who used hormonal therapy for menopausal symptoms had an increased risk for ovarian cancer (relative risk 1.41 with current use), that the elevated risk with combined current and recent use (discontinued use within 5 years before cancer diagnosis) was significant for both estrogen-alone and estrogen plus progestin products, and that the exact duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown. Its gallbladder disease warning states that a 2- to 4-fold increase in the risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery has been reported in postmenopausal women receiving estrogens. The cited estradiol tablet label warns that estrogen can cause severe hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and bone metastases. It directs the treating clinician to stop the estrogen medication and reduce serum calcium if that reaction occurs. Its visual abnormalities warning notes that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogens, and it states that medication should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that estrogens should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions. Its precautions section notes that, in a small number of case reports, substantial increases in blood pressure have been attributed to idiosyncratic reactions to estrogens and that a generalized effect of estrogens on blood pressure was not seen in a large, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial, and it states that blood pressure should be monitored at regular intervals with estrogen use. It states that in patients with pre-existing hypertriglyceridemia, estrogen therapy may be associated with elevations of plasma triglycerides leading to pancreatitis and other complications. Under its precautions, the labeling notes that estrogens may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function, and that for patients with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or with pregnancy, caution should be exercised and, in the case of recurrence, medication should be discontinued. It states that estrogen administration leads to increased thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels, that patients dependent on thyroid hormone replacement therapy who are also receiving estrogens may require increased doses of their thyroid replacement therapy, and that these patients should have their thyroid function monitored in order to maintain their free thyroid hormone levels in an acceptable range. It states that because estrogens may cause some degree of fluid retention, patients with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as asthma, epilepsy, migraine, and cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation when estrogens are prescribed, and that estrogens should be used with caution in individuals with severe hypocalcemia. It notes that endometriosis may be exacerbated with administration of estrogens and that a few cases of malignant transformation of residual endometrial implants have been reported in women treated post-hysterectomy with estrogen alone therapy, and it states that for patients known to have residual endometriosis post-hysterectomy, the addition of progestin should be considered. It states that estrogens may cause an exacerbation of asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraine or porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas and should be used with caution in women with these conditions. Its clinical pharmacology section states that estrogens are metabolized partially by cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), and that inducers or inhibitors of CYP3A4 may therefore affect estrogen drug metabolism. It gives St. John’s Wort preparations (Hypericum perforatum), phenobarbital, carbamazepine and rifampin as examples of CYP3A4 inducers that may reduce plasma concentrations of estrogens, possibly resulting in a decrease in therapeutic effects and/or changes in the uterine bleeding profile. It gives erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice as examples of CYP3A4 inhibitors that may increase plasma concentrations of estrogens and may result in side effects. The labeling states that estrogen administration to nursing mothers has been shown to decrease the quantity and quality of the milk, that detectable amounts of estrogens have been identified in the milk of mothers receiving the drug the labeling describes, and that caution should be exercised when estradiol is administered to a nursing woman. Its patient information lists these common side effects: headache; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach/abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; and hair loss. It also lists these other side effects: high blood pressure; liver problems; high blood sugar; fluid retention; enlargement of benign tumors (“fibroids”) of the uterus; a spotty darkening of the skin, particularly on the face; and vaginal yeast infection; it states that these are not all the possible side effects of estradiol tablets. Its patient information advises calling the doctor immediately if any of the warning signals it lists, or any other unusual symptoms, happen while using estrogens; those signals include abnormal bleeding from the vagina (possible uterine cancer); pains in the calves or chest, sudden shortness of breath, or coughing blood (possible clot in the legs, or lungs); and severe headache or vomiting, dizziness, faintness, changes in vision or speech, weakness or numbness of an arm or leg (possible clot in the brain or eye). The other warning signals it lists are breast lumps (possible breast cancer; it advises asking a doctor or health professional to show how to examine the breasts monthly); yellowing of the skin or eyes (possible liver problem); and pain, swelling, or tenderness in the abdomen (possible gallbladder problem). This listing does not state the capsule's inactive ingredients, capsule shell or storage, or what active ingredients it contains and in what amounts.

content.summary: Progesterone 150 mg capsules are a prescription hormone. Their reference labeling, for 100 mg and 200 mg PROMETRIUM capsules rather than this one, covers preventing endometrial hyperplasia (overgrowth of the uterine lining) in women after menopause who still have a uterus and take conjugated estrogens tablets, and secondary amenorrhea (periods that have stopped). Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These capsules are listed at 150 mg of progesterone, a prescription hormone. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information cited here describes 100 mg and 200 mg capsules of micronized progesterone made with peanut oil; it does not describe this capsule, and the listing does not say whether this capsule's progesterone is micronized or what its vehicle is. PROMETRIUM is labeled for preventing endometrial hyperplasia (overgrowth of the uterine lining) in women after menopause who still have a uterus and take conjugated estrogens tablets, and for secondary amenorrhea (periods that have stopped); it is not for children. Because PROMETRIUM capsules are made with peanut oil, that labeling rules them out for people allergic to peanuts; the listing does not state this capsule's ingredients. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed at 150 mg of progesterone. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the reference label cited here, describes capsules containing 100 mg or 200 mg of micronized progesterone with peanut oil among their inactive ingredients. 150 mg is not a strength it describes, and the listing does not state whether this capsule's progesterone is micronized, what its vehicle is or how it is prepared, so the label's statements describe PROMETRIUM capsules and do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. According to the PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the progesterone in PROMETRIUM capsules is synthesized from a starting material from a plant source and is chemically identical to progesterone of human ovarian origin, and the oral bioavailability of progesterone is increased through micronization. For PROMETRIUM's micronized soft-gelatin capsules, it reports that maximum serum concentrations were attained within 3 hours after oral administration, and that the absolute bioavailability of micronized progesterone is not known. It states that progesterone is approximately 96 percent to 99 percent bound to serum proteins, that it is metabolized primarily by the liver largely to pregnanediols and pregnanolones, and that its metabolites are eliminated mainly by the kidneys. The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules are indicated for use in the prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets, and also for use in secondary amenorrhea. It notes that the effect of hepatic impairment and of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of PROMETRIUM capsules has not been studied. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule, how it is prepared, or whether its progesterone is micronized or its vehicle contains peanut oil as PROMETRIUM capsules do; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (PROMETRIUM prescribing information), which describe PROMETRIUM capsules of 100 mg or 200 mg micronized progesterone and not this capsule: prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets; and secondary amenorrhea. The labeling also states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The PROMETRIUM prescribing information contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with hypersensitivity to its ingredients and, because PROMETRIUM capsules contain peanut oil, in patients allergic to peanuts; this listing does not state the capsule's ingredients or vehicle.

It also contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with abnormal genital bleeding of unknown etiology; known, suspected, or history of breast cancer; active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease (for example, stroke and myocardial infarction) or a history of these conditions; or known liver dysfunction or disease.

Its warnings state that PROMETRIUM should be immediately discontinued if a pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction occurs or is suspected, and that, if feasible, it should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization.

The labeling states that the safety and efficacy of estrogen plus progestogen for the prevention of cardiovascular disorders has not been established, and that the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin trial reported increased risks of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke and myocardial infarction in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age, average age 63.4 years) during 5.6 years of treatment with daily oral conjugated estrogens (0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (2.5 mg), relative to placebo.

It states that only daily oral 0.625 mg conjugated estrogens and 2.5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate were studied in that trial, so the relevance of the WHI findings regarding adverse cardiovascular events to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, and that without such data it is not possible to definitively exclude these risks or determine their extent for other products.

For venous thromboembolism in the overall WHI study population, the labeling reports a relative risk for pulmonary embolism of 1.98 (95% CI, 1.36, 2.87) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (18 versus 9), and a relative risk for deep vein thrombosis of 1.87 (95% CI, 1.37, 2.54), with a risk difference of 12 per 10,000 women-years (25 versus 14).

For the overall WHI population it also reports a relative risk for stroke of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.07, 1.76) with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (33 versus 24), and a relative risk of coronary heart disease of 1.18 (95% CI, 0.95, 1.45) with a risk difference of 6 per 10,000 women-years (41 versus 35), for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo.

Its breast cancer warning states that PROMETRIUM is contraindicated in women with breast cancer, a history of breast cancer, or estrogen-dependent neoplasia, that PROMETRIUM should be discontinued if a hormone-sensitive malignancy is diagnosed, and that the use of estrogen plus progestin therapy has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation.

In the overall WHI population, the labeling reports a relative risk for invasive breast cancer of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01, 1.53) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (43 versus 35); it states that invasive breast cancers were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage in that group, and that the trial did not show a statistically significant difference in breast cancer mortality.

It adds that, consistent with the WHI trial, observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy, and that a large meta-analysis including 24 prospective studies of postmenopausal women comparing current use of estrogen plus progestin products for 5 to 14 years (average of 9 years) versus never use reported a relative risk for breast cancer of 2.08 (95% CI, 2.02 to 2.15). It states that these studies have not generally found significant variation in the risk of breast cancer among different estrogen plus progestin combinations, doses, or routes of administration, and that the relevance of the WHI findings regarding breast cancer to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, so that these risks cannot be definitively excluded or their extent determined for other products.

Its ovarian cancer warning reports, for the overall WHI population, a relative risk for ovarian cancer of 1.41 (95% CI, 0.75 to 2.66) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate versus placebo after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, with a risk difference of 1 per 10,000 women-years (5 versus 4), and a large meta-analysis of 17 prospective studies of postmenopausal women reporting a relative risk of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.26 to 1.48) for current use of estrogen plus progestin products versus never use; it states that the duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown.

Its vision warning states that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogen, that estrogen plus progestin therapy should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that it should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions.

Its precautions state that progesterone may cause some degree of fluid retention, so women with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation.

They also state that PROMETRIUM capsules may cause transient dizziness and drowsiness and should be used with caution when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery; the patient information adds that some women may experience extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness during initial therapy, in a few cases with blurred vision, difficulty speaking, difficulty with walking and feeling abnormal, and says to discuss these symptoms with the healthcare provider right away.

Its drug-interaction section reports that the metabolism of progesterone by human liver microsomes was inhibited by ketoconazole, a known inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, so these data suggest that ketoconazole or other known inhibitors of this enzyme may increase the bioavailability of progesterone, and that the clinical relevance of the in vitro findings is unknown.

It reports that coadministration of conjugated estrogens and PROMETRIUM capsules to 29 postmenopausal women over a 12-day period increased total estrone and total equilin concentrations and decreased circulating 17β estradiol concentrations, while the half-life of the conjugated estrogens was similar with coadministration.

Its precautions also list laboratory results that may be altered by estrogen plus progestin therapy: increased sulfobromophthalein retention and other hepatic function tests; coagulation tests (an increase in prothrombin factors VII, VIII, IX and X); pregnanediol determination; and thyroid function (an increase in PBI and butanol extractable protein bound iodine and a decrease in T3 uptake values).

Its precautions state that exogenously administered progesterone has been shown to inhibit ovulation in a number of species, and that high doses given for an extended duration are expected to impair fertility until the cessation of treatment.

The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules should not be used during pregnancy, and its patient information lists, among serious but less common side effects, risk to the fetus: cases of cleft palate, cleft lip, hypospadias, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, and other congenital heart defects.

It states that detectable amounts of progestin have been identified in the milk of nursing women receiving progestins, that caution should be exercised when PROMETRIUM capsules are administered to a nursing woman, and, in the patient information, that the hormone in PROMETRIUM capsules can pass into breast milk.

It states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children, that clinical studies have not been conducted in the pediatric population, and that there have not been sufficient numbers of geriatric women in clinical studies to determine whether those over 65 years of age differ from younger subjects in their response.

For women over 65, it reports that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy showed a higher relative risk of nonfatal stroke and invasive breast cancer. It also reports that the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study of postmenopausal women 65 to 79 years of age found an increased risk of developing probable dementia with estrogen plus progestin compared to placebo (after an average follow-up of 4 years, a relative risk of 2.05, 95 percent CI 1.21 to 3.48, and an absolute risk of 45 versus 22 per 10,000 women-years), and that it is unknown whether these findings apply to younger postmenopausal women.

Its table of adverse reactions comes from a 3-year, placebo-controlled trial of cyclic PROMETRIUM capsules 200 mg with conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg in postmenopausal women (875 women studied; the table's arms are n = 178 and placebo n = 174) and lists the reactions reported by 2% or more of women. Those are headache (31% versus 27% on placebo), breast tenderness (27% versus 6%), joint pain (20% versus 29%), depression (19% versus 12%), dizziness (15% versus 9%), abdominal bloating (12% versus 5%), hot flashes (11% versus 35%), urinary problems (11% versus 9%), abdominal pain (10% versus 10%), vaginal discharge (10% versus 3%), nausea or vomiting (8% versus 7%), worry (8% versus 4%), chest pain (7% versus 5%), diarrhea (7% versus 4%), night sweats (7% versus 17%), breast pain (6% versus 2%), swelling of hands and feet (6% versus 9%), vaginal dryness (6% versus 10%), constipation (3% versus 2%), and breast carcinoma, breast excisional biopsy and cholecystectomy (2% each versus less than 1%).

In a placebo-controlled trial of PROMETRIUM capsules at 400 mg/day in 49 estrogen-primed postmenopausal women, its table of adverse reactions reported by 5% or more lists fatigue (8% versus 4% on placebo), headache (16% versus 8%), dizziness (24% versus 4%), abdominal distention or bloating (8% versus 8%), abdominal pain or cramping (20% versus 13%), diarrhea (8% versus 4%), nausea (8% versus 0%), back pain (8% versus 8%), musculoskeletal pain (12% versus 4%), irritability (8% versus 4%), breast pain (16% versus 8%), viral infection (12% versus 0%) and coughing (8% versus 0%).

In an open-label postmarketing study of 220 premenopausal women with secondary amenorrhea who received conjugated estrogens with PROMETRIUM capsules, the labeling lists the most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse reactions (5% or more) as nausea, fatigue, vaginal mycosis, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness, abdominal distension, acne, dysmenorrhea, mood swing, and urinary tract infection.

Among additional adverse reactions reported with PROMETRIUM capsules after marketing, which the labeling notes are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size so that their frequency or a causal relationship to drug exposure cannot always be reliably established, it lists genitourinary reactions (endometrial carcinoma, hypospadia, intra-uterine death, menorrhagia, menstrual disorder, metrorrhagia, ovarian cyst, spontaneous abortion) and cardiovascular reactions (circulatory collapse, congenital heart disease including ventricular septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus, hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia).

It also lists gastrointestinal reactions (acute pancreatitis, cholestasis, cholestatic hepatitis, dysphagia, hepatic failure, hepatic necrosis, hepatitis, increased liver function tests, jaundice, swollen tongue), skin reactions (alopecia, pruritus, urticaria) and eye reactions (blurred vision, diplopia, visual disturbance).

Its central nervous system list includes aggression, convulsion, depersonalization, depressed consciousness, disorientation, dysarthria, loss of consciousness, paresthesia, sedation, stupor, syncope (with and without hypotension), transient ischemic attack and suicidal ideation, and it notes that during initial therapy a few women have experienced a constellation of many or all of the following: extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness, blurred vision, slurred speech, difficulty walking, loss of consciousness, vertigo, confusion, disorientation, feeling drunk, and shortness of breath.

Among miscellaneous postmarketing reactions it lists abnormal gait, anaphylactic reaction, arthralgia, blood glucose increased, choking, cleft lip, cleft palate, difficulty walking, dyspnea, face edema, feeling abnormal, feeling drunk, hypersensitivity, asthma, muscle cramp, throat tightness, tinnitus and vertigo, among others.

Its patient information lists abnormal blood clotting (stroke, heart attack, pulmonary embolus, visual loss or blindness) among serious but less common side effects, gives changes in vision or speech, sudden new severe headaches, severe pains in the chest or legs with or without shortness of breath, weakness and fatigue, dizziness and faintness, and vomiting as warning signs of serious side effects, and says to call the healthcare provider right away for any of these warning signs or any other unusual symptoms that concern the patient.

Its patient information lists these less serious but common side effects: headaches; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach or abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; hair loss; fluid retention; and vaginal yeast infection.

Its patient information advises seeing the healthcare provider right away for unusual vaginal bleeding while taking PROMETRIUM capsules. It advises a pelvic exam, breast exam and mammogram every year unless the healthcare provider says otherwise, and says that women whose family members have had breast cancer, or who have ever had breast lumps or an abnormal mammogram, may need breast exams more often. It also advises telling the healthcare provider about all medical problems, since closer checks may be needed with conditions such as asthma, epilepsy, diabetes, migraine, endometriosis, lupus, problems with the heart, liver, thyroid or kidneys, or high calcium levels in the blood, and about all medicines taken, including nonprescription medicines, vitamins and herbal supplements, since some medicines may affect how PROMETRIUM capsules work and PROMETRIUM capsules may affect how other medicines work.

content.summary: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) injection listed at 500 mg/mL in a 10 mL vial, prescription only. Labels for ascorbic acid pharmacy bulk package injections, which the listing does not identify as this vial, cover short-term treatment of scurvy when it cannot be treated by mouth, not vitamin C deficiency without signs of scurvy. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
This listing is ascorbic acid (vitamin C) injection at 500 mg/mL in a 10 mL vial. The ASCOR prescribing information cited here and three other ascorbic acid injection labels describe pharmacy bulk package vials, not this vial. Those labels cover short-term (up to 1 week) treatment of scurvy, a disorder of severe vitamin C deficiency, in adults and children 5 months and older who cannot be treated by mouth, and not other vitamin C deficiency or long-term use. The exact way ascorbic acid treats scurvy is unknown; it is thought to restore the body's supply of vitamin C. The ASCOR label's warnings concern kidney damage from oxalate and kidney stones, breakdown of red blood cells in people with an enzyme deficiency called G6PD deficiency, and effects on laboratory tests. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

This listing is ascorbic acid 500 mg/mL injection in a 10 mL vial, as the pharmacy catalog describes it. The prescribing information cited here is for ASCOR (ascorbic acid injection), for intravenous use, whose label describes a 25,000 mg/50 mL (500 mg/mL) pharmacy bulk package vial intended for dispensing single doses to multiple patients in a pharmacy admixture program. Three other ascorbic acid injection labels, from Zydus Pharmaceuticals (USA), Renova Pharmaceuticals and Fresenius Kabi, describe the same 25,000 mg/50 mL (500 mg/mL) pharmacy bulk package presentation. The Zydus label also lists 5,000 mg/10 mL and 2,500 mg/5 mL pharmacy bulk package vials at the same concentration. The listed 10 mL size matches the 5,000 mg/10 mL pharmacy bulk package size that the Zydus label describes, and a matching concentration or package size does not by itself make the listed vial that product. The listing does not identify its vial as any of those labeled products, and the label statements on this page describe the labeled products, not this vial. The ASCOR label identifies ascorbic acid as vitamin C; it states that the exact mechanism of action of ascorbic acid for the treatment of the symptoms and signs of scurvy, a disorder caused by severe deficiency in vitamin C, is unknown, and that giving ascorbic acid to patients with scurvy is thought to restore the body's pool of it. ASCOR is labeled for the short-term (up to 1 week) treatment of scurvy in adult and pediatric patients age 5 months and older for whom oral administration is not possible, insufficient or contraindicated, and its label states that it is not indicated for vitamin C deficiency that is not associated with signs and symptoms of scurvy or for prolonged administration; the three other labels state the same indication and limitation of use. The ASCOR label reports that ascorbic acid is distributed widely in the body, with large concentrations in the liver, leukocytes, platelets, glandular tissues and the lens of the eye, that a major route of its metabolism is conversion to urinary oxalate, and that the kidney excretes it in large amounts only when the plasma concentration exceeds a renal threshold of approximately 1.4 mg/100 mL. In the single pharmacokinetic study the ASCOR label describes, eight healthy adults given a single intravenous dose of 1000 mg of ascorbic acid, which the label describes as five times its largest recommended single dose, over 30 minutes had a mean peak exposure of 436.2 µM at the end of the infusion, and the mean half-life observed in three of them was 7.4 ± 1.4 hours. The ASCOR label lists no contraindications, and its warnings concern oxalate nephropathy and kidney stones, hemolysis in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and interference with laboratory tests, each detailed under cautions. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the vial, how it is prepared, or whether it is any of the labeled products cited here or a different preparation; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.

specifications.label: Reference prescribing information
specifications.value: ASCOR (ascorbic acid injection) 25,000 mg/50 mL (500 mg/mL) pharmacy bulk package, McGuff Pharmaceuticals; also cited for their presentations and indication: the ascorbic acid injection labels of Zydus Pharmaceuticals (USA), Renova Pharmaceuticals and Fresenius Kabi. Each describes its own product, not this vial.

content.purpose: Labeled indication(s) (ASCOR ascorbic acid injection; the label describes that pharmacy bulk package product, not this vial): short-term (up to 1 week) treatment of scurvy in adult and pediatric patients age 5 months and older for whom oral administration is not possible, insufficient or contraindicated. The label states that ASCOR is not indicated for treatment of vitamin C deficiency that is not associated with signs and symptoms of scurvy, is not indicated for prolonged administration, and is not indicated for use in pediatric patients less than 5 months of age. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions: The ASCOR label lists no contraindications. It reports that acute and chronic oxalate nephropathy have been reported with prolonged administration of high doses of ascorbic acid, and that acidification of the urine by ascorbic acid may cause precipitation of cysteine, urate or oxalate stones. It names patients with renal disease including renal impairment, patients with a history of oxalate kidney stones, and geriatric patients as groups that may be at increased risk for oxalate nephropathy while receiving ascorbic acid, and pediatric patients less than 2 years of age as at increased risk because their kidneys are immature. It directs monitoring of renal function in patients at increased risk receiving ASCOR and discontinuation of ASCOR in patients who develop oxalate nephropathy. The label advises caution with ASCOR in scorbutic patients with a history of or risk of developing renal oxalate stones or evidence of renal impairment or other issues, giving patients on dialysis, patients with diabetic nephropathy and renal transplant recipients as examples, since they may be at increased risk of acute or chronic oxalate nephropathy following high-dose ascorbic acid administration. The label reports that hemolysis has been reported with administration of ascorbic acid in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, who may be at increased risk for severe hemolysis during treatment with ascorbic acid; it directs monitoring of hemoglobin and blood count in these patients and discontinuation of ASCOR if hemolysis is suspected. The label provides dosage reductions for pregnant women, lactating women and patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. The label states that, because ascorbic acid is a strong reducing agent, it can interfere with laboratory tests based on oxidation-reduction reactions, including blood and urine glucose, nitrite and bilirubin levels and leukocyte counts, and may produce false negatives if testing occurs during or within 24 hours after infusion; it advises delaying such tests, if possible, until 24 hours after infusion of ASCOR. Adverse reactions the label identifies from the literature, for which it says neither frequency nor a causal relationship to the drug can always be established, are administration-site pain and swelling; the label also states that rapid intravenous administration of ASCOR may cause temporary faintness or nausea, lethargy, flushing, dizziness and headache. The label states that ascorbic acid may decrease the activities of erythromycin, kanamycin, streptomycin, doxycycline and lincomycin, and that bleomycin is inactivated in vitro by ascorbic acid; it directs discontinuing ASCOR if an antibiotic's efficacy is suspected to be decreased by concomitant administration. The label states that ascorbic acid may acidify the urine and lower serum concentrations of amphetamine by increasing renal excretion, and that acidification of urine by ascorbic acid will alter the excretion of other drugs affected by urine pH, such as fluphenazine, whose plasma concentrations have been reported to decrease with concurrent ascorbic acid. It calls for standard monitoring of such therapy and for discontinuing ASCOR in case of decreased amphetamine efficacy. The label states that limited case reports have suggested interference of ascorbic acid with the anticoagulation effects of warfarin, although no effect was observed in patients on warfarin therapy treated with ascorbic acid doses up to 1000 mg/day for 2 weeks, which the label describes as five times its largest recommended single dose for twice its maximum recommended duration, and that standard monitoring for anticoagulation therapy should continue during ascorbic acid treatment. The label states that there are no available data on use of ASCOR or another ascorbic acid injection in pregnant women, that ascorbic acid (vitamin C) has been used during pregnancy for several decades with no adverse developmental outcomes reported in the published literature, and that animal reproduction studies have not been conducted with ASCOR. The label cites a published meta-analysis of randomized studies of pregnant women who took oral ascorbic acid at 500 to 1000 mg/day, which it describes as 2.5 to 5 times its recommended daily intravenous dose, between the 9th and 16th weeks of pregnancy, which showed no increased risk of miscarriage, preterm premature rupture of membranes, preterm delivery or pregnancy-induced hypertension compared with placebo, while stating that these data cannot definitely establish or exclude the absence of a risk with ascorbic acid during pregnancy. The label states that there are no data on the presence of ascorbic acid in human milk following intravenous dosing in lactating women, although ascorbic acid is present in human milk after maternal oral intake, and that maternal oral intake exceeding the U.S. Recommended Dietary Allowance for lactation does not influence its content in breast milk or the estimated daily amount a breastfed infant receives. It states that there are no data on its effect on milk production or the breastfed infant, and that the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother's clinical need for ASCOR and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child from ASCOR or from the underlying maternal condition. Its pharmacokinetics section adds that, based on data from oral exposure, ascorbic acid is known to be distributed into breast milk and to cross the placental barrier. The label states that the safety profile of ascorbic acid in pediatric patients is similar to adults, that patients less than 2 years of age may be at higher risk of oxalate nephropathy due to age-related decreased glomerular filtration, that ASCOR is not indicated for use in pediatric patients less than 5 months of age, and that the decrease in glomerular filtration rate with age may likewise increase the risk of oxalate nephropathy in elderly patients. The label states that carcinogenicity, mutagenicity and fertility studies have not been performed with ASCOR. The label states that overdose with ascorbic acid may cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, facial flushing, rash, headache, fatigue or disturbed sleep, and directs immediate discontinuation and treatment of the signs and symptoms of overdose, avoiding additional intake of ascorbic acid. The label directs that patients be informed that treatment with ASCOR may increase their risk of oxalate nephropathy, may affect laboratory results including blood and urine glucose tests for up to 24 hours after infusion, and, in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, may increase their risk of hemolysis. Everything above is drawn from the ASCOR label and describes that product or ascorbic acid generally; whether it applies to the listed vial depends on what the dispensed product is, which this listing does not state.

content.summary: Anastrozole 1 mg capsules, a prescription aromatase inhibitor. ARIMIDEX's labeling, written for 1 mg tablets and not this capsule, says anastrozole lowers estrogen and covers certain breast cancers in women after menopause. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These capsules are listed at 1 mg of anastrozole, a prescription medicine called an aromatase inhibitor. According to the ARIMIDEX prescribing information, many breast cancers grow in response to estrogen, which after menopause comes mainly from the aromatase enzyme; anastrozole blocks that enzyme and lowers estradiol, an estrogen. ARIMIDEX is labeled for certain breast cancers in women after menopause, including early hormone receptor-positive breast cancer and advanced breast cancer, and its patient information states that ARIMIDEX does not work in women with breast cancer who have not gone through menopause. That labeling describes 1 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed at 1 mg of anastrozole, a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor. A capsule is a different dosage form from the tablets covered by the ARIMIDEX prescribing information cited here, which describes 1 mg tablets; the statements below describe those tablets and do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. According to the ARIMIDEX prescribing information, the growth of many breast cancers is stimulated or maintained by estrogens, and in postmenopausal women estrogens come mainly from the aromatase enzyme, which converts adrenal androgens (primarily androstenedione and testosterone) to estrone and estradiol. The same labeling describes anastrozole as a selective non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor that significantly lowers serum estradiol concentrations and has no detectable effect on the formation of adrenal corticosteroids or aldosterone. The ARIMIDEX prescribing information indicates ARIMIDEX for adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer, for first-line treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive or hormone receptor-unknown locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer, and for treatment of advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease progression following tamoxifen therapy. It notes that patients with estrogen receptor-negative disease, and patients who did not respond to previous tamoxifen therapy, rarely responded to ARIMIDEX. Its patient information states that ARIMIDEX does not work in women with breast cancer who have not gone through menopause. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule or how it is prepared; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (ARIMIDEX prescribing information), which describe ARIMIDEX tablets and not this capsule: adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer; first-line treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive or hormone receptor-unknown locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer; and treatment of advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease progression following tamoxifen therapy; the labeling notes that patients with estrogen receptor-negative disease and patients who did not respond to previous tamoxifen therapy rarely responded to ARIMIDEX. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The ARIMIDEX prescribing information contraindicates ARIMIDEX in any patient who has shown a hypersensitivity reaction to the drug or to any of its excipients; observed reactions include anaphylaxis, angioedema and urticaria.

Based on findings from animal studies and its mechanism of action, the labeling states that ARIMIDEX can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman, and it notes that there are no studies of ARIMIDEX use in pregnant women; it advises verifying the pregnancy status of females of reproductive potential before starting and using effective contraception during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose, and it advises females to contact their healthcare provider if they become pregnant, or if pregnancy is suspected, during treatment.

Based on studies in female animals, the labeling says ARIMIDEX may impair fertility in females of reproductive potential.

It advises lactating women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 2 weeks after the last dose.

It states that tamoxifen should not be administered with anastrozole, and that estrogen-containing therapies should not be used with ARIMIDEX because they may diminish its pharmacological action.

The labeling reports that in the ATAC trial, women with pre-existing ischemic heart disease had more ischemic cardiovascular events on ARIMIDEX than on tamoxifen (17% versus 10%), and it advises considering the risks and benefits of ARIMIDEX therapy in these patients.

Its patient counseling information says to inform patients of the possibility of serious allergic reactions with swelling of the face, lips, tongue and/or throat, which may cause difficulty in swallowing and/or breathing, and to seek medical attention immediately; it also says that patients with pre-existing ischemic heart disease should be informed that an increased incidence of cardiovascular events has been observed with ARIMIDEX use compared to tamoxifen use, and it advises patients to seek medical attention immediately if new or worsening chest pain or shortness of breath occurs.

It reports that patients receiving ARIMIDEX in the ATAC bone substudy had mean decreases in lumbar spine and total hip bone mineral density, and it advises considering bone mineral density monitoring; it also reports that more patients on ARIMIDEX than on tamoxifen had elevated serum cholesterol (9% versus 3.5%), and its patient counseling information says to inform patients that an increased level of cholesterol might be seen while receiving ARIMIDEX.

It also reports that in the adjuvant trial patients receiving ARIMIDEX had an increase in the incidence of all fractures (specifically fractures of the spine, hip and wrist), 10% versus 7% on tamoxifen, and its patient counseling information notes that a possible consequence of decreased mineral content of bones is an increase in the risk of fractures.

The labeling lists the serious adverse reactions occurring in fewer than 1 in 10,000 patients as skin reactions such as lesions, ulcers or blisters; allergic reactions with swelling of the face, lips, tongue and/or throat, which may cause difficulty swallowing and/or breathing; and changes in liver function blood tests, including inflammation of the liver.

Its patient information says to stop taking ARIMIDEX and call the healthcare provider right away for any skin lesions, ulcers or blisters, or for signs or symptoms of a liver problem such as a general feeling of not being well, yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, or pain on the right side of the stomach area.

It lists the common adverse reactions (10% or more) in women taking ARIMIDEX as hot flashes, asthenia, arthritis, pain, arthralgia, hypertension, depression, nausea and vomiting, rash, osteoporosis, fractures, back pain, insomnia, headache, bone pain, peripheral edema, increased cough, dyspnea, pharyngitis and lymphedema.

The labeling reports that in the adjuvant trial, patients receiving ARIMIDEX had a higher incidence of carpal tunnel syndrome (2.5%) than patients receiving tamoxifen (0.7%), and it says patients should be informed that if they experience tickling, tingling or numbness they should notify their health care provider.

Post-marketing reports, which the labeling says come from a population of uncertain size and cannot always be used to estimate frequency or establish causation, include hepatobiliary events (increases in alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, gamma-GT and bilirubin; hepatitis), rash including erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, allergic reactions including angioedema, urticaria and anaphylaxis, myalgia and hypercalcemia (with or without an increase in parathyroid hormone), and tendon disorders including tendon rupture, tendonitis, tenosynovitis and trigger finger.

content.summary: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) injection listed at 500 mg/mL in a 30 mL vial, prescription only. Labels for ascorbic acid pharmacy bulk package injections, which the listing does not identify as this vial, cover short-term treatment of scurvy when it cannot be treated by mouth, not vitamin C deficiency without signs of scurvy. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
This listing is ascorbic acid (vitamin C) injection at 500 mg/mL in a 30 mL vial. The ASCOR prescribing information cited here and three other ascorbic acid injection labels describe pharmacy bulk package vials, not this vial. Those labels cover short-term (up to 1 week) treatment of scurvy, a disorder of severe vitamin C deficiency, in adults and children 5 months and older who cannot be treated by mouth, and not other vitamin C deficiency or long-term use. The exact way ascorbic acid treats scurvy is unknown; it is thought to restore the body's supply of vitamin C. The ASCOR label's warnings concern kidney damage from oxalate and kidney stones, breakdown of red blood cells in people with an enzyme deficiency called G6PD deficiency, and effects on laboratory tests. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

This listing is ascorbic acid 500 mg/mL injection in a 30 mL vial, as the pharmacy catalog describes it. The prescribing information cited here is for ASCOR (ascorbic acid injection), for intravenous use, whose label describes a 25,000 mg/50 mL (500 mg/mL) pharmacy bulk package vial intended for dispensing single doses to multiple patients in a pharmacy admixture program. Three other ascorbic acid injection labels, from Zydus Pharmaceuticals (USA), Renova Pharmaceuticals and Fresenius Kabi, describe the same 25,000 mg/50 mL (500 mg/mL) pharmacy bulk package presentation. The Zydus label also lists 5,000 mg/10 mL and 2,500 mg/5 mL pharmacy bulk package vials at the same concentration. None of those labels describes a 30 mL presentation, so the listed 30 mL size matches no labeled package, and a matching concentration alone does not make the listed vial any of those products. The listing does not identify its vial as any of those labeled products, and the label statements on this page describe the labeled products, not this vial. The ASCOR label identifies ascorbic acid as vitamin C; it states that the exact mechanism of action of ascorbic acid for the treatment of the symptoms and signs of scurvy, a disorder caused by severe deficiency in vitamin C, is unknown, and that giving ascorbic acid to patients with scurvy is thought to restore the body's pool of it.
