It reports that large doses of estrogen (5 mg conjugated estrogens per day), comparable to those used to treat cancer of the prostate and breast, have been shown in a large prospective clinical trial in men to increase the risks of nonfatal myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism and thrombophlebitis.

The labeling states that, if feasible, estrogens should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization.

Its breast cancer warning states that, after a mean follow-up of 5.6 years, the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy reported an increased risk of invasive breast cancer in women who took daily CE plus MPA (relative risk 1.24; absolute risk 41 versus 33 cases per 10,000 women-years compared with placebo), and that invasive breast cancers in the CE plus MPA group were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage than in the placebo group.

It states that in the WHI estrogen-alone substudy, after an average follow-up of 7.1 years, daily CE (0.625 mg)-alone was not associated with an increased risk of invasive breast cancer (relative risk 0.80).

It adds that observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer for estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller, but still increased, risk for estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use, and that one large meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies reported increased risks that were dependent upon duration of use and could last up to more than 10 years after discontinuation of estrogen plus progestin therapy and estrogen-alone therapy.

It notes that the use of estrogen-alone and estrogen plus progestin has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation, and it states that all women should receive yearly breast examinations by a healthcare provider and perform monthly breast self-examinations, and that mammography examinations should be scheduled based on patient age, risk factors and prior mammogram results.

Its ovarian cancer warning states that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy reported a statistically non-significant increased risk of ovarian cancer: after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, the relative risk for CE plus MPA versus placebo was 1.58 (95 percent CI, 0.77-3.24), and the absolute risk was 4 versus 3 cases per 10,000 women-years.

It adds that a meta-analysis of 17 prospective and 35 retrospective epidemiology studies found that women who used hormonal therapy for menopausal symptoms had an increased risk for ovarian cancer (relative risk 1.41 with current use), that the elevated risk with combined current and recent use (discontinued use within 5 years before cancer diagnosis) was significant for both estrogen-alone and estrogen plus progestin products, and that the exact duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown.

Its gallbladder disease warning states that a 2- to 4-fold increase in the risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery has been reported in postmenopausal women receiving estrogens.

Its hypercalcemia warning states that estrogen administration may lead to severe hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and bone metastases, and that if hypercalcemia occurs, use of the drug should be stopped and appropriate measures taken to reduce the serum calcium level.

Its visual abnormalities warning notes that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogens, and it states that medication should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision, or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that estrogens should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions.

Its precautions section notes that, in a small number of case reports, substantial increases in blood pressure have been attributed to idiosyncratic reactions to estrogens and that a generalized effect of estrogens on blood pressure was not seen in a large, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial, and it states that blood pressure should be monitored at regular intervals with estrogen use.

It states that in patients with pre-existing hypertriglyceridemia, estrogen therapy may be associated with elevations of plasma triglycerides leading to pancreatitis and other complications.

Under its precautions, the labeling notes that estrogens may be poorly metabolized in patients with impaired liver function, and that for patients with a history of cholestatic jaundice associated with past estrogen use or with pregnancy, caution should be exercised and, in the case of recurrence, medication should be discontinued.

It states that estrogen administration leads to increased thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels, that patients dependent on thyroid hormone replacement therapy who are also receiving estrogens may require increased doses of their thyroid replacement therapy, and that these patients should have their thyroid function monitored in order to maintain their free thyroid hormone levels in an acceptable range.

It states that because estrogens may cause some degree of fluid retention, patients with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as asthma, epilepsy, migraine, and cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation when estrogens are prescribed, and that estrogens should be used with caution in individuals with severe hypocalcemia.

It notes that endometriosis may be exacerbated with administration of estrogens and that a few cases of malignant transformation of residual endometrial implants have been reported in women treated post-hysterectomy with estrogen alone therapy, and it states that for patients known to have residual endometriosis post-hysterectomy, the addition of progestin should be considered.

It states that estrogens may cause an exacerbation of asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraine or porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas and should be used with caution in women with these conditions.

Its clinical pharmacology section states that estrogens are metabolized partially by cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), and that inducers or inhibitors of CYP3A4 may therefore affect estrogen drug metabolism.

It gives St. John’s Wort preparations (Hypericum perforatum), phenobarbital, carbamazepine and rifampin as examples of CYP3A4 inducers that may reduce plasma concentrations of estrogens, possibly resulting in a decrease in therapeutic effects and/or changes in the uterine bleeding profile.

It gives erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and grapefruit juice as examples of CYP3A4 inhibitors that may increase plasma concentrations of estrogens and may result in side effects.

The labeling states that estrogen administration to nursing mothers has been shown to decrease the quantity and quality of the milk, that detectable amounts of estrogens have been identified in the milk of mothers receiving this drug, and that caution should be exercised when estradiol is administered to a nursing woman.

Its patient information lists these common side effects: headache; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach/abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; and hair loss.

It also lists these other side effects: high blood pressure; liver problems; high blood sugar; fluid retention; enlargement of benign tumors (“fibroids”) of the uterus; a spotty darkening of the skin, particularly on the face; and vaginal yeast infection.

Its patient information advises calling the doctor immediately if any of the warning signals it lists, or any other unusual symptoms, happen while using estrogens; those signals include abnormal bleeding from the vagina (possible uterine cancer); pains in the calves or chest, sudden shortness of breath, or coughing blood (possible clot in the legs, or lungs); and severe headache or vomiting, dizziness, faintness, changes in vision or speech, weakness or numbness of an arm or leg (possible clot in the brain or eye).

The other warning signals it lists are breast lumps (possible breast cancer; it advises asking a doctor or health professional to show how to examine the breasts monthly); yellowing of the skin or eyes (possible liver problem); and pain, swelling, or tenderness in the abdomen (possible gallbladder problem).

content.summary: Sildenafil 110 mg capsules, a prescription capsule form of sildenafil, a PDE5 inhibitor. VIAGRA labeling, written for 25, 50 and 100 mg tablets and not this capsule, says sildenafil helps blood flow into the penis during sexual stimulation and covers erectile dysfunction. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
The catalog lists each capsule as sildenafil 110 mg, a PDE5 inhibitor; a capsule is a different form from the VIAGRA tablets cited here. According to the VIAGRA prescribing information, sexual stimulation releases nitric oxide, which relaxes smooth muscle so blood can flow into the penis; sildenafil strengthens this by blocking PDE5 and, at the doses the label recommends for VIAGRA tablets, has no effect without sexual stimulation. VIAGRA is labeled for the treatment of erectile dysfunction. That labeling describes 25, 50 and 100 mg tablets, so it does not show how this capsule is absorbed or how well it works. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

The catalog lists each capsule as sildenafil 110 mg. Sildenafil is a selective inhibitor of cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5). A capsule is a different dosage form from the film-coated tablets covered by the VIAGRA prescribing information cited here. According to the VIAGRA prescribing information, erection involves the release of nitric oxide in the corpus cavernosum during sexual stimulation; nitric oxide activates the enzyme guanylate cyclase, which raises cyclic GMP (cGMP), relaxing smooth muscle and allowing blood to flow in. The VIAGRA label states that sildenafil enhances the effect of nitric oxide by inhibiting PDE5, the enzyme responsible for breaking down cGMP in the corpus cavernosum, and that sildenafil at the doses it recommends for VIAGRA tablets has no effect in the absence of sexual stimulation. The VIAGRA prescribing information indicates VIAGRA for the treatment of erectile dysfunction and describes its tablets as containing sildenafil citrate equivalent to 25 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg of sildenafil. Those statements describe VIAGRA tablets; they do not establish how this capsule is absorbed or how it performs. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule, how it is prepared, or whether its strength is expressed as sildenafil or as the citrate salt; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.

content.cautions: The VIAGRA prescribing information contraindicates VIAGRA with nitric oxide donors such as organic nitrates or nitrites in any form, taken regularly or intermittently, with guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat, and in people with a known hypersensitivity to sildenafil or any component of the tablet. It notes a potential cardiac risk of sexual activity in people with preexisting cardiovascular disease, and advises stopping all PDE5 inhibitors and seeking prompt medical attention after a sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes or a sudden decrease or loss of hearing. It states that treatments for erectile dysfunction, including VIAGRA, should not generally be used in men for whom sexual activity is inadvisable because of their underlying cardiovascular status. It reports prolonged erections lasting more than 4 hours and priapism, and states that a patient with an erection that persists longer than 4 hours should seek immediate medical assistance, because priapism that is not treated immediately could result in penile tissue damage and permanent loss of potency. It also advises caution with alpha-blockers and other blood-pressure medicines, and notes that ritonavir substantially increases sildenafil levels. The VIAGRA label states that the safety and efficacy of combinations of VIAGRA with other PDE5 inhibitors, including REVATIO or other pulmonary arterial hypertension treatments containing sildenafil, or with other treatments for erectile dysfunction have not been studied. The VIAGRA label states that such combinations may further lower blood pressure and that their use is not recommended. The VIAGRA label also notes postmarketing reports of bleeding events in patients who have taken VIAGRA, and states that a causal relationship between VIAGRA and these events has not been established. It also states that VIAGRA offers no protection against sexually transmitted diseases.

The catalog lists Bi-Est 1.25 mg (80/20) capsules; it does not name the ingredients, say which ingredient each figure of the ratio refers to, or say whether the stated milligram amount is the total of the ingredients or that of one of them. The FDA reports that, at its request, the National Academies (NASEM) evaluated the scientific evidence and in July 2020 provided the FDA with an analysis of compounded bioidentical hormone therapy. That report includes an appendix table of such formulations with two or more active ingredients, drawn from resources its note lists (peer-reviewed literature, adverse event reports, information provided by practitioners, outsourcing facility preparation reports and pharmacies’ online marketing); the table lists “Bi-Estrogen” and “Bi-Est” preparations whose active ingredients are estradiol and estriol, writes the ratios of a capsule entry and a cream entry as estriol/estradiol (for example 80/20) and describes “Bi-Est 50:50” as 50% estradiol and 50% estriol, but it does not describe this capsule, and the catalog does not say that its ratio follows the same order. It adds that circulating estrogens modulate the pituitary secretion of the gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), through a negative feedback mechanism, and that estrogens act to reduce the elevated levels of these hormones seen in postmenopausal women. Its boxed warning states that estrogens increase the risk of endometrial cancer, and it also addresses cardiovascular and other risks, including findings from the Women’s Health Initiative studies. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule or how it is prepared; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.

content.cautions: The VIAGRA prescribing information contraindicates VIAGRA with nitric oxide donors such as organic nitrates or nitrites in any form, taken regularly or intermittently, with guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat, and in people with a known hypersensitivity to sildenafil or any component of the tablet. It notes a potential cardiac risk of sexual activity in people with preexisting cardiovascular disease, and advises stopping all PDE5 inhibitors and seeking prompt medical attention after a sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes or a sudden decrease or loss of hearing. It states that treatments for erectile dysfunction, including VIAGRA, should not generally be used in men for whom sexual activity is inadvisable because of their underlying cardiovascular status. It reports prolonged erections lasting more than 4 hours and priapism, and states that a patient with an erection that persists longer than 4 hours should seek immediate medical assistance, because priapism that is not treated immediately could result in penile tissue damage and permanent loss of potency. It also advises caution with alpha-blockers and other blood-pressure medicines, and notes that ritonavir substantially increases sildenafil levels. The VIAGRA label states that the safety and efficacy of combinations of VIAGRA with other PDE5 inhibitors, including REVATIO or other pulmonary arterial hypertension treatments containing sildenafil, or with other treatments for erectile dysfunction have not been studied. The VIAGRA label states that such combinations may further lower blood pressure and that their use is not recommended. The VIAGRA label also notes postmarketing reports of bleeding events in patients who have taken VIAGRA, and states that a causal relationship between VIAGRA and these events has not been established. It also states that VIAGRA offers no protection against sexually transmitted diseases.

content.summary: Progesterone 25 mg sustained-release capsules are a prescription hormone. Their reference labeling, for 100 mg and 200 mg PROMETRIUM capsules and no sustained-release product, covers preventing endometrial hyperplasia (overgrowth of the uterine lining) in women after menopause who still have a uterus and take conjugated estrogens tablets, and secondary amenorrhea (periods that have stopped). Clinical review required.
content.overview:
These sustained-release capsules are listed at 25 mg of progesterone, a prescription hormone. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information cited here describes 100 mg and 200 mg capsules of micronized progesterone made with peanut oil and no sustained-release product, and the listing does not say how this capsule releases its progesterone or what its vehicle is. PROMETRIUM is labeled for preventing endometrial hyperplasia (overgrowth of the uterine lining) in women after menopause who still have a uterus and take conjugated estrogens tablets, and for secondary amenorrhea (periods that have stopped); it is not for children. Because PROMETRIUM capsules are made with peanut oil, that labeling rules them out for people allergic to peanuts; the listing does not state this capsule's ingredients. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

Each capsule is listed as a sustained-release capsule at 25 mg of progesterone. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the reference label cited here, describes capsules containing 100 mg or 200 mg of micronized progesterone with peanut oil among their inactive ingredients. It describes no sustained-release product, and the listing does not state how this capsule releases its progesterone, whether the progesterone is micronized, what the vehicle is or how the capsule is prepared, so the label's statements describe PROMETRIUM capsules and do not establish how this sustained-release capsule releases or absorbs progesterone or how it performs. According to the PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the progesterone in PROMETRIUM capsules is synthesized from a starting material from a plant source and is chemically identical to progesterone of human ovarian origin, and the oral bioavailability of progesterone is increased through micronization. For PROMETRIUM's micronized soft-gelatin capsules, it reports that maximum serum concentrations were attained within 3 hours after oral administration, and that the absolute bioavailability of micronized progesterone is not known. It states that progesterone is approximately 96 percent to 99 percent bound to serum proteins, that it is metabolized primarily by the liver largely to pregnanediols and pregnanolones, and that its metabolites are eliminated mainly by the kidneys. The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules are indicated for use in the prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets, and also for use in secondary amenorrhea. It notes that the effect of hepatic impairment and of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of PROMETRIUM capsules has not been studied. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the capsule, how it is prepared, or whether its progesterone is micronized or its vehicle contains peanut oil as PROMETRIUM capsules do; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Labeled indications (PROMETRIUM prescribing information), which describe PROMETRIUM capsules of 100 mg or 200 mg micronized progesterone and not this sustained-release capsule: prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets; and secondary amenorrhea. The labeling also states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions:
The PROMETRIUM prescribing information contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with hypersensitivity to its ingredients and, because PROMETRIUM capsules contain peanut oil, in patients allergic to peanuts; this listing does not state the capsule's ingredients or vehicle.

It also contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with abnormal genital bleeding of unknown etiology; known, suspected, or history of breast cancer; active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease (for example, stroke and myocardial infarction) or a history of these conditions; or known liver dysfunction or disease.

Its warnings state that PROMETRIUM should be immediately discontinued if a pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction occurs or is suspected, and that, if feasible, it should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization.

The labeling states that the safety and efficacy of estrogen plus progestogen for the prevention of cardiovascular disorders has not been established, and that the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin trial reported increased risks of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke and myocardial infarction in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age, average age 63.4 years) during 5.6 years of treatment with daily oral conjugated estrogens (0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (2.5 mg), relative to placebo.

It states that only daily oral 0.625 mg conjugated estrogens and 2.5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate were studied in that trial, so the relevance of the WHI findings regarding adverse cardiovascular events to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, and that without such data it is not possible to definitively exclude these risks or determine their extent for other products.

For venous thromboembolism in the overall WHI study population, the labeling reports a relative risk for pulmonary embolism of 1.98 (95% CI, 1.36, 2.87) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (18 versus 9), and a relative risk for deep vein thrombosis of 1.87 (95% CI, 1.37, 2.54), with a risk difference of 12 per 10,000 women-years (25 versus 14).

For the overall WHI population it also reports a relative risk for stroke of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.07, 1.76) with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (33 versus 24), and a relative risk of coronary heart disease of 1.18 (95% CI, 0.95, 1.45) with a risk difference of 6 per 10,000 women-years (41 versus 35), for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo.

Its breast cancer warning states that PROMETRIUM is contraindicated in women with breast cancer, a history of breast cancer, or estrogen-dependent neoplasia, that PROMETRIUM should be discontinued if a hormone-sensitive malignancy is diagnosed, and that the use of estrogen plus progestin therapy has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation.

In the overall WHI population, the labeling reports a relative risk for invasive breast cancer of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01, 1.53) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (43 versus 35); it states that invasive breast cancers were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage in that group, and that the trial did not show a statistically significant difference in breast cancer mortality.

It adds that, consistent with the WHI trial, observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy, and that a large meta-analysis including 24 prospective studies of postmenopausal women comparing current use of estrogen plus progestin products for 5 to 14 years (average of 9 years) versus never use reported a relative risk for breast cancer of 2.08 (95% CI, 2.02 to 2.15). It states that these studies have not generally found significant variation in the risk of breast cancer among different estrogen plus progestin combinations, doses, or routes of administration, and that the relevance of the WHI findings regarding breast cancer to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, so that these risks cannot be definitively excluded or their extent determined for other products.

Its ovarian cancer warning reports, for the overall WHI population, a relative risk for ovarian cancer of 1.41 (95% CI, 0.75 to 2.66) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate versus placebo after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, with a risk difference of 1 per 10,000 women-years (5 versus 4), and a large meta-analysis of 17 prospective studies of postmenopausal women reporting a relative risk of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.26 to 1.48) for current use of estrogen plus progestin products versus never use; it states that the duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown.

Its vision warning states that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogen, that estrogen plus progestin therapy should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that it should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions.

Its precautions state that progesterone may cause some degree of fluid retention, so women with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation.

They also state that PROMETRIUM capsules may cause transient dizziness and drowsiness and should be used with caution when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery; the patient information adds that some women may experience extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness during initial therapy, in a few cases with blurred vision, difficulty speaking, difficulty with walking and feeling abnormal, and says to discuss these symptoms with the healthcare provider right away.

Its drug-interaction section reports that the metabolism of progesterone by human liver microsomes was inhibited by ketoconazole, a known inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, so these data suggest that ketoconazole or other known inhibitors of this enzyme may increase the bioavailability of progesterone, and that the clinical relevance of the in vitro findings is unknown.

It reports that coadministration of conjugated estrogens and PROMETRIUM capsules to 29 postmenopausal women over a 12-day period increased total estrone and total equilin concentrations and decreased circulating 17β estradiol concentrations, while the half-life of the conjugated estrogens was similar with coadministration.

Its precautions also list laboratory results that may be altered by estrogen plus progestin therapy: increased sulfobromophthalein retention and other hepatic function tests; coagulation tests (an increase in prothrombin factors VII, VIII, IX and X); pregnanediol determination; and thyroid function (an increase in PBI and butanol extractable protein bound iodine and a decrease in T3 uptake values).

Its precautions state that exogenously administered progesterone has been shown to inhibit ovulation in a number of species, and that high doses given for an extended duration are expected to impair fertility until the cessation of treatment.

The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules should not be used during pregnancy, and its patient information lists, among serious but less common side effects, risk to the fetus: cases of cleft palate, cleft lip, hypospadias, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, and other congenital heart defects.

It states that detectable amounts of progestin have been identified in the milk of nursing women receiving progestins, that caution should be exercised when PROMETRIUM capsules are administered to a nursing woman, and, in the patient information, that the hormone in PROMETRIUM capsules can pass into breast milk.

It states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children, that clinical studies have not been conducted in the pediatric population, and that there have not been sufficient numbers of geriatric women in clinical studies to determine whether those over 65 years of age differ from younger subjects in their response.

For women over 65, it reports that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy showed a higher relative risk of nonfatal stroke and invasive breast cancer. It also reports that the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study of postmenopausal women 65 to 79 years of age found an increased risk of developing probable dementia with estrogen plus progestin compared to placebo (after an average follow-up of 4 years, a relative risk of 2.05, 95 percent CI 1.21 to 3.48, and an absolute risk of 45 versus 22 per 10,000 women-years), and that it is unknown whether these findings apply to younger postmenopausal women.

Its table of adverse reactions comes from a 3-year, placebo-controlled trial of cyclic PROMETRIUM capsules 200 mg with conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg in postmenopausal women (875 women studied; the table's arms are n = 178 and placebo n = 174) and lists the reactions reported by 2% or more of women. Those are headache (31% versus 27% on placebo), breast tenderness (27% versus 6%), joint pain (20% versus 29%), depression (19% versus 12%), dizziness (15% versus 9%), abdominal bloating (12% versus 5%), hot flashes (11% versus 35%), urinary problems (11% versus 9%), abdominal pain (10% versus 10%), vaginal discharge (10% versus 3%), nausea or vomiting (8% versus 7%), worry (8% versus 4%), chest pain (7% versus 5%), diarrhea (7% versus 4%), night sweats (7% versus 17%), breast pain (6% versus 2%), swelling of hands and feet (6% versus 9%), vaginal dryness (6% versus 10%), constipation (3% versus 2%), and breast carcinoma, breast excisional biopsy and cholecystectomy (2% each versus less than 1%).

In a placebo-controlled trial of PROMETRIUM capsules at 400 mg/day in 49 estrogen-primed postmenopausal women, its table of adverse reactions reported by 5% or more lists fatigue (8% versus 4% on placebo), headache (16% versus 8%), dizziness (24% versus 4%), abdominal distention or bloating (8% versus 8%), abdominal pain or cramping (20% versus 13%), diarrhea (8% versus 4%), nausea (8% versus 0%), back pain (8% versus 8%), musculoskeletal pain (12% versus 4%), irritability (8% versus 4%), breast pain (16% versus 8%), viral infection (12% versus 0%) and coughing (8% versus 0%).

In an open-label postmarketing study of 220 premenopausal women with secondary amenorrhea who received conjugated estrogens with PROMETRIUM capsules, the labeling lists the most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse reactions (5% or more) as nausea, fatigue, vaginal mycosis, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness, abdominal distension, acne, dysmenorrhea, mood swing, and urinary tract infection.

Among additional adverse reactions reported with PROMETRIUM capsules after marketing, which the labeling notes are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size so that their frequency or a causal relationship to drug exposure cannot always be reliably established, it lists genitourinary reactions (endometrial carcinoma, hypospadia, intra-uterine death, menorrhagia, menstrual disorder, metrorrhagia, ovarian cyst, spontaneous abortion) and cardiovascular reactions (circulatory collapse, congenital heart disease including ventricular septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus, hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia).

It also lists gastrointestinal reactions (acute pancreatitis, cholestasis, cholestatic hepatitis, dysphagia, hepatic failure, hepatic necrosis, hepatitis, increased liver function tests, jaundice, swollen tongue), skin reactions (alopecia, pruritus, urticaria) and eye reactions (blurred vision, diplopia, visual disturbance).

Its central nervous system list includes aggression, convulsion, depersonalization, depressed consciousness, disorientation, dysarthria, loss of consciousness, paresthesia, sedation, stupor, syncope (with and without hypotension), transient ischemic attack and suicidal ideation, and it notes that during initial therapy a few women have experienced a constellation of many or all of the following: extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness, blurred vision, slurred speech, difficulty walking, loss of consciousness, vertigo, confusion, disorientation, feeling drunk, and shortness of breath.

Among miscellaneous postmarketing reactions it lists abnormal gait, anaphylactic reaction, arthralgia, blood glucose increased, choking, cleft lip, cleft palate, difficulty walking, dyspnea, face edema, feeling abnormal, feeling drunk, hypersensitivity, asthma, muscle cramp, throat tightness, tinnitus and vertigo, among others.

Its patient information lists abnormal blood clotting (stroke, heart attack, pulmonary embolus, visual loss or blindness) among serious but less common side effects, gives changes in vision or speech, sudden new severe headaches, severe pains in the chest or legs with or without shortness of breath, weakness and fatigue, dizziness and faintness, and vomiting as warning signs of serious side effects, and says to call the healthcare provider right away for any of these warning signs or any other unusual symptoms that concern the patient.

Its patient information lists these less serious but common side effects: headaches; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach or abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; hair loss; fluid retention; and vaginal yeast infection.

Its patient information advises seeing the healthcare provider right away for unusual vaginal bleeding while taking PROMETRIUM capsules. It advises a pelvic exam, breast exam and mammogram every year unless the healthcare provider says otherwise, and says that women whose family members have had breast cancer, or who have ever had breast lumps or an abnormal mammogram, may need breast exams more often. It also advises telling the healthcare provider about all medical problems, since closer checks may be needed with conditions such as asthma, epilepsy, diabetes, migraine, endometriosis, lupus, problems with the heart, liver, thyroid or kidneys, or high calcium levels in the blood, and about all medicines taken, including nonprescription medicines, vitamins and herbal supplements, since some medicines may affect how PROMETRIUM capsules work and PROMETRIUM capsules may affect how other medicines work.

content.summary: Prescription topical solution for hair loss, listed at minoxidil 5% and finasteride 0.1% in a 60 mL fill. Minoxidil 5% alone is sold over the counter to regrow hair in men, but the FDA states there is no FDA-approved topical finasteride. Clinical review required.
content.overview:
This prescription solution, for use on the skin, is listed at minoxidil 5% and finasteride 0.1% in a 60 mL fill. Minoxidil 5% solution is sold over the counter to regrow hair on the top of the scalp in men; its label says regrowth takes time, differs from person to person and will not work for all men. Finasteride blocks the enzyme that turns testosterone into DHT, a hormone found at higher levels in balding scalp. Finasteride 1 mg tablets are labeled for male pattern hair loss in men only, and the FDA states there is no FDA-approved topical finasteride. A licensed clinician reviews each request and decides whether it is appropriate.

This topical solution is listed at minoxidil 5% and finasteride 0.1% in a 60 mL fill. Minoxidil 5% topical solution is sold over the counter as an FDA-approved hair regrowth treatment for men, labeled to regrow hair on the top of the scalp. That Drug Facts label notes that regrowth takes time, that the amount differs from person to person, and that it will not work for all men. Finasteride is a competitive and specific inhibitor of Type II 5α-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT); according to the PROPECIA prescribing information, the balding scalp contains miniaturized hair follicles and more DHT than hairy scalp. Oral finasteride 1 mg is FDA-approved for male pattern hair loss in men only, but the FDA states that there is no FDA-approved topical formulation of finasteride and that compounded topical finasteride products do not have FDA-approved labeling. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.
content.purpose: Clinician-directed topical hair-loss therapy. The FDA states that there is no FDA-approved topical formulation of finasteride.
content.cautions: The FDA has alerted providers and consumers to adverse events reported with compounded topical finasteride, including erectile dysfunction, decreased libido, anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, brain fog, fatigue, insomnia and testicular pain, as well as skin irritation, redness, dryness, stinging and burning. The FDA also noted a greater potential for transfer of the applied product to others, particularly females; finasteride is contraindicated in women who are or may become pregnant because of the risk to a male fetus. The FDA-approved minoxidil 5% Drug Facts label advises avoiding contact with the eyes and stopping use and asking a doctor if chest pain, rapid heartbeat, faintness or dizziness, sudden unexplained weight gain, swelling of the hands or feet, or scalp irritation occurs. Discuss these risks with the prescribing clinician before starting.

content.summary: This listing states two components, BPC-157 and TB-500, described separately. No source cited studied them together, and the findings for each do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed amounts: BPC-157 10 mg and TB-500 10 mg, for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this listing states two separate materials in one product: BPC-157 and TB-500. Each is described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. What the cited work establishes is reported for one of them at a time, in the cell and animal models described for that material. What none of it establishes is anything about the combination, because the properties of a combination do not follow from the separate literature of its parts. The amounts are the catalog's own, stated below. The full technical description follows.

This listing states two components at the amounts given in its label: BPC-157 at 10 mg and TB-500 at 10 mg. The two are described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide (Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val) whose sequence is a partial sequence of body protection compound, a protein first isolated from human gastric juice. In cultured rat Achilles tendon explants, it accelerated the outgrowth of tendon fibroblasts. In isolated rat tendon fibroblasts, it did not directly change proliferation but improved cell survival under hydrogen peroxide stress, and it increased cell migration and spreading in a concentration-dependent way, with increased phosphorylation of the focal adhesion proteins FAK and paxillin. A follow-up study in these fibroblasts found that BPC-157 increased growth hormone receptor expression, and that adding growth hormone then increased proliferation and activated Janus kinase 2 signaling. A pharmacokinetic study measured a plasma elimination half-life of under 30 minutes for the intact peptide in rats and beagle dogs; in that study's separate experiment with tritium-labeled BPC-157 in rats, the excreted radioactivity was found mainly in urine and bile, and the authors reported that the peptide was broken down within minutes into small peptide fragments and, ultimately, single amino acids. A 2025 systematic review of BPC-157 in orthopaedic sports medicine included 35 preclinical studies and one retrospective clinical report, and reported that it found no clinical safety data in the literature it reviewed. TB-500 is a product name rather than a chemical name. A 2012 analytical study identified the peptide in TB-500 as Ac-LKKTETQ, the N-terminally acetylated 17 to 23 fragment of human thymosin beta-4, using high-performance liquid chromatography with high-resolution mass spectrometry, and prepared Ac-LKKTETQ separately by solid-phase peptide synthesis for comparison. That study examined a product sold under the name, so it establishes what the name has been shown to denote and not the composition of this listing. The seven-residue peptide is not thymosin beta-4 itself: reference records give the mature thymosin beta-4 chain as 43 residues, against the seven of this acetylated fragment, so findings reported for the 43-residue protein cannot be assumed to apply to a seven-residue fragment, and what this listing contains is not established. A 2015 evaluation of in vitro models for the metabolism of small peptide hormones included TB-500 among the peptides examined in human liver microsome and S9 fraction preparations. Nothing about a combination of the two is asserted. Each finding above is reported for one peptide on its own, and the properties of a combination are not established by the separate literature of its parts. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The laboratory and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with listed amounts of 10 mg of BPC-157 and 10 mg of TB-500, for nonclinical laboratory research.
content.purpose: Nonclinical research on each listed peptide separately, in the cell and animal models described for it.
content.label: For laboratory research use only.
content.cautions: For nonclinical laboratory research only. Not for human or veterinary use.

content.summary: This listing states two components, CJC-1295 (No DAC) and IPAMORELIN, described separately. In plain terms, this listing states two separate materials in one product: CJC-1295 (No DAC) and IPAMORELIN. Each is described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. What the cited work establishes is reported for one of them at a time, in the studies described for each below. What none of it establishes is anything about the combination, because the properties of a combination do not follow from the separate literature of its parts. The amounts are the catalog's own, stated below. The full technical description follows.

This listing states 2 components at the amounts given in its label: CJC-1295 (No DAC) at 10 mg and IPAMORELIN at 10 mg. Each is described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. CJC-1295 is a synthetic analogue of human growth-hormone-releasing factor, and this listing's label states the form without the drug affinity complex. That distinction is drawn in the published record: a 2021 analytical study of growth-hormone-releasing-hormone analogues counts CJC-1295 and CJC-1295 with drug affinity complex as two separate analytes. The 2005 study that identified the compound describes CJC-1295 as a tetrasubstituted form of hGRF(1-29) with an added N-epsilon-3-maleimidopropionamide derivative of lysine at the C terminus, and a 2026 analytical report describes a drug affinity complex as chemically crosslinking the peptide to plasma proteins that carry free cysteine residues. The findings reported for the complex-forming compound therefore do not carry over to this listing: its persistence in plasma beyond 72 hours, and the immunoreactivity seen on the serum-albumin band, were properties of the maleimide-bearing molecule, and the qualifier on this label states the form without that group. What the 2005 work does report for the unmodified parent is that hGRF(1-29) itself gave a smaller area under the growth-hormone curve over two hours in rats than the conjugated compound. In the sources read for this listing, the form without the complex is not separately characterised under this name, so this description states what the name denotes and what the qualifier excludes rather than what this material is. Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide (Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2) developed as a growth hormone secretagogue. It came from a series of compounds that lack the central Ala-Trp dipeptide of growth hormone-releasing peptide 1 (GHRP-1). In primary rat pituitary cells, anaesthetised rats and conscious swine it released growth hormone with potency and efficacy comparable to GHRP-6, and antagonist studies indicated that, like GHRP-6, it acts through a GHRP-type receptor. In swine, none of the tested secretagogues changed FSH, LH, prolactin or TSH; GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 increased ACTH and cortisol, whereas the levels after ipamorelin did not differ significantly from those after GHRH, even at more than 200 times the amount needed for half-maximal growth hormone release. In adult female rats given ipamorelin for 15 days, longitudinal bone growth and body-weight gain increased with the amount given, while total IGF-I and serum markers of bone turnover did not change. A small randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 study in 117 adults after bowel resection, which described ipamorelin as a ghrelin-receptor agonist, found no significant difference from placebo in its efficacy measures. These cell, animal and early clinical findings do not establish that this research material is safe or effective in people. Nothing about a combination of them is asserted. Each finding above is reported for one substance on its own, and the properties of a combination are not established by the separate literature of its parts. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The laboratory and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with listed amounts of 10 mg of CJC-1295 (No DAC) and 10 mg of IPAMORELIN, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.overview:
In plain terms, this listing states two separate materials in one product: CAGRILINTIDE and SEMAGLUTIDE. Each is described separately below. Three of the sources cited here name both components - the developer's 2021 and 2025 reports and a 2026 systematic review - and the 2025 report describes cagrilintide adding to the effects of semaglutide in diet-induced obese rats. What is still not asserted is any property of the two together for this listing: the cited findings do not establish what the listed material contains or how it performs. The amounts are the catalog's own, stated below. The full technical description follows.

This listing states 2 components at the amounts given in its label: CAGRILINTIDE at 10 mg and SEMAGLUTIDE at 10 mg. Each is described separately below. Three sources cited here name both components: the developer's 2021 and 2025 reports and a 2026 systematic review. No property of the two together is asserted for this listing. Cagrilintide is a lipidated analogue of amylin, a pancreatic hormone whose native form readily forms amyloid fibrils; its developer reported it in 2021 as a stable, long-acting amylin analogue selected for clinical development. The PubChem record describes it as a 37-amino-acid peptide amide with one disulfide bridge and a C20 fatty diacid attached through a γ-glutamyl spacer to its N-terminal lysine. A 2026 structural study reported cryo-electron-microscopy structures of cagrilintide bound to the amylin-1 receptor and to the calcitonin receptor, each with a Gs protein, and described it as a dual agonist that activates Gs signaling through both receptors with a similar binding mode at each; the authors noted a salt bridge between residues 14 and 17 that stabilizes its helix and a phenylalanine at position 23 that anchors the peptide at the receptor's transmembrane bundle. In a 2025 report from its developer, cagrilintide and a closely related tool compound reduced food intake in normal-weight rats after acute administration, had small and transient effects on food intake and body weight in diet-induced obese mice, and in diet-induced obese rats markedly reduced food intake and body weight, mainly through loss of fat mass, while adding to the effects of semaglutide. As of its developer's 2025 report and a 2026 systematic review of trials published to March 2026, cagrilintide was in clinical development alone and in a combination with semaglutide. Semaglutide is an analogue of human glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) with two amino-acid substitutions, aminoisobutyric acid at position 8 and arginine at position 34, and a C18 fatty diacid attached through a hydrophilic spacer to the lysine at position 26; the fatty diacid binds albumin reversibly, which prolongs the peptide's presence in circulation. Position 8 was changed because native GLP-1 is cleaved there by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, and in the developer's early work aminoisobutyric acid at that position was the only substitution that gave both enzyme stability and high receptor affinity. In the discovery report, semaglutide bound the GLP-1 receptor with an affinity of 0.38 nM, about three-fold lower than liraglutide, while binding albumin more strongly, and among fatty diacids of 12 to 20 carbons tested with the same linker, the C18 diacid gave the highest albumin affinity together with receptor potency. In a 2020 rodent study, semaglutide changed food preference, reduced food intake and lowered body weight without decreasing energy expenditure; in mice, fluorescently labeled semaglutide reached the brainstem, septal nucleus and hypothalamus through circumventricular organs and sites next to the ventricles rather than by crossing the blood-brain barrier, with the signal clearly decreased in every brain region except the choroid plexus in animals lacking a functional GLP-1 receptor; separately, in a cohort whose species the report does not state, whole-brain mapping of c-Fos, a marker of neuronal activation, four hours after acute administration showed increased activation in ten brain regions, overlapping the compound's direct access only in the area postrema, the nucleus of the solitary tract and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, with the activation elsewhere, including the lateral parabrachial nucleus, interpreted by the authors as secondary. Nothing about a combination of them is asserted. Apart from the rat finding with semaglutide reported above, each finding is reported for one substance on its own, and none establishes the properties of this listing. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The laboratory and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with listed amounts of 10 mg of CAGRILINTIDE and 10 mg of SEMAGLUTIDE, for nonclinical laboratory research.

This listing states 2 components at the amounts given in its label: DSIP at 2 mg and SELANK at 10 mg. Each is described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. Delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP) is a nine-amino-acid peptide, Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu, isolated in 1977 from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits by a research group in Basel and named for its effect on the electroencephalogram (EEG). In the original double-blind study in rabbits, synthetic DSIP infused into the brain ventricles significantly increased delta-wave and spindle EEG activity compared with controls. Of the other eight peptides tested, rabbits given one of the three shortest (two fragments and a related tripeptide) showed less significant differences from controls, and rabbits given one of the remaining five, three longer fragments and two analogues with two amino acids exchanged, did not differ significantly from controls. A 2006 review noted that this link to sleep had never been further characterized, partly because no gene, precursor protein or receptor for DSIP had been isolated by then, and that its natural occurrence and biological activity remained unclear. The same review describes the structure of DSIP as unlike any other known peptide family, and notes that DSIP-like immunoreactivity has a highly specific distribution in neurosecretory nuclei of the hypothalamus in several vertebrate species, regions not particularly relevant to sleep regulation. The review's authors also report that certain synthetic DSIP analogues, but not DSIP itself, promoted slow-wave sleep in their own rabbit and rat studies, and they propose that a related, still unidentified peptide may account, at least in part, for the activity attributed to DSIP. These animal findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. Selank is a synthetic heptapeptide (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro) designed as an analogue of the endogenous peptide tuftsin. The selected studies examine GABA-related signaling, gene expression and behavior in rodent and tissue models. In brain membrane binding assays, Selank changed [3H]GABA binding in a way consistent with positive allosteric modulation of GABA receptors, and it blocked the modulatory effect of diazepam and olanzapine on that binding. In the rat frontal cortex, Selank altered the expression of many of 84 neurotransmission-related genes at one and three hours; the one-hour changes correlated positively with those produced by GABA, and the three-hour changes correlated negatively. In mouse spleen, Selank and its C-terminal Gly-Pro fragment changed the expression of immune-related genes such as complement C3 within 30 to 90 minutes, with similar profiles for both peptides. In rats given ethanol as their only fluid for 30 weeks, Selank prevented memory and attention deficits during withdrawal and prevented the ethanol-related rise in BDNF in the hippocampus and frontal cortex. These findings come from rodent and tissue studies and do not establish effects of this research material in people. Nothing about a combination of them is asserted. Each finding above is reported for one substance on its own, and the properties of a combination are not established by the separate literature of its parts. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The laboratory and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. This listing states 2 components at the amounts given in its label: GHK-Cu at 50 mg and EPITHALON at 10 mg. Each is described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. GHK (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine) is a tripeptide with high affinity for copper(II) ions, and GHK-Cu is its copper complex. The tripeptide later identified as GHK was first reported in human serum in 1973 as a factor that prolonged the survival of normal liver cells. In fibroblast cultures, the copper complex GHK-Cu stimulated collagen synthesis beginning at picomolar concentrations and peaking near 1 nanomolar, independently of any change in cell number. Those authors noted that a GHK sequence occurs within the alpha 2 chain of type I collagen and proposed that proteases could release it at a wound site. These cell-culture findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. Epithalon, also called Epitalon or Epithalone, is the synthetic tetrapeptide Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly, abbreviated AEDG, which was synthesized on the basis of the amino-acid composition of epithalamin, a bovine pineal gland polypeptide preparation. The two are chemically distinct: epithalamin is a heterogeneous pineal-derived polypeptide preparation, whereas this compound is the defined tetrapeptide, and a 2026 review states that findings obtained with epithalamin should not be extrapolated directly to it. The telomere work is a single line of cellular evidence. A 2025 study measured telomere length, human telomerase reverse transcriptase expression, telomerase activity and alternative lengthening of telomeres, in two breast cancer lines exposed daily for four days and in normal epithelial and fibroblast cells exposed for three weeks; a correction published in November 2025 replaced three figures covering those endpoints, stating that the wrong figures had appeared. Because the published comparisons for those endpoints rest on the figures the correction replaced, this study is described here by the endpoints it measured rather than by established effects, and the 2026 review characterises this line of work as cellular evidence with limited independent replication whose clinical benefit remains unproven. The reported neuroendocrine findings depend on the model. In a 2001 experiment with six young and six senescent female rhesus monkeys, in groups of three by age and by whether the peptide was given, the authors reported higher evening melatonin production in the senescent animals and described their rhythm of cortisol production as normalized. In isolated pineal glands from young and old male Wistar rats studied in a perifusion device, the tetrapeptide at concentrations from 1 to 100 micromolar had no significant effect on melatonin secretion at either age and did not modify the increase produced by the beta-adrenergic agonist isoproterenol, from which those authors concluded that it does not appear to play a role in vitro in the control of melatonin secretion by the rat pineal gland. The 2026 review reads the two together as meaning the effects cannot be attributed simply to direct stimulation of pineal melatonin release. In human pineal-gland cell cultures undergoing replicative aging, compared at passage 3 and passage 14 with the tetrapeptide at 100 nanograms per millilitre added at each subculture, the tetrapeptide raised the area of MitoTracker Red mitochondrial staining about 1.5-fold and lowered expression of the ribosomal protein L7A by about 22 per cent, while senescence alone moved both measures the other way; the 2026 review records this as a single in vitro study without independent replication. Two 2002 reports in mouse cells concern separate immune endpoints. In splenocytes from CBA mice the tetrapeptide activated interleukin-2 messenger RNA synthesis in the absence of a specific inducer, with an intensity the authors reported as depending on which peptide was used, on its concentration and on how long the cells were exposed to it. In mouse thymocytes it produced a comitogenic effect on proliferation, an effect measured together with an added mitogenic stimulus, which those authors reported as less potent than that of the dipeptide Lys-Glu studied alongside it. A 2025 overview notes that it remains uncertain whether the reported mechanisms are the sole mechanisms of action and that physico-chemical and structural investigations of the peptide remain limited. Nothing about a combination of them is asserted. Each finding above is reported for one substance on its own, and the properties of a combination are not established by the separate literature of its parts. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The laboratory and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. content.summary: A synthetic hexapeptide whose structure is that of an analogue described in 1984 as a growth hormone-releasing peptide. Animal studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic hexapeptide - a chain of six amino acids - whose structure is that of an analogue described in 1984 as a growth hormone-releasing peptide. It is listed for laboratory work on the growth hormone secretagogue receptor and on growth hormone release in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is in animals: it released growth hormone in pituitary incubates and in rats, monkeys, lambs and calves without releasing luteinizing, follicle-stimulating or thyroid-stimulating hormone or prolactin, and immature rats given it gained more weight than controls. What it does not establish is any effect in a person - and the natural hormone whose action these peptides were thought to reflect was only identified later, as ghrelin, in 1999. The full technical description follows.

GHRP-6 is a synthetic hexapeptide, His-D-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2, whose structure is that of the analogue described in 1984 as [His1,Lys6] growth hormone-releasing peptide. In that 1984 report the hexapeptide released growth hormone in pituitary incubates at 1 to 10 nanograms per millilitre and in rats, monkeys, lambs, calves and, under special experimental conditions, chicks, without a concomitant release of luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone or prolactin, and in limited work insulin or glucagon; its growth hormone response lasted longer than that of the larger growth hormone-releasing factors of 44 and 40 residues, and both the 14- and 28-residue forms of somatotropin release-inhibiting factor suppressed it, the longer form being about four times as active in pituitary incubates and about seven and a half times as active in animals. In the same report, body weight gain in immature rats given the peptide for 9 or 25 days rose above that of controls, and the pituitary remained fully responsive to the peptide at the end of those studies. A 1998 review by the author of that 1984 report described growth hormone-releasing peptides as a class of synthetic growth hormone secretagogues that act on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary, and argued that, although the peptides themselves are of unnatural origin, their action reflects that of a natural hypothalamic hormone not yet isolated at the time. The receptor through which such secretagogues act was cloned from the pituitary and hypothalamus of swine and humans in 1996, and in 1999 an endogenous ligand for it was purified from rat stomach and named ghrelin, a 28-amino-acid peptide whose serine 3 is octanoylated, an acylation the authors found essential for its activity. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

This listing states 3 components at the amounts given in its label: BPC-157 at 10 mg, TB-500 at 10 mg and GHK-Cu at 50 mg. Each is described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide (Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val) whose sequence is a partial sequence of body protection compound, a protein first isolated from human gastric juice. In cultured rat Achilles tendon explants, it accelerated the outgrowth of tendon fibroblasts. In isolated rat tendon fibroblasts, it did not directly change proliferation but improved cell survival under hydrogen peroxide stress, and it increased cell migration and spreading in a concentration-dependent way, with increased phosphorylation of the focal adhesion proteins FAK and paxillin. content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a lipidated peptide of 39 amino acids - one carrying an attached fatty chain - designed to activate three receptors with a single molecule: those for glucagon, for glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and for glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). It is listed for laboratory work on those three receptors, on energy balance and on liver fat in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is in mice, hamsters and isolated mouse tissue: it lowered body weight and liver fat in obese animals, and it raised the beating rate of the right atrium. What it does not establish is any effect in a person - as of a review covering evidence through September 2026 it was an investigational medicine in phase 3 development and was not approved. The full technical description follows.

Retatrutide, also designated LY3437943, is a lipidated peptide of 39 amino acids designed to activate three receptors with a single molecule: the receptors for glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). In its developer's 2022 report, it showed balanced glucagon- and GLP-1-receptor activity but more GIP-receptor activity in vitro, and in obese mice it decreased body weight and improved glycemic control; the authors reported that glucagon-receptor-mediated increases in energy expenditure added to the weight loss from reduced calorie intake driven by the GIP and GLP-1 receptors. In a separate 2026 study in diet-induced obese mice used as a model of steatohepatitis, retatrutide reduced body weight, both fat and lean mass, an index of insulin resistance and liver lipid content without significantly changing energy expenditure, and in a hamster model it halved liver triglycerides without reducing liver histology scores. In a 2025 mouse model of steatohepatitis induced by a Western diet with fructose and sucrose in the drinking water, retatrutide significantly lowered body weight, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, liver triglycerides and cholesterol, and hepatic inflammatory markers in female mice compared with vehicle controls. In isolated mouse atria, retatrutide did not increase the force of contraction of the left atrium but raised the beating rate of the right atrium, an effect antagonized by a glucagon-receptor antagonist. As of a review covering evidence through September 2026, retatrutide was an investigational medicine in phase 3 clinical development and was not approved; this listing is a laboratory research material, not a medicine. These laboratory and animal findings do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 20 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

Semax is a synthetic seven-amino-acid peptide, Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro, described in the literature as an analogue of the N-terminal fragment 4-10 of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In membranes from the rat basal forebrain, tritium-labelled Semax bound to specific, reversible, calcium-dependent binding sites, and giving the peptide to rats raised brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) protein in the basal forebrain 3 hours later but not in the cerebellum. In the rat hippocampus, a single administration increased BDNF protein, tyrosine phosphorylation of its receptor trkB, and BDNF (exon III) and trkB mRNA levels, and rats that received it made more conditioned avoidance responses. In rodents, Semax raised striatal levels of the serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA without changing dopamine or its metabolites on its own, but it enhanced the dopamine release and locomotor activity produced by D-amphetamine. In a rat model of permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion, a genome-wide analysis of the cortex found that Semax mainly altered the expression of immune-system genes, notably those encoding immunoglobulins and chemokines, as well as genes related to the vascular system. These rodent findings do not establish effects of this research material in people. Selank is a synthetic heptapeptide (Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro) designed as an analogue of the endogenous peptide tuftsin. The selected studies examine GABA-related signaling, gene expression and behavior in rodent and tissue models. In brain membrane binding assays, Selank changed [3H]GABA binding in a way consistent with positive allosteric modulation of GABA receptors, and it blocked the modulatory effect of diazepam and olanzapine on that binding. In the rat frontal cortex, Selank altered the expression of many of 84 neurotransmission-related genes at one and three hours; the one-hour changes correlated positively with those produced by GABA, and the three-hour changes correlated negatively. In mouse spleen, Selank and its C-terminal Gly-Pro fragment changed the expression of immune-related genes such as complement C3 within 30 to 90 minutes, with similar profiles for both peptides. In rats given ethanol as their only fluid for 30 weeks, Selank prevented memory and attention deficits during withdrawal and prevented the ethanol-related rise in BDNF in the hippocampus and frontal cortex. These findings come from rodent and tissue studies and do not establish effects of this research material in people. Delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP) is a nine-amino-acid peptide, Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu, isolated in 1977 from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits by a research group in Basel and named for its effect on the electroencephalogram (EEG). In the original double-blind study in rabbits, synthetic DSIP infused into the brain ventricles significantly increased delta-wave and spindle EEG activity compared with controls. Of the other eight peptides tested, rabbits given one of the three shortest (two fragments and a related tripeptide) showed less significant differences from controls, and rabbits given one of the remaining five, three longer fragments and two analogues with two amino acids exchanged, did not differ significantly from controls. A 2006 review noted that this link to sleep had never been further characterized, partly because no gene, precursor protein or receptor for DSIP had been isolated by then, and that its natural occurrence and biological activity remained unclear. The same review describes the structure of DSIP as unlike any other known peptide family, and notes that DSIP-like immunoreactivity has a highly specific distribution in neurosecretory nuclei of the hypothalamus in several vertebrate species, regions not particularly relevant to sleep regulation. The review's authors also report that certain synthetic DSIP analogues, but not DSIP itself, promoted slow-wave sleep in their own rabbit and rat studies, and they propose that a related, still unidentified peptide may account, at least in part, for the activity attributed to DSIP. This listing states 3 components at the amounts given in its label: Thymosin Alpha-1 at 10 mg, KPV at 10 mg and LL-37 at 5 mg. Each is described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. Thymosin alpha-1 is a heat-stable, highly acidic peptide of 28 amino acids, first isolated from calf thymus and sequenced in 1977. It corresponds to the N-terminal region of the larger precursor protein prothymosin alpha. It was one of several polypeptides in the thymic extract thymosin fraction 5 proposed to take part in the differentiation and function of T cells. In dendritic cells exposed to the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus, thymosin alpha-1 induced functional maturation and interleukin-12 production through MyD88-dependent Toll-like receptor signaling involving p38 MAP kinase and NF-kappaB. In highly susceptible mice that had received hematopoietic transplants, the synthetic peptide activated T-helper 1 antifungal immunity, accelerated myeloid cell recovery and protected against aspergillosis. A separate literature review discusses clinical studies of thymosin alpha-1. KPV is the tripeptide lysine-proline-valine, corresponding to residues 11 to 13 of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), a melanocortin peptide with described anti-inflammatory effects. In the Caco2-BBE human intestinal epithelial cell line, nanomolar KPV reduced NF-kappaB and MAP kinase inflammatory signaling and lowered secretion of the cytokine IL-8; in Jurkat T cells it reduced inflammatory signaling and IL-8 mRNA. Its uptake depended on PepT1, a di- and tripeptide transporter normally expressed in the small intestine and induced in the colon during inflammatory bowel disease. In mice, KPV given in drinking water reduced colitis induced by dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) or TNBS. A separate mouse study reported earlier recovery, regain of body weight and fewer inflammatory infiltrates in DSS and T-cell transfer colitis. In mice with a nonfunctional melanocortin-1 receptor, that study reported that all KPV-treated animals survived DSS colitis, and the authors concluded that the effects were at least partly independent of that receptor. These are cell and mouse findings and do not establish effects in people. LL-37 is a 37-amino-acid peptide released from the C-terminal end of the human cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide precursor, a 170-residue protein in which LL-37 occupies residues 134 to 170. That precursor is also called CAP-18, and it is not the same molecule as LL-37; it also yields the shorter peptides FALL-39, LL-29, LL-23, FF-33, RK-31, KS-30 and KR-20. A 1999 study describes LL-37 as a member of the cathelicidin family and as the first amphipathic alpha-helical peptide isolated from human, and examined its structure and organization in phospholipid membranes in relation to the molecular basis of its non-cell-selective activity. A 2011 study reported that the peptide binds membranes in an alpha-helical form and forms transmembrane pores. A 2014 study reported that it inhibits the lipopolysaccharide- and ATP-induced pyroptosis of macrophages by a dual mechanism. A 2012 review describes it as an important effector molecule of innate immunity in the skin. Nothing about a combination of them is asserted. Each finding above is reported for one substance on its own, and the properties of a combination are not established by the separate literature of its parts. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The laboratory and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. This listing states 2 components at the amounts given in its label: TESAMORELIN at 10 mg and IPAMORELIN at 5 mg. Each is described separately below, and no source cited here studied them together. Tesamorelin, developed under the code TH9507, is an analogue of the 44-amino-acid human growth hormone-releasing factor, hGRF(1-44)NH2, modified only by a trans-3-hexenoyl group added to the N-terminal tyrosine. That modification made it resistant to inactivation by dipeptidyl aminopeptidase IV, slowed its breakdown in rat, dog and human plasma in vitro, and prolonged its plasma elimination in vivo compared with the natural peptide. In pigs, rats and dogs, repeated administration markedly increased plasma growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), and its apparent elimination half-life in dogs was 21 to 45 minutes. In subchronic studies of up to four months, rats and dogs gained more body weight, and dogs showed reversible liver, kidney and blood findings that the authors attributed to sustained supraphysiological growth hormone and IGF-1 exposure. Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide (Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2) developed as a growth hormone secretagogue. It came from a series of compounds that lack the central Ala-Trp dipeptide of growth hormone-releasing peptide 1 (GHRP-1). In primary rat pituitary cells, anaesthetised rats and conscious swine it released growth hormone with potency and efficacy comparable to GHRP-6, and antagonist studies indicated that, like GHRP-6, it acts through a GHRP-type receptor. In swine, none of the tested secretagogues changed FSH, LH, prolactin or TSH; GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 increased ACTH and cortisol, whereas the levels after ipamorelin did not differ significantly from those after GHRH, even at more than 200 times the amount needed for half-maximal growth hormone release. In adult female rats given ipamorelin for 15 days, longitudinal bone growth and body-weight gain increased with the amount given, while total IGF-I and serum markers of bone turnover did not change. A small randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 study in 117 adults after bowel resection, which described ipamorelin as a ghrelin-receptor agonist, found no significant difference from placebo in its efficacy measures. These cell, animal and early clinical findings do not establish that this research material is safe or effective in people. Nothing about a combination of them is asserted. Each finding above is reported for one substance on its own, and the properties of a combination are not established by the separate literature of its parts.
