content.purpose: Labeled indications (KYZATREX prescribing information): testosterone replacement therapy in adult males for conditions associated with a deficiency or absence of endogenous testosterone, namely primary hypogonadism (congenital or acquired) and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (congenital or acquired). The labeling states that the safety and efficacy of KYZATREX in males less than 18 years old and in men with “age-related hypogonadism” (also referred to as “late-onset hypogonadism”) have not been established, and that KYZATREX is not indicated for use in women. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions: The KYZATREX labeling contraindicates it in patients with carcinoma of the breast or known or suspected carcinoma of the prostate, in women who are pregnant, stating that testosterone can cause virilization of the female fetus when administered to a pregnant woman, and in patients with known hypersensitivity to KYZATREX or any of its ingredients. It states that testosterone is teratogenic and may cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman, based on data from animal studies and its mechanism of action, and that exposure of a female fetus to androgens may result in varying degrees of virilization. Citing the lack of controlled studies in women and potential virilizing effects, the labeling states that KYZATREX is not indicated for use in women. Its warnings state that androgens, including KYZATREX, can cause an increase in hemoglobin or hematocrit, reflective of an increase in red blood cell mass, and that an increase in red blood cell mass may increase the risk of thromboembolic events. The labeling says to check hematocrit before starting KYZATREX and to evaluate it approximately every 3 months during treatment; if hematocrit becomes elevated, KYZATREX is stopped until hematocrit decreases to an acceptable concentration, and if it again causes elevated hematocrit after a restart, it is permanently discontinued. The labeling states that there have been post-marketing reports of venous thromboembolic events, including deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), in patients using testosterone replacement products such as KYZATREX. It adds that in TRAVERSE, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled cardiovascular outcomes study, topical testosterone gel was associated with a numerically higher incidence of venous thromboembolism than placebo (1.7% vs 1.2%), including DVT (0.6% vs 0.5%) and PE (0.9% vs 0.5%). If a venous thromboembolic event is suspected, the labeling says to discontinue KYZATREX and initiate appropriate workup and management. It states that patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) who are treated with androgens are at an increased risk for worsening of signs and symptoms of BPH, that patients treated with androgens may be at increased risk for prostate cancer, and that patients should be evaluated for prostate cancer before starting and during treatment with androgens. The labeling states that KYZATREX can increase blood pressure. Based on ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in its study MRS-TU-2019EXT, it reports mean systolic/diastolic increases of 1.7/0.6 mm Hg from baseline after 4 months and 1.8/0.6 mm Hg after 6 months, and in patients with hypertension on antihypertensive therapy, 3.4/0.7 mm Hg and 3.1/1.0 mm Hg; the labeling adds that blood pressure increases can increase cardiovascular (CV) risk over time. For TRAVERSE, which enrolled men with a history of cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors, the labeling reports that topical testosterone gel increased mean systolic blood pressure by 1.0 mm Hg from baseline to 36 months, and that the incidences of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction and non-fatal stroke) were nevertheless similar with topical testosterone gel and placebo (7% vs 7.3%). It also reports that adverse reactions in TRAVERSE with an incidence above 2% in either group and higher with topical testosterone gel than placebo included nonfatal arrhythmias warranting intervention (5.2% vs 3.3%), atrial fibrillation (3.5% vs 2.4%), acute kidney injury (2.3% vs 1.5%) and bone fracture (3.5% vs 2.5%). It says to monitor blood pressure periodically in men using KYZATREX, especially men with hypertension, and states that KYZATREX is not recommended for use in patients with uncontrolled hypertension. For interactions, the labeling states that some prescription medications and nonprescription analgesic and cold medications contain drugs known to increase blood pressure, and that taking them with KYZATREX may lead to additional increases in blood pressure. It states that changes in insulin sensitivity or glycemic control may occur in patients treated with androgens, and that in diabetic patients the metabolic effects of androgens may decrease blood glucose and may therefore necessitate a decrease in the dose of anti-diabetic medication; that changes in anticoagulant activity may be seen with androgens, so more frequent monitoring of INR and prothrombin time is recommended in patients taking warfarin, especially at the start and end of androgen therapy; and that testosterone used with corticosteroids may result in increased fluid retention and requires careful monitoring, particularly in patients with cardiac, renal or hepatic disease. The labeling states that testosterone has been subject to abuse, typically at doses higher than recommended and in combination with other anabolic androgenic steroids, and that anabolic androgenic steroid abuse can lead to serious cardiovascular and psychiatric adverse reactions. It reports that serious adverse reactions in individuals who abuse anabolic androgenic steroids include cardiac arrest, myocardial infarction, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular accident, hepatotoxicity and serious psychiatric manifestations, including major depression, mania, paranoia, psychosis, delusions, hallucinations, hostility and aggression, and that testicular atrophy, subfertility and infertility have been reported in men. Reactions reported in women who abuse these steroids include hirsutism, virilization, deepening of voice, clitoral enlargement, breast atrophy, male-pattern baldness and menstrual irregularities, and in adolescents, premature closure of bony epiphyses with termination of growth, and precocious puberty; the labeling notes that these reports are voluntary and may include abuse of other agents, so frequency and causality cannot always be established. It states that individuals taking supratherapeutic doses of testosterone may experience withdrawal symptoms lasting for weeks or months, which may include depressed mood, major depression, fatigue, craving, restlessness, irritability, anorexia, insomnia, decreased libido and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. The labeling states that with large doses of exogenous androgens, including KYZATREX, spermatogenesis may be suppressed through feedback inhibition of pituitary FSH, possibly leading to adverse effects on semen parameters including sperm count; that reduced fertility has been observed in some men taking testosterone replacement therapy; and that the impact on fertility may be irreversible. It states that KYZATREX is not a 17-alpha-alkyl androgen and is not known to cause hepatic adverse effects, but that prolonged use of high doses of orally active 17-alpha-alkyl androgens (for example, methyltestosterone) has been associated with serious hepatic adverse effects (peliosis hepatis, hepatic neoplasms, cholestatic hepatitis and jaundice), that peliosis hepatis can be a life-threatening or fatal complication, and that long-term therapy with intramuscular testosterone enanthate has produced multiple hepatic adenomas. The labeling says patients should be instructed to report any signs or symptoms of hepatic dysfunction, such as jaundice, and that if these occur KYZATREX is promptly discontinued while the cause is evaluated. The labeling states that androgens, including KYZATREX, may promote retention of sodium and water, and that edema, with or without congestive heart failure, may be a serious complication in patients with pre-existing cardiac, renal or hepatic disease, for which diuretic therapy may be required in addition to discontinuation of the drug. It states that treatment of hypogonadal men with testosterone may potentiate sleep apnea in some patients, especially those with the risk factors the labeling names, which include chronic lung disease, and that gynecomastia may develop and persist in patients being treated for hypogonadism. The labeling reports that in clinical trials patients receiving KYZATREX had reductions in lipid parameters, including total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides; that changes in the serum lipid profile may require adjustment of lipid-lowering drugs or discontinuation of testosterone therapy; and that the lipid profile should be monitored periodically, particularly after starting testosterone therapy. It states that androgens, including KYZATREX, should be used with caution in cancer patients at risk of hypercalcemia (and associated hypercalciuria), with serum calcium monitored periodically in these patients, and that androgens may decrease concentrations of thyroxin-binding globulin, resulting in decreased total T4 serum concentrations and increased resin uptake of T3 and T4, while free thyroid hormone concentrations remain unchanged and there is no clinical evidence of thyroid dysfunction. In the labeling’s 6-month study of 155 hypogonadal men, the adverse reaction reported in at least 2% of patients was hypertension (2.6%, based on blood pressure cuff measurements); one patient (0.8%) stopped early because of acne. Increases in hemoglobin were reported in 4.5% of patients and headaches in 1.9%, and 2.6% had an increase in PSA from baseline greater than 1.4 ng/mL. In a 12-month open-label study of 212 hypogonadal adult men, the labeling reports these additional adverse reactions: headache, arthralgia, diarrhea, increased hemoglobin, anxiety, constipation, peripheral edema and increased PSA. It lists myocardial infarction, stroke and venous thromboembolism among reactions in the labeling’s postmarketing experience with testosterone. It states that the safety and efficacy of KYZATREX in patients less than 18 years old have not been established and that it is not recommended for them because of the potential for acceleration of bone age and premature closure of epiphyses. It reports that clinical studies of KYZATREX did not include any patients 65 years of age and older, and that there are insufficient long-term safety data in geriatric patients to assess the potentially increased risk of cardiovascular disease and prostate cancer. These statements come from the KYZATREX prescribing information; the catalog does not state which bottle or NDC is dispensed or who supplies it, and the dispensed product’s own label and the prescribing clinician govern its use.

content.summary: Progesterone 50 mg/mL cream, listed for clinician-directed care through the provider pathway. A prescription is required.
content.overview: The catalog lists this item as a progesterone cream at 50 mg/mL; it does not state the cream’s base or inactive ingredients, its route or site of application, or the basis of the listed concentration. This description cites the PROMETRIUM prescribing information, which describes capsules containing 100 mg or 200 mg of micronized progesterone for oral administration, with peanut oil among their inactive ingredients; a cream is a different dosage form, and the label was written for those capsules, does not address this cream, and does not establish how this cream is absorbed or how it performs. According to the PROMETRIUM prescribing information, the progesterone in PROMETRIUM capsules is synthesized from a starting material from a plant source and is chemically identical to progesterone of human ovarian origin, and the oral bioavailability of progesterone is increased through micronization. For PROMETRIUM's micronized soft-gelatin capsules, it reports that maximum serum concentrations were attained within 3 hours after oral administration, and that the absolute bioavailability of micronized progesterone is not known. It states that progesterone is approximately 96 percent to 99 percent bound to serum proteins, that it is metabolized primarily by the liver largely to pregnanediols and pregnanolones, and that its metabolites are eliminated mainly by the kidneys. The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules are indicated for use in the prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets, and also for use in secondary amenorrhea. It notes that the effect of hepatic impairment and of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of PROMETRIUM capsules has not been studied. Which use applies to a given patient, if any, is a clinical decision that this listing does not make. This listing does not state who prepares or supplies the cream, how it is prepared, or whether its progesterone is micronized or its base and inactive ingredients include peanut oil as PROMETRIUM capsules do; the dispensed product's own label governs. A prescription is required. Requests go through the provider pathway, where a licensed clinician decides whether it is appropriate. Fulfillment depends on state availability and pharmacy requirements, and it is not available for direct purchase.

content.purpose: Labeled indications (PROMETRIUM prescribing information), which describe PROMETRIUM capsules of 100 mg or 200 mg micronized progesterone and not this cream: prevention of endometrial hyperplasia in nonhysterectomized postmenopausal women who are receiving conjugated estrogens tablets; and secondary amenorrhea. The labeling also states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children. The labeling does not establish that this cream serves either use. Whether a labeled use applies to a given patient is decided in clinician-directed review.
content.cautions: The cautions below come from the PROMETRIUM prescribing information, which states them for its own PROMETRIUM capsules, not for this cream; the dispensed product's own label governs, and the prescribing clinician decides whether the cream is appropriate. The PROMETRIUM prescribing information contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with hypersensitivity to its ingredients and, because PROMETRIUM capsules contain peanut oil, in patients allergic to peanuts; this listing does not state the cream's ingredients or base. It also contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with abnormal genital bleeding of unknown etiology; known, suspected, or history of breast cancer; active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease (for example, stroke and myocardial infarction) or a history of these conditions; or known liver dysfunction or disease. Its warnings state that PROMETRIUM should be immediately discontinued if a pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction occurs or is suspected, and that, if feasible, it should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization. The labeling states that the safety and efficacy of estrogen plus progestogen for the prevention of cardiovascular disorders has not been established, and that the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) estrogen plus progestin trial reported increased risks of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke and myocardial infarction in postmenopausal women (50 to 79 years of age, average age 63.4 years) during 5.6 years of treatment with daily oral conjugated estrogens (0.625 mg) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (2.5 mg), relative to placebo. It states that only daily oral 0.625 mg conjugated estrogens and 2.5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate were studied in that trial, so the relevance of the WHI findings regarding adverse cardiovascular events to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, and that without such data it is not possible to definitively exclude these risks or determine their extent for other products. For venous thromboembolism in the overall WHI study population, the labeling reports a relative risk for pulmonary embolism of 1.98 (95% CI, 1.36, 2.87) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (18 versus 9), and a relative risk for deep vein thrombosis of 1.87 (95% CI, 1.37, 2.54), with a risk difference of 12 per 10,000 women-years (25 versus 14). For the overall WHI population it also reports a relative risk for stroke of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.07, 1.76) with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (33 versus 24), and a relative risk of coronary heart disease of 1.18 (95% CI, 0.95, 1.45) with a risk difference of 6 per 10,000 women-years (41 versus 35), for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo. Its breast cancer warning states that PROMETRIUM is contraindicated in women with breast cancer, a history of breast cancer, or estrogen-dependent neoplasia, that PROMETRIUM should be discontinued if a hormone-sensitive malignancy is diagnosed, and that the use of estrogen plus progestin therapy has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation. In the overall WHI population, the labeling reports a relative risk for invasive breast cancer of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01, 1.53) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (43 versus 35); it states that invasive breast cancers were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage in that group, and that the trial did not show a statistically significant difference in breast cancer mortality. It adds that, consistent with the WHI trial, observational studies have also reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy, and that a large meta-analysis including 24 prospective studies of postmenopausal women comparing current use of estrogen plus progestin products for 5 to 14 years (average of 9 years) versus never use reported a relative risk for breast cancer of 2.08 (95% CI, 2.02 to 2.15). It states that these studies have not generally found significant variation in the risk of breast cancer among different estrogen plus progestin combinations, doses, or routes of administration, and that the relevance of the WHI findings regarding breast cancer to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, so that these risks cannot be definitively excluded or their extent determined for other products. Its ovarian cancer warning reports, for the overall WHI population, a relative risk for ovarian cancer of 1.41 (95% CI, 0.75 to 2.66) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate versus placebo after an average follow-up of 5.6 years, with a risk difference of 1 per 10,000 women-years (5 versus 4), and a large meta-analysis of 17 prospective studies of postmenopausal women reporting a relative risk of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.26 to 1.48) for current use of estrogen plus progestin products versus never use; it states that the duration of hormone therapy use associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer is unknown. Its vision warning states that retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported in patients receiving estrogen, that estrogen plus progestin therapy should be discontinued pending examination if there is sudden partial or complete loss of vision or a sudden onset of proptosis, diplopia or migraine, and that it should be permanently discontinued if examination reveals papilledema or retinal vascular lesions. Its precautions state that progesterone may cause some degree of fluid retention, so women with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation. They also state that PROMETRIUM capsules may cause transient dizziness and drowsiness and should be used with caution when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery; the patient information adds that some women may experience extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness during initial therapy, in a few cases with blurred vision, difficulty speaking, difficulty with walking and feeling abnormal, and says to discuss these symptoms with the healthcare provider right away. Its drug-interaction section reports that the metabolism of progesterone by human liver microsomes was inhibited by ketoconazole, a known inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, so these data suggest that ketoconazole or other known inhibitors of this enzyme may increase the bioavailability of progesterone, and that the clinical relevance of the in vitro findings is unknown. It reports that coadministration of conjugated estrogens and PROMETRIUM capsules to 29 postmenopausal women over a 12-day period increased total estrone and total equilin concentrations and decreased circulating 17β estradiol concentrations, while the half-life of the conjugated estrogens was similar with coadministration. Its precautions also list laboratory results that may be altered by estrogen plus progestin therapy: increased sulfobromophthalein retention and other hepatic function tests; coagulation tests (an increase in prothrombin factors VII, VIII, IX and X); pregnanediol determination; and thyroid function (an increase in PBI and butanol extractable protein bound iodine and a decrease in T3 uptake values). Its precautions state that exogenously administered progesterone has been shown to inhibit ovulation in a number of species, and that high doses given for an extended duration are expected to impair fertility until the cessation of treatment. The labeling states that PROMETRIUM capsules should not be used during pregnancy, and its patient information lists, among serious but less common side effects, risk to the fetus: cases of cleft palate, cleft lip, hypospadias, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, and other congenital heart defects. It states that detectable amounts of progestin have been identified in the milk of nursing women receiving progestins, that caution should be exercised when PROMETRIUM capsules are administered to a nursing woman, and, in the patient information, that the hormone in PROMETRIUM capsules can pass into breast milk. It states that PROMETRIUM capsules are not indicated in children, that clinical studies have not been conducted in the pediatric population, and that there have not been sufficient numbers of geriatric women in clinical studies to determine whether those over 65 years of age differ from younger subjects in their response. For women over 65, it reports that the WHI estrogen plus progestin substudy showed a higher relative risk of nonfatal stroke and invasive breast cancer. It also reports that the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study of postmenopausal women 65 to 79 years of age found an increased risk of developing probable dementia with estrogen plus progestin compared to placebo (after an average follow-up of 4 years, a relative risk of 2.05, 95 percent CI 1.21 to 3.48, and an absolute risk of 45 versus 22 per 10,000 women-years), and that it is unknown whether these findings apply to younger postmenopausal women. Its table of adverse reactions comes from a 3-year, placebo-controlled trial of cyclic PROMETRIUM capsules 200 mg with conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg in postmenopausal women (875 women studied; the table's arms are n = 178 and placebo n = 174) and lists the reactions reported by 2% or more of women. Those are headache (31% versus 27% on placebo), breast tenderness (27% versus 6%), joint pain (20% versus 29%), depression (19% versus 12%), dizziness (15% versus 9%), abdominal bloating (12% versus 5%), hot flashes (11% versus 35%), urinary problems (11% versus 9%), abdominal pain (10% versus 10%), vaginal discharge (10% versus 3%), nausea or vomiting (8% versus 7%), worry (8% versus 4%), chest pain (7% versus 5%), diarrhea (7% versus 4%), night sweats (7% versus 17%), breast pain (6% versus 2%), swelling of hands and feet (6% versus 9%), vaginal dryness (6% versus 10%), constipation (3% versus 2%), and breast carcinoma, breast excisional biopsy and cholecystectomy (2% each versus less than 1%). In a placebo-controlled trial of PROMETRIUM capsules at 400 mg/day in 49 estrogen-primed postmenopausal women, its table of adverse reactions reported by 5% or more lists fatigue (8% versus 4% on placebo), headache (16% versus 8%), dizziness (24% versus 4%), abdominal distention or bloating (8% versus 8%), abdominal pain or cramping (20% versus 13%), diarrhea (8% versus 4%), nausea (8% versus 0%), back pain (8% versus 8%), musculoskeletal pain (12% versus 4%), irritability (8% versus 4%), breast pain (16% versus 8%), viral infection (12% versus 0%) and coughing (8% versus 0%). In an open-label postmarketing study of 220 premenopausal women with secondary amenorrhea who received conjugated estrogens with PROMETRIUM capsules, the labeling lists the most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse reactions (5% or more) as nausea, fatigue, vaginal mycosis, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness, abdominal distension, acne, dysmenorrhea, mood swing, and urinary tract infection. Among additional adverse reactions reported with PROMETRIUM capsules after marketing, which the labeling notes are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size so that their frequency or a causal relationship to drug exposure cannot always be reliably established, it lists genitourinary reactions (endometrial carcinoma, hypospadia, intra-uterine death, menorrhagia, menstrual disorder, metrorrhagia, ovarian cyst, spontaneous abortion) and cardiovascular reactions (circulatory collapse, congenital heart disease including ventricular septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus, hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia). It also lists gastrointestinal reactions (acute pancreatitis, cholestasis, cholestatic hepatitis, dysphagia, hepatic failure, hepatic necrosis, hepatitis, increased liver function tests, jaundice, swollen tongue), skin reactions (alopecia, pruritus, urticaria) and eye reactions (blurred vision, diplopia, visual disturbance). Its central nervous system list includes aggression, convulsion, depersonalization, depressed consciousness, disorientation, dysarthria, loss of consciousness, paresthesia, sedation, stupor, syncope (with and without hypotension), transient ischemic attack and suicidal ideation, and it notes that during initial therapy a few women have experienced a constellation of many or all of the following: extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness, blurred vision, slurred speech, difficulty walking, loss of consciousness, vertigo, confusion, disorientation, feeling drunk, and shortness of breath. Among miscellaneous postmarketing reactions it lists abnormal gait, anaphylactic reaction, arthralgia, blood glucose increased, choking, cleft lip, cleft palate, difficulty walking, dyspnea, face edema, feeling abnormal, feeling drunk, hypersensitivity, asthma, muscle cramp, throat tightness, tinnitus and vertigo, among others. Its patient information lists abnormal blood clotting (stroke, heart attack, pulmonary embolus, visual loss or blindness) among serious but less common side effects, gives changes in vision or speech, sudden new severe headaches, severe pains in the chest or legs with or without shortness of breath, weakness and fatigue, dizziness and faintness, and vomiting as warning signs of serious side effects, and says to call the healthcare provider right away for any of these warning signs or any other unusual symptoms that concern the patient. Its patient information lists these less serious but common side effects: headaches; breast pain; irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting; stomach or abdominal cramps, bloating; nausea and vomiting; hair loss; fluid retention; and vaginal yeast infection. Its patient information advises seeing the healthcare provider right away for unusual vaginal bleeding while taking PROMETRIUM capsules. It advises a pelvic exam, breast exam and mammogram every year unless the healthcare provider says otherwise, and says that women whose family members have had breast cancer, or who have ever had breast lumps or an abnormal mammogram, may need breast exams more often. It also advises telling the healthcare provider about all medical problems, since closer checks may be needed with conditions such as asthma, epilepsy, diabetes, migraine, endometriosis, lupus, problems with the heart, liver, thyroid or kidneys, or high calcium levels in the blood, and about all medicines taken, including nonprescription medicines, vitamins and herbal supplements, since some medicines may affect how PROMETRIUM capsules work and PROMETRIUM capsules may affect how other medicines work. This listing does not state the cream's route or site of application, base, inactive ingredients, fill, applicator or storage, or the basis of the listed concentration.

It also contraindicates PROMETRIUM in women with abnormal genital bleeding of unknown etiology; known, suspected, or history of breast cancer; active deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease (for example, stroke and myocardial infarction) or a history of these conditions; or known liver dysfunction or disease. Its warnings state that PROMETRIUM should be immediately discontinued if a pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction occurs or is suspected, and that, if feasible, it should be discontinued at least 4 to 6 weeks before surgery of the type associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism, or during periods of prolonged immobilization. It states that only daily oral 0.625 mg conjugated estrogens and 2.5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate were studied in that trial, so the relevance of the WHI findings regarding adverse cardiovascular events to lower conjugated estrogens plus other medroxyprogesterone acetate doses, other routes of administration, or other estrogen plus progestogen products is not known, and that without such data it is not possible to definitively exclude these risks or determine their extent for other products. For venous thromboembolism in the overall WHI study population, the labeling reports a relative risk for pulmonary embolism of 1.98 (95% CI, 1.36, 2.87) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (18 versus 9), and a relative risk for deep vein thrombosis of 1.87 (95% CI, 1.37, 2.54), with a risk difference of 12 per 10,000 women-years (25 versus 14). For the overall WHI population it also reports a relative risk for stroke of 1.37 (95% CI, 1.07, 1.76) with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (33 versus 24), and a relative risk of coronary heart disease of 1.18 (95% CI, 0.95, 1.45) with a risk difference of 6 per 10,000 women-years (41 versus 35), for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo. Its breast cancer warning states that PROMETRIUM is contraindicated in women with breast cancer, a history of breast cancer, or estrogen-dependent neoplasia, that PROMETRIUM should be discontinued if a hormone-sensitive malignancy is diagnosed, and that the use of estrogen plus progestin therapy has been reported to result in an increase in abnormal mammograms requiring further evaluation. In the overall WHI population, the labeling reports a relative risk for invasive breast cancer of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.01, 1.53) for conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate compared to placebo, with a risk difference of 9 per 10,000 women-years (43 versus 35); it states that invasive breast cancers were larger, more likely to be node positive and diagnosed at a more advanced stage in that group, and that the trial did not show a statistically significant difference in breast cancer mortality. Its precautions state that progesterone may cause some degree of fluid retention, so women with conditions that might be influenced by this factor, such as cardiac or renal dysfunction, warrant careful observation. They also state that PROMETRIUM capsules may cause transient dizziness and drowsiness and should be used with caution when driving a motor vehicle or operating machinery; the patient information adds that some women may experience extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness during initial therapy, in a few cases with blurred vision, difficulty speaking, difficulty with walking and feeling abnormal, and says to discuss these symptoms with the healthcare provider right away. Its drug-interaction section reports that the metabolism of progesterone by human liver microsomes was inhibited by ketoconazole, a known inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, so these data suggest that ketoconazole or other known inhibitors of this enzyme may increase the bioavailability of progesterone, and that the clinical relevance of the in vitro findings is unknown. It also lists gastrointestinal reactions (acute pancreatitis, cholestasis, cholestatic hepatitis, dysphagia, hepatic failure, hepatic necrosis, hepatitis, increased liver function tests, jaundice, swollen tongue), skin reactions (alopecia, pruritus, urticaria) and eye reactions (blurred vision, diplopia, visual disturbance). Its central nervous system list includes aggression, convulsion, depersonalization, depressed consciousness, disorientation, dysarthria, loss of consciousness, paresthesia, sedation, stupor, syncope (with and without hypotension), transient ischemic attack and suicidal ideation, and it notes that during initial therapy a few women have experienced a constellation of many or all of the following: extreme dizziness and/or drowsiness, blurred vision, slurred speech, difficulty walking, loss of consciousness, vertigo, confusion, disorientation, feeling drunk, and shortness of breath. Among miscellaneous postmarketing reactions it lists abnormal gait, anaphylactic reaction, arthralgia, blood glucose increased, choking, cleft lip, cleft palate, difficulty walking, dyspnea, face edema, feeling abnormal, feeling drunk, hypersensitivity, asthma, muscle cramp, throat tightness, tinnitus and vertigo, among others. It advises a pelvic exam, breast exam and mammogram every year unless the healthcare provider says otherwise, and says that women whose family members have had breast cancer, or who have ever had breast lumps or an abnormal mammogram, may need breast exams more often. This listing does not state the cream's route or site of application, base, inactive ingredients, fill, applicator or storage, or the basis of the listed concentration.

content.summary: This listing's label names CJC-1295, a synthetic analogue of human growth-hormone-releasing factor, in the form without the drug affinity complex. Cell-assay and animal studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this listing's label names CJC-1295 without the drug affinity complex, the chemical group that lets the peptide crosslink to blood proteins. It is listed for laboratory work on the chemistry of such growth-hormone-releasing-factor analogues and on the difference between the conjugating and non-conjugating forms. What the cited work establishes is that the two are counted as separate analytes, and that the persistence in plasma beyond 72 hours and the signal on the serum-albumin band belong to the form that carries that group, not to this one. What it does not establish is what this material is: in the sources read, the form without the complex is not separately characterised under this name, so this description says what the name denotes and what the qualifier excludes. The full technical description follows.

content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic tetrapeptide - a chain of four amino acids - made on the basis of the amino-acid composition of epithalamin, a polypeptide preparation from the bovine pineal gland. The two are chemically distinct, and findings obtained with the preparation should not be read across to this compound. It is listed for laboratory work on telomere maintenance, on circadian and neuroendocrine signaling, and on cell-ageing markers in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is thin and contested: the telomere work is a single line of cellular evidence whose published figures were replaced by a November 2025 correction, and the neuroendocrine findings point in different directions in monkeys and in isolated rat pineal glands. What it does not establish is clinical benefit, which a 2026 review describes as unproven. The full technical description follows.

Epithalon, also called Epitalon or Epithalone, is the synthetic tetrapeptide Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly, abbreviated AEDG, which was synthesized on the basis of the amino-acid composition of epithalamin, a bovine pineal gland polypeptide preparation. The two are chemically distinct: epithalamin is a heterogeneous pineal-derived polypeptide preparation, whereas this compound is the defined tetrapeptide, and a 2026 review states that findings obtained with epithalamin should not be extrapolated directly to it. The telomere work is a single line of cellular evidence. A 2025 study measured telomere length, human telomerase reverse transcriptase expression, telomerase activity and alternative lengthening of telomeres, in two breast cancer lines exposed daily for four days and in normal epithelial and fibroblast cells exposed for three weeks; a correction published in November 2025 replaced three figures covering those endpoints, stating that the wrong figures had appeared. Because the published comparisons for those endpoints rest on the figures the correction replaced, this study is described here by the endpoints it measured rather than by established effects, and the 2026 review characterises this line of work as cellular evidence with limited independent replication whose clinical benefit remains unproven. The reported neuroendocrine findings depend on the model. In a 2001 experiment with six young and six senescent female rhesus monkeys, in groups of three by age and by whether the peptide was given, the authors reported higher evening melatonin production in the senescent animals and described their rhythm of cortisol production as normalized. In isolated pineal glands from young and old male Wistar rats studied in a perifusion device, the tetrapeptide at concentrations from 1 to 100 micromolar had no significant effect on melatonin secretion at either age and did not modify the increase produced by the beta-adrenergic agonist isoproterenol, from which those authors concluded that it does not appear to play a role in vitro in the control of melatonin secretion by the rat pineal gland. The 2026 review reads the two together as meaning the effects cannot be attributed simply to direct stimulation of pineal melatonin release. In human pineal-gland cell cultures undergoing replicative aging, compared at passage 3 and passage 14 with the tetrapeptide at 100 nanograms per millilitre added at each subculture, the tetrapeptide raised the area of MitoTracker Red mitochondrial staining about 1.5-fold and lowered expression of the ribosomal protein L7A by about 22 per cent, while senescence alone moved both measures the other way; the 2026 review records this as a single in vitro study without independent replication. Two 2002 reports in mouse cells concern separate immune endpoints. In splenocytes from CBA mice the tetrapeptide activated interleukin-2 messenger RNA synthesis in the absence of a specific inducer, with an intensity the authors reported as depending on which peptide was used, on its concentration and on how long the cells were exposed to it. In mouse thymocytes it produced a comitogenic effect on proliferation, an effect measured together with an added mitogenic stimulus, which those authors reported as less potent than that of the dipeptide Lys-Glu studied alongside it. A 2025 overview notes that it remains uncertain whether the reported mechanisms are the sole mechanisms of action and that physico-chemical and structural investigations of the peptide remain limited. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine; the 2026 review describes the compound as biologically active but clinically unproven, with human evidence limited to small physiological or biomarker studies and one older controlled report, no adequately powered randomized trial establishing efficacy, inadequate pharmacokinetic and long-term safety data, and open questions about immunogenicity, product quality and the oncological implications of telomerase activation. The cell and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.overview:

IGF-1 LR3 is a product name for Long [Arg3] insulin-like growth factor-I, a recombinant analogue of insulin-like growth factor 1 and not the native protein. The 1992 study that introduced the analogue describes the series as comprising an insulin-like growth factor 1 sequence together with the first 11 amino acids of methionyl porcine growth hormone, and writes this member as [Met1]-pGH(1-11)-Val-Asn-[Arg3]-IGF-I, where glutamate 3 of the human insulin-like growth factor 1 sequence has been replaced by arginine. That same study reports the analogues were more potent than authentic insulin-like growth factor 1 at stimulating protein and DNA synthesis in rat L6 myoblasts, and that in a cell line secreting no detectable insulin-like growth factor binding proteins Long [Arg3]-IGF-I was less potent than insulin-like growth factor 1 itself; it attributes the increased potency of N-terminal analogues to changes in their interaction with those binding proteins rather than to receptor binding. The name has also been shown to cover tagged constructs: a 2010 analytical report characterised the protein in one product sold under this name as Long-R3-IGF-I carrying a six-residue histidine tag on its C-terminus, joined by leucine and glutamate linker residues. That analytical work examined products sold under these names, so it establishes what the names have been shown to cover and not the composition of this listing. content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic tetrapeptide - a chain of four amino acids - also known as elamipretide, which binds cardiolipin, a phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is listed for laboratory work on that interaction, on mitochondrial energy production and on redox biology in laboratory systems and animals. What the cited work establishes is in rats and mice: it protected mitochondrial cristae during kidney ischemia, reversed age-related declines in mitochondrial ATP production in the skeletal muscle of aged mice, and improved dilation of small brain vessels in 24-month-old mice. What it does not establish is any effect in a person, and the separate prescription formulation of elamipretide is approved on its own evidence, which does not transfer to this research listing. The full technical description follows.

SS-31, also known as elamipretide and as MTP-131, is a synthetic tetrapeptide, D-arginyl-2′,6′-dimethyl-L-tyrosyl-L-lysyl-L-phenylalaninamide (D-Arg-Dmt-Lys-Phe-NH2). A 2013 study used a fluorescent analog of SS-31 to show that SS-31 binds with high affinity to cardiolipin, a phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane that is required for cristae formation; the SS-31–cardiolipin complex inhibited cytochrome c peroxidase activity, and pretreating rats with SS-31 protected mitochondrial cristae during kidney ischemia. In aged mice, SS-31 rapidly reversed age-related declines in resting and maximal mitochondrial ATP production in skeletal muscle and made the muscle more fatigue resistant. With longer exposure in aged female mice, it also shifted the glutathione redox state toward a more reduced balance, generally reversed the age-associated increases in S-glutathionylation measured on cysteine residues across muscle proteins, and increased fatigue resistance and treadmill endurance. In 24-month-old mice, SS-31 improved neurovascular coupling responses by increasing nitric-oxide-mediated dilation of small brain vessels, and this was associated with better spatial working memory and motor skill learning, while gait measures did not differ significantly between treated and untreated aged mice. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine; separately, a prescription formulation of elamipretide received accelerated approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in September 2025 to improve muscle strength in adult and pediatric patients with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg. The animal findings above, and the approval of that separate medicine, do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. What LL-37 itself is, the published record settles: a 37-amino-acid peptide released from the end of a 170-residue human precursor protein, which also yields several shorter peptides. It is listed for laboratory work on that peptide's chemistry, within the limits of an unstated formulation. This listing's name adds the word Complex to the name of a defined peptide, and that word states a formulation rather than a substance. What LL-37 itself is, the published record settles, and the description of it below is the one already written for the LL-37 listing in this catalog. That precursor is also called CAP-18, and it is not the same molecule as LL-37; it also yields the shorter peptides FALL-39, LL-29, LL-23, FF-33, RK-31, KS-30 and KR-20. A 1999 study describes LL-37 as a member of the cathelicidin family and as the first amphipathic alpha-helical peptide isolated from human, and examined its structure and organization in phospholipid membranes in relation to the molecular basis of its non-cell-selective activity. A 2011 study reported that the peptide binds membranes in an alpha-helical form and forms transmembrane pores. A 2014 study reported that it inhibits the lipopolysaccharide- and ATP-induced pyroptosis of macrophages by a dual mechanism. A 2012 review describes it as an important effector molecule of innate immunity in the skin. What no source read here states is what this listing's formulation holds besides that peptide, in what proportion, or whether the stated amount refers to the peptide, to a mixture, or to a total. The 5 mg is therefore reproduced as the catalog gives it, and this description does not assert that it is 5 mg of LL-37. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. content.summary: Mechano growth factor is a name for a splice variant of insulin-like growth factor 1. Work on a product sold under the name does not establish this listing's composition, or the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, mechano growth factor is a name for a splice variant of insulin-like growth factor 1, and the published record applies that name to more than one material - which matters for a listing that states an amount and nothing more. It is listed for laboratory work on those splice variants, on E-domain peptide chemistry and on receptor activation. What the cited work establishes is that the readings differ: a product sold as full-length mechano growth factor was characterised as a protein of monoisotopic mass 12264.9, and in receptor assays that full-length form activated the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor while a shorter mechano growth factor and a stabilised analogue produced no activation at all. What it does not establish is the composition of this listing: a 24-residue E-domain peptide and a protein of that mass are not interchangeable. The full technical description follows.

Mechano growth factor, written MGF, is a name for a splice variant of insulin-like growth factor 1: published work states that human insulin-like growth factor 1 Ec, also called mechano growth factor, is a splice variant of insulin-like growth factor 1, and reference records list mechano growth factor as an alternative name for insulin-like growth factor 1. Those reference records give the human insulin-like growth factor 1 precursor as 195 residues, with a signal region at 1 to 21, a propeptide at 22 to 48, the mature insulin-like growth factor 1 chain at 49 to 118, and the E peptide as residues 119 to 195. A 2014 review describes IGF-1Ec as arising from alternative splicing of exons 4, 5 and 6, and notes that a synthetic analogue corresponding to the last 24 amino acids of the E domain of the IGF-1Ec isoform has been used to study what that domain does. The name is applied in the published record to more than one material, which matters for a listing that states an amount and nothing more. A 2014 analytical study characterised a product sold as full-length mechano growth factor and reported a protein of monoisotopic molecular mass 12264.9 whose sequence is closely related to IGF-1Ec without the signal and propeptide regions, its C-terminus altered by loss of the terminal lysine and by an R109H substitution. That study examined a product sold under the name, so it establishes what the name has been shown to denote and not the composition of this listing. A 2016 receptor-activation study compared the two readings directly: in kinase-specific receptor activation assays, full-length mechano growth factor stimulated the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor to a maximal effect similar to recombinant human insulin-like growth factor 1 at high equimolar concentrations, while human mechano growth factor and a stabilised mechano growth factor analogue produced no activation of that receptor in the same assays. A 24-residue E-domain peptide and a protein of about that mass are therefore not interchangeable, and findings reported for one do not carry over to the other. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The analytical and cell-assay findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.summary: An eleven-amino-acid peptide, also called cibinetide, whose sequence reproduces the water-facing side of one helix of erythropoietin. content.overview:
In plain terms, this is an eleven-amino-acid peptide, also called cibinetide, whose sequence reproduces one face of a helix of erythropoietin. It is listed for laboratory work on the erythropoietin receptor, on the beta common receptor and on tissue protection in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is in rats and mice: it was not erythropoietic, meaning it did not drive red-cell production, yet on a molar basis it was as active as erythropoietin in a sciatic nerve compression model, reduced infarct volume in a stroke model and gave long-lasting relief of nerve-injury pain in a way that depended on the beta common receptor. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

ARA-290, also called cibinetide, is an eleven-amino-acid peptide whose sequence pGlu-Glu-Gln-Leu-Glu-Arg-Ala-Leu-Asn-Ser-Ser reproduces the water-facing side of helix B of erythropoietin, with the first residue present as pyroglutamate. In the 2008 report that described this family of peptides, the tissue-protective effects of erythropoietin were attributed to a receptor complex of the erythropoietin receptor with CD131, the β common receptor, separate from the erythropoietin receptor homodimer that drives red-cell production; crystallographic work showed the water-facing side of helix B to be the sequence QEQLERAL, the eleven-residue peptide QEQLERALNSS was synthesized from it, and its N-terminal glutamine was found to cyclize spontaneously to pyroglutamate, giving the peptide of this listing. In that report neither the helix B peptide nor the eleven-residue peptide was erythropoietic in a cell assay or in animals; the eleven-residue peptide was as active as erythropoietin and as the longer helix B peptide, on a molar basis, in a sciatic nerve compression model; the pyroglutamate form reduced infarct volume (225 ± 20 against 291 ± 23 cubic millimetres, P < 0.05) and improved a neurological score in a stroke model, lowered markers of kidney injury after renal ischaemia and reperfusion in mice, and sped the closure of skin punch wounds in rats; the longer helix B peptide held retinal leakage in a rat model of diabetes to the level of animals without diabetes, and the authors also summarize the peptide as augmenting cognitive function in rodents. A 2011 study reported long-lasting relief of tactile and cold allodynia in rats after a peripheral nerve injury, and concluded from work in rats and in mice lacking the β common receptor that the relief depended on activation of that receptor. A 2012 review by the peptide's investigators describes it as a short-lived mimic of erythropoietin, with a plasma half-life of about two minutes, whose single administration suppressed a histamine-induced skin wheal in rats for more than twenty-four hours, and attributes such effects to the tissue-protective receptor rather than to erythropoiesis. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The cell and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.summary: A synthetic peptide derived from the carboxy-terminal region of human growth hormone. Cell, tissue and animal studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 5 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic peptide taken from the tail end of human growth hormone - the investigators who studied it describe it as a C-terminal fragment of that hormone, and the reference record shows a sequence beginning with tyrosine and closed by a disulfide bridge. It is listed for laboratory work on how such fragments affect fat breakdown and fat formation. What the cited work establishes is in rats, mice and isolated tissue, much of it on related analogues: the fragment reduced fat formation as strongly as the intact hormone and slowed weight gain in obese mice, without the high blood glucose or the reduced insulin secretion that followed the intact hormone. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

AOD-9604 is a synthetic peptide derived from the carboxy-terminal region of human growth hormone, described by the investigators who studied it as a C-terminal fragment of that hormone; the PubChem record shows a sequence that begins with tyrosine and is closed by a disulfide bridge. The antilipogenic activity of this region of the hormone was reported from 1993: a synthetic peptide of human growth hormone residues 177 to 191 had antilipogenic activity identical to that of the intact hormone, while showing no significant lipolytic effect as measured by glycerol release from the fat pads of rats given the peptide, and in 1994 long-term administration of the same peptide to obese mice reduced cumulative body weight gain, decreased adipose tissue mass and inhibited lipogenesis in adipose tissue. In one 2000 report on AOD9401, an analogue of that domain spanning residues 177 to 191, the peptide stimulated hormone-sensitive lipase and inhibited acetyl-coenzyme A carboxylase in isolated rat adipose tissue, mimicked the intact hormone's effect on diacylglycerol release in adipocytes, and over 20 days in obese Zucker rats reduced body weight gain and lowered mean adipocyte diameter from about 110 to about 80 micrometres, without the insulin resistance or glucose intolerance that followed the intact hormone. In a second 2000 report, administration of AOD9401 to obese mice over 30 days lowered body weight gain from day 16 with no difference in food consumption, reduced lipogenic and raised lipolytic activity in adipose tissue examined afterwards, acutely raised energy expenditure and glucose and fat oxidation, and raised lipolytic and lowered lipogenic activity in isolated adipose tissue from obese rodents and from people. Two 2001 reports on AOD9604 itself found that over 14 days it reduced body weight gain and body fat in obese mice with increased fat oxidation and raised plasma glycerol, did not produce the high blood glucose or the reduced insulin secretion that followed the intact hormone, did not compete with the intact hormone for its receptor and did not induce cell proliferation through that receptor; the same work found the weight and lipolysis changes absent over the long term in mice lacking the β3-adrenergic receptor, while a single administration still raised energy expenditure and fat oxidation in those mice, from which the authors concluded that the lipolytic action is not mediated directly through that receptor, although both the hormone and the peptide raised its expression. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The cell, tissue and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 5 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.summary: Glutathione is a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine and glycine. The catalog states only 'Glutathione' without saying which redox form this listing supplies. Biochemical studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 500 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is glutathione, a tripeptide - a chain of three amino acids - that cells use to keep their own chemistry in a reduced state and to tag other molecules for disposal. It is listed for laboratory work on that thiol chemistry, on glutathione metabolism and on how glutathione status is measured. What the cited work establishes is biochemical: it is the most abundant non-protein thiol in mammalian tissues, it is made in two enzyme steps whose rate depends on the supply of cysteine, and one review describes how its status is assessed in cells. What it does not establish is which redox form this listing supplies, since the catalog says only Glutathione, nor any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

Glutathione is the tripeptide γ-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine, in which the glutamate is joined to cysteine through its side-chain carboxyl group; the reductant and conjugating chemistry below belongs to its reduced form, reduced glutathione, whose free cysteine thiol carries it, and the catalog states only 'Glutathione' without saying which redox form this listing supplies. A 1983 article placed this thiol in virtually every cell, with roles in metabolism, in transport and in cellular protection: it reduces disulfides and other molecules, forms conjugates with compounds arising both outside and inside the cell, and shields cells from reactive oxygen intermediates and free radicals. Later reviews describe it as the most abundant non-protein thiol in mammalian tissues and as the most abundant low-molecular-weight thiol compound synthesized in cells, a determinant of redox signalling, and a participant in the detoxification of xenobiotics and xenobiotic electrophiles and in maintaining redox homeostasis. Its biosynthesis occurs in the cytosol in two enzymatic steps, the first catalysed by glutamate cysteine ligase, the rate-limiting enzyme, which is composed of a catalytic and a modifier subunit, and the second by glutathione synthetase; the key determinants are the availability of the sulfur amino acid precursor cysteine and the activity of that ligase, whose subunit genes are regulated through transcription factors including NF-E2 related factor 2 acting at the antioxidant response element. One of them also describes methods of assessing glutathione status in cells. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The biochemical findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. content.summary: The oxidized form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, also called coenzyme I, a dinucleotide on which the cell's redox state depends. content.overview:
In plain terms, this is the oxidized form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, also called coenzyme I - a molecule central to the chemistry by which cells move electrons about. It is listed for laboratory work on that redox chemistry and on the enzymes that depend on it, in cell and biochemical assays. What the cited work establishes is biochemical: a cell's redox state depends both on the absolute concentrations of these dinucleotides and on the ratios of their oxidized and reduced forms, and in 2000 yeast and mouse Sir2 proteins were shown to deacetylate histones in a manner that required it. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

NAD+ is the oxidized form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, also called coenzyme I, a dinucleotide in which a nicotinamide ribonucleotide is joined through a pyrophosphate bridge to adenosine 5'-monophosphate. A 2008 review of mammalian nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide metabolism notes that the cellular redox state depends both on the absolute concentrations of the pyridine dinucleotides and on the ratios of their oxidized and reduced forms, and surveys the enzymes of both the de novo and the reutilization routes of its biosynthesis as well as those that cleave it, alongside what the review calls its non-redox functions. In 2000, yeast and mouse Sir2 proteins were shown to deacetylate lysines 9 and 14 of histone H3 in a manner dependent on nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, with the deacetylation of lysine 16 of histone H4 reported for the yeast protein, whose activity the authors tied to transcriptional silencing and to replicative life span in yeast. A 2015 review of cellular research gathers work in which the level of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide within a cell bears on metabolic adaptation, on sirtuin activity and on mitochondrial stress responses, among them the mitochondrial unfolded protein response. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The biochemical and laboratory findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 1000 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.summary: A synthetic tripeptide of glutamate, aspartate and arginine. The review reporting its effects presents its mechanism as an assumption rather than a demonstration. Cell and animal studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a synthetic tripeptide - a chain of three amino acids: glutamate, aspartate and arginine. It is listed for laboratory work on oxidative stress, neuronal survival and dendrite shape in cells and animals. What the cited work establishes is in cells and rats: it restricted the accumulation of reactive oxygen species and necrotic cell death in several cell types under oxidative stress, improved spatial orientation and learning in the offspring of rats loaded with dietary methionine, and increased the number of processes and the total length of dendrites in neurons derived from elderly donors' skin cells. What it does not establish is a mechanism: the review reporting these effects presents entry into cells and binding to histone proteins or nucleic acids as an assumption rather than a demonstration. The full technical description follows.

Pinealon is the synthetic tripeptide L-glutamyl-L-aspartyl-L-arginine, written Glu-Asp-Arg and abbreviated EDR. In a 2011 cell study, the tripeptide restricted the accumulation of reactive oxygen species in cerebellar granule cells, in neutrophils and in pheochromocytoma PC12 cells under oxidative stress raised by both receptor-dependent and receptor-independent means, and reduced necrotic cell death measured by propidium iodide staining, alongside a delayed time course of ERK 1/2 activation and a change in the cell cycle; because the limit on reactive oxygen species and on cell mortality saturated at lower concentrations while the cell-cycle effect continued at higher ones, the authors concluded that it may act directly on the cell genome in addition to its antioxidant activity. In a 2012 study, rats were loaded with dietary methionine during pregnancy to produce experimental hyperhomocysteinemia; giving the tripeptide under those conditions improved the offspring's spatial orientation and learning and lowered both reactive oxygen species accumulation and the number of necrotic cells among neurons isolated from the offspring's cerebellum. In a 2024 study using cortical neurons transdifferentiated from the dermal fibroblasts of elderly donors, this tripeptide and two related short peptides increased the number of primary processes and the total length of dendrites, while none of the three changed the activity of mitochondria or lysosomes or the level of the p16 protein; this tripeptide lowered oxidative DNA damage in those neurons. A 2020 review of the same tripeptide reports that it activates the expression of genes and the synthesis of proteins that maintain neuronal activity and lowers the intensity of apoptosis in cell and animal studies, that it interferes with the loss of dendritic spines in neuronal cultures from mouse models of Alzheimer's and Huntington's diseases, and that it promotes the synthesis of antioxidant enzymes in cultured rat cerebellum neurons; the review presents entry into cells and binding to histone proteins or nucleic acids as an assumption rather than a demonstrated mechanism. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The cell and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 10 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.overview:
In plain terms, SNAP-8 is a product name rather than a chemical name. A 2026 report gives it as acetyl octapeptide-3, a name that states an acetylated peptide of eight residues and nothing further - no source read here gives a sequence for it, so this description states none. It is listed for laboratory work on synthetic peptide chemistry and on distinguishing this peptide from other acetylated ones. What the cited work does not establish is any shared property with acetyl hexapeptide-8, a different peptide and not a clinically interchangeable substitute; a 2026 review states that its evidence does not justify assigning direct collagen stimulation or equivalent efficacy to these sequences. The full technical description follows.

content.summary: Thymalin is a product name for a polypeptide preparation obtained from the thymus, not a single defined molecule. Studies name components of it, not a full composition. content.overview:
In plain terms, Thymalin is a product name for a polypeptide preparation obtained from the thymus, not a single defined molecule. It is listed for laboratory work on such thymus preparations in cell assays of cytokine synthesis and blood-cell differentiation. What the cited work establishes is in human cells: the preparation and two named dipeptides each lowered the measured synthesis of three inflammatory signalling proteins by between 1.4 and 6.0 times, and in haematopoietic stem cells it shifted several surface markers. What it does not establish is a composition, a potency basis, or any equivalence to thymulin, which the published record keeps distinct and which database records listing both names alongside each other do not make the same substance. The full technical description follows.

Thymalin is a product name for a polypeptide preparation obtained from the thymus rather than for a single defined molecule: a 2020 study describes it as a polypeptide complex isolated from the thymus, and a 2023 study describes it as an immunomodulatory preparation holding a polypeptide extract of thymus. That 2023 study names the dipeptides KE and EW as active substances of the preparation, which identifies components rather than a full composition. The published record keeps this preparation distinct from thymulin, which one review describes as a well-characterised thymic hormone existing as a nonapeptide coupled to equimolar amounts of zinc ions, and a 1997 review lists thymalin and thymulin among separate thymus preparations; a listing of one is not a listing of the other, and database records that carry both names alongside each other do not make them the same substance. In a 2023 in vitro model of an inflammatory reaction using human peripheral blood mononuclear cells stimulated with lipopolysaccharide, the preparation and the two dipeptides each lowered the measured synthesis of interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor alpha by between 1.4 and 6.0 times. In a 2020 cell study of human haematopoietic stem cells, exposure lowered the expression of CD44 and CD117 by two to three times and raised the expression of CD28 by 6.8 times, which the authors read as a shift towards mature T lymphocytes. Because the preparation is defined by its source material rather than by a structure, this listing states no composition, no potency basis and no equivalence to any single peptide. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The cell-level findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. content.summary: The catalog's four-pack of one compound, tesamorelin, an analogue of human growth hormone-releasing factor. The pack count is the catalog's wording; the selling unit is not established. The findings do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 8 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is the catalog's four-pack of a single compound rather than a single unit. Tesamorelin itself is a version of a 44-amino-acid human hormone that prompts growth-hormone release, with one chemical group added at one end so that it breaks down more slowly. It is listed for laboratory work on that analogue chemistry, as described for the single-unit listings. What the cited work establishes is in animals: it resisted the enzyme that inactivates the natural hormone, lasted longer in plasma, and raised growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 in pigs, rats and dogs. What it does not establish is what a customer receives - the per-unit amount is reproduced as the label gives it, and the pack count is the catalog's own wording, because a multipack is not a customer unit until a source says so. The full technical description follows.

This listing is the catalog's four-pack of a single compound rather than a single unit, and the description of the compound below is the one already written for the tesamorelin listings. Tesamorelin, developed under the code TH9507, is an analogue of the 44-amino-acid human growth hormone-releasing factor, hGRF(1-44)NH2, modified only by a trans-3-hexenoyl group added to the N-terminal tyrosine. That modification made it resistant to inactivation by dipeptidyl aminopeptidase IV, slowed its breakdown in rat, dog and human plasma in vitro, and prolonged its plasma elimination in vivo compared with the natural peptide. In pigs, rats and dogs, repeated administration markedly increased plasma growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), and its apparent elimination half-life in dogs was 21 to 45 minutes. In subchronic studies of up to four months, rats and dogs gained more body weight, and dogs showed reversible liver, kidney and blood findings that the authors attributed to sustained supraphysiological growth hormone and IGF-1 exposure. The catalog's label for this listing states 8 mg and a four-pack. The per-unit amount is reproduced as the label gives it; the pack count is the catalog's own wording and not a statement about what a customer receives, because the selling unit for this listing is not established by any source read here. A multipack is not a customer unit until a source says so. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. The catalog lists this item with a listed amount of 8 mg, for nonclinical laboratory research.

content.summary: A 16-residue synthetic peptide based on residues 177 to 191 of human growth hormone, with an added N-terminal tyrosine and a disulfide bond. Cell, tissue and animal studies of this compound do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people. Listed at 10 mg for laboratory research.
content.overview:
In plain terms, this is a 16-amino-acid synthetic peptide based on residues 177 to 191 of human growth hormone, with an extra tyrosine added at one end and a disulfide bond inside it. It is listed for laboratory work on how that fragment affects fat breakdown and fat formation in cells, tissue and animals. What the cited work establishes is in rats, mice, isolated tissue and cell assays, much of it on related analogues: the fragment reduced fat formation as strongly as the intact hormone and slowed weight gain in obese mice without raising plasma glucose or reducing insulin secretion, and in cell assays it did not compete for the growth hormone receptor. What it does not establish is any effect in a person. The full technical description follows.

The reference compound AOD-9604 is a 16-residue synthetic peptide based on residues 177 to 191 of human growth hormone, with an added N-terminal tyrosine and a disulfide bond linking two internal cysteines. The antilipogenic activity of this region of the hormone was reported from 1993: a synthetic peptide of human growth hormone residues 177 to 191 had antilipogenic activity identical to that of the intact hormone, while showing no significant lipolytic effect as measured by glycerol release from the fat pads of rats given the peptide, and in 1994 long-term administration of the same peptide to obese mice reduced cumulative body weight gain, decreased adipose tissue mass and inhibited lipogenesis in adipose tissue. In one 2000 report on AOD9401, an analogue of that domain spanning residues 177 to 191, the peptide stimulated hormone-sensitive lipase and inhibited acetyl-coenzyme A carboxylase in isolated rat adipose tissue, mimicked the intact hormone's effect on diacylglycerol release in adipocytes, and over 20 days in obese Zucker rats reduced body weight gain and lowered mean adipocyte diameter from about 110 to about 80 micrometres, without the insulin resistance or glucose intolerance that followed the intact hormone. In a second AOD-9401 study, obese mice gained weight more slowly from day 16 during a 30-day experiment. Food intake was similar between groups, and resting energy expenditure showed no detectable increase. A separate acute challenge at the end of the experiment increased energy expenditure and the oxidation of both glucose and fat in the mice tested. In isolated adipose tissue assays, AOD-9401 increased lipolytic activity and lowered lipogenic activity in rodent and human samples. In one 14-day AOD-9604 study, obese mice gained weight more slowly and had higher fat oxidation and plasma glycerol. The fragment did not raise plasma glucose or reduce insulin secretion in that comparison, and in separate cell assays it neither competed for growth hormone receptor binding nor stimulated proliferation. A second AOD-9604 study reported lower body weight and body fat in obese mice and higher levels of β3-adrenergic receptor RNA after chronic exposure to AOD-9604 or intact growth hormone. The chronic weight and lipolysis effects were absent in mice lacking that receptor, although a separate acute AOD-9604 challenge still increased energy expenditure and fat oxidation in the knockout mice. This listing is a laboratory research material and not a medicine. The cell, tissue and animal findings above do not establish the safety or effects of this research material in people.
